events.title: Taiwan agrees to buy 30% of gas from Alaska LNG project, Trump says
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the gas from a pipeline project in Alaska. The terms of the deal remain unclear, though Taiwan's state-owned CPC Corp reached an agreement last year to purchase LNG and invest in the project. Trump's remarks come amid uncertainty over South Korea's participation in the $50 billion Alaska LNG project, despite his repeated claims that Seoul had agreed to join. U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the gas from a proposed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska. "Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years," Trump said at a rally in Alaska. "That guarantees a success." His latest remarks follow repeated claims earlier this month that South Korea had agreed to join the $50 billion Alaska LNG project, even as Seoul maintained that its participation had not been finalized. "We'll also invest $4.4 billion into the project, on top of $50 billion already committed by South Korea to Alaska," Trump said. However, the terms of the Taiwan deal cited by Trump were not immediately clear. Last year, Taiwan's state-owned energy company CPC Corp reportedly reached an agreement with Alaska Gasline Development Corp to purchase LNG and invest in the pipeline project. Taiwan, home to critical semiconductor giant TSMC, has seen energy demand climb due to AI-related growth. However, the island relies on imports for more than 90% of its energy supply and this summer projected its average electricity demand growth rate through 2035 would exceed that of Japan and South Korea. Taiwan's economic affairs ministry said that growth rate would climb by about 2.5% a year, the second-highest forecast in its history. The democratically self-ruled island is still waiting on major new arms sales from the U.S. Beijing considers Taiwan part of its territory. Glenfarne, the developer of the Alaska LNG pipeline, told the U.S. government in a report this month the project aims to deliver its first gas in 2029. Trump has also stepped up pressure on South Korea over its participation in the project, warning earlier this month that he would charge the country more and threatened to double the charges if Seoul failed to sign soon, without specifying what would be doubled. That prompted speculation in South Korean media that he was referring to higher tariffs. The White House, Taiwan's energy ministry and CPC Corp. did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

events.title: Producer prices in China rise at fastest pace since June 2022, beating expectations
events.summary: China's PPI rose 5% year on year in September, sharply up from August's 3.8% and beating the 4.5% rise expected. CPI rose 0.9%, up from 0.8% in August, but missing the 1% expected by economists. China's producer price index climbed at its fastest pace in over four years, rising 5% in September as higher fuel prices pushed up costs for businesses. The increase was higher than the 4.5% expected by economists polled by Reuters, and sharply up from the 3.8% seen in the previous month. China's National Bureau of Statistics said higher prices were also seen in the country's coal sector, due to increased demand for coal for winter heating, temporary tight supply in major coal-producing areas, and expectations of rising international coal prices. Consumer prices saw a 0.9% rise, marginally missing expectations of 1%, but up from 0.8% in the month before. The increase in the consumer inflation rate was due to gasoline prices, which climbed 16.6% and contributed approximately 0.47 percentage points to the year-on-year CPI increase, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the Urban Division at the NBS. This was partially offset by a wider fall in food prices, which declined 1.7% and pulled down the CPI by 0.29 percentage points, Dong added. The core CPI rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed 1%. The higher inflation figures come as China's economy grapples with its lowest growth rate in more than three years . GDP growth for the second quarter of the year missed expectations at 4.3%. While economic data for August showed that retail sales expanded more slowly than expected, industrial output beat expectations. On Sept 28, a State Council readout signaled that more policy support could be on the way for the Chinese economy, saying that "In response to emerging challenges in the economy's operation, efforts should be made to intensify counter-cyclical adjustment of macro policies." Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, wrote that "It marks a bit of a shift in tone," adding that more policy support rollouts will be coming so as to reach both short- and long-term growth targets. "These include the 4.5%-5.0% GDP growth target for 2026, and the longstanding goal to double GDP from 2020 to 2035." — This is breaking news, please check back for updates.

events.title: South Korean carmaker Hyundai plans 'strategic' investment of $15.5 billion in India by 2032
events.summary: Korean car company Hyundai Motor Group says India is a strategic core market. Hyundai will invest $15.5 billion from 2026 through 2032 in India. Hyundai has a total production capacity of 1.4 million vehicles across India and exports cars from these locations. South Korea's Hyundai Motor Group on Tuesday said it plans to invest $15.5 billion from 2026 through 2032 in India, a market it considers core to the company's emerging-market growth and expansion . "India remains one of Hyundai Motor Group's most important and strategic markets globally," Euisun Chung, the executive chair of Hyundai Motor Group, said in a release following his meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He added that this investment "reaffirms" the company's commitment to the Indian market for the next 30 years and beyond. Over the seven-year plan, Hyundai said it will invest across manufacturing expansion and in developing research and development infrastructure, local supplier cultivation for parts localization, and future technology innovation. To execute these investments, Hyundai will set up a dedicated investment entity in India, it said in the release. The Indian car market has been hitting new records every month, driven by strong demand. In August, passenger car sales hit a new monthly record with sales of 439,000 units, over 36% higher year-on-year, as per data from industry body Society of Indian Auto Manufacturers. Hyundai is the third-largest car company in India and sold 247,980 passenger cars in the country between April and August this year, according to data released last month. Japanese carmaker Maruti Suzuki was the top seller in the country over that period, followed by India's Mahindra & Mahindra, as per SIAM's data. However, in the financial year ended March 2026, Hyundai came in fourth, edged out by M&M and Tata Motors . In 2024, the South Korean company listed its India business unit, Hyundai Motors India , raising $3.3 billion in the largest-ever initial public offer in the country.

events.title: Reassessment of billion-dollar silver mine sparks tractor protest
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Opponents hold tractor protest as IPC begins reassessment of Bowdens silver mine Fifteen tractors and dozens of trucks and utes weave through Mudgee, honking horns and receiving waves of support from locals. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) is reassessing the proposed Bowdens silver mine near Mudgee. Protesters drove tractors through the town today to express their opposition to the development. Three days of hearings are being held by the IPC before a determination is made. Plans for a $1 billion silver and lead mine in Central West New South Wales are being reassessed as opponents take to the streets of Mudgee in tractors to protest. Approval of the Bowdens Silver Mines Limited project was deemed "void" by the NSW Court of Appeal in August 2024. It had been approved by the state's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) in April the previous year. That decision was overturned when the court ruled the IPC should have examined the potential environmental impacts of the project's transmission line. The IPC has now started three days of hearings as part of its reassessment. Silver Mines Limited managing director Jo Batershill told the panel today the merits of the project were now stronger than when it was approved in 2023. He said it was in the best interests of the local and regional economy, the state's strategic minerals goals and the nation's contribution to the global renewable energy transition. A group of protesters gathered in Mudgee ahead of the public hearing on the Bowdens silver project. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Today's "tractorcade" was similar to a protest held in 2023 when residents of Lue, about 26 kilometres east of Mudgee, disrupted traffic through the famous wine region. Protester Tom Combes, who farms sheep and cattle at Lue, described the mine proposal as "just nuts". Tom Combes was one of more than 40 residents outside the IPC hearing in Mudgee with signs and shirts voicing their opposition to the development. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) "All the people that live out there, all of their lifestyle, their health and their amenity is going to be destroyed," he said. Mr Combes is one of 97 speakers set to give evidence over the next three days. The application approved in 2023 involved extracting 30 million tonnes of silver, lead and zinc over 23-years. The mine site is about 2km from the village of Lue and its local primary school. The decision was successfully challenged by the Bingman Catchment Landcare Group. The court found the panel failed to consider the impacts of a 13km transmission line that the Department of Planning and Environment had deemed required a separate application. Dozens of people drove tractors from Lue to Mudgee, where the IPC is holding a three-day hearing into the Bowdens silver mine application. In response, the state government passed legislative changes that allow off-site infrastructure for state significant projects to be assessed separately. With the original project approval still considered void, the project must now be reassessed. A new three-person panel of commissioners was appointed in September to make a new determination on Bowdens's proposal, with the IPC stating the "previous determination has no influence on this new assessment". Under the new laws, the proposed transmission infrastructure will not form part of the application being reassessed. No changes have been made to the original project application, but Silver Mines Limited has provided additional advice to the state's planning department that will be considered. The proponents of the Bowdens silver mine are seeking approval to extract 30 million tonnes of ore over 23 years. ( ABC Central West: Mollie Gorman ) Mr Battershill told the panel that additional assessments, including biodiversity and climate change reports, showed "the merits of the project before the commission today remain unchanged". While admitting that the project was not supported by everyone in the community, Mr Battershill pointed to a supplementary report provided by the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure that found the "project benefits outweigh its residual costs and that the project is in the public interest and is approvable". He referred to a survey conducted for the company in August 2026 that concluded 84 per cent of people in the surrounding region held positive or neutral views on the project. The IPC initially scheduled two days for the hearing but added a third following significant community interest in the development. It is expected to make a determination by December 9.

events.title: Oil rises amid growing Mideast tensions between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia
events.summary: A Saudi-led coalition reportedly struck Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen. U.S. Central Command rejected Iran's claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under Tehran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk." Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and notable commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on on CNBC's "Squawk Box." Oil rises Wednesday, amid worries over supply disruptions as tensions continue to escalate in the Middle East with fighting between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery gained 1.24% at $107.02 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November advanced 1.18% at $95.25 per barrel. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate, following a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport by Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen. According to Al Jazeera, Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen were struck by a Saudi-led coalition, though a spokesperson said that precautions were taken to avoid "collateral damage on civilians." Meanwhile, tensions also continued to simmer between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. Central Command rejected claims by the commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy that the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk." "RGC's navy commander has no navy," CENTCOM said in an X post , adding that "American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz." Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and noted commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said the founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment. "If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms," he added.

events.title: Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Opposition leaders in Jamaica have questioned why the deportation deal with the Trump White House has not been made public. The Caribbean country of Jamaica has received its first third-country deportations from the United States, as part of an expanding set of international agreements under President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, 22 deportees from the US arrived at Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston, Jamaica. list 1 of 3 Key takeaways from US Senate debate in Michigan between El-Sayed, Rogers list 2 of 3 ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests list 3 of 3 US ICE releases Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh from custody Media reports indicate they were subsequently boarded onto a bus and taken to an undisclosed location. Such deportations – which often involve non-citizens who have no ties to their destinations – have faced widespread condemnation from human rights groups and advocates who have questioned their legality. But Jamaica is among a growing number of countries to accept third-country deportations, as part of Trump’s effort to implement the largest mass deportation campaign in US history. At least 35 countries have entered into third-country deportation agreements with the US, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, an advocacy project affiliated with the groups Refugees International and Human Rights First. The Washington Post reported last month that the Trump administration has earmarked roughly $410m to support such efforts. Jamaica signed a bilateral memorandum of understanding in June to receive third-country deportations. Under the plan, Jamaica will transfer any deportees to their home countries or other destinations after their arrival. The country’s government has also pledged not to accept any deportees with criminal records. “The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries,” Jamaica’s Ministry of National Security and Peace and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade said in a joint statement. It added that care for the deportees will be supported by the International Organization for Migration, a United Nations organisation. “The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica,” the joint statement added. Opposition leaders in Jamaica, however, spoke out against the deportation, framing the deal as a threat to the island’s security. They also questioned why the agreement had not been debated publicly. “Jamaicans are being asked to trust a secret document that touches their security, their communities and their public services,” said Fitz Jackson, the opposition spokesperson on national security. In response to Jackson’s statement, Foreign Minister Kamina Johnson Smith argued that any questions about the deportation deal “have all been answered”. She also indicated that the US has not agreed to make the deal public. “As I explained before, some countries have agreed to receive criminals, we have not,” she wrote on social media. “Some countries have had their agreements made public, but our partner has not agreed for this one to be.” Legal challenges against the third-country deportations are ongoing in the US, where advocates have argued that deportees are being removed from the country without due process of law, the constitutional right to a fair hearing. Critics have also argued that third-country deportations sometimes send immigrants to countries where they may face danger. Some of the recipient countries, such as South Sudan, are in the midst of ongoing conflict or have faced accusations of serious human rights abuses. Opponents have even said the third-country deportations are being used as a backdoor method for circumventing court protection orders . Such orders may prohibit the US government from returning certain immigrants to their home countries, for fear of violence and persecution. But by sending immigrants to third countries, critics say the Trump administration avoids violating such protection orders – though in some cases, the third country has then returned the deportee to the country identified in the US protection order. In a February report by Democrats on the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, one official said anonymously that the purpose of such far-flung deportations was to instil fear. “The point is that the administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere,” the official said. “The point is to scare people.”

events.title: Colombia peace tribunal charges ex-FARC members with anti-Indigenous crimes
events.summary: The former rebels are accused of abuses such as torture, murder and the displacement of Indigenous leaders during Colombia’s civil conflict. Colombia’s transitional justice system, established to address crimes committed during the country’s decades-long civil conflict , has indicted several former members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), formerly the country’s largest rebel group. A group of 10 ex-rebels were charged on Tuesday with alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity between 1996 and 2016. list 1 of 3 Colombia extradites leader of armed group to US in shift towards Washington list 2 of 3 Three minors killed in Colombia armed group crackdown list 3 of 3 Car bomb attack rattles Colombia after inauguration of hardline president The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), the transitional justice tribunal, said that the accused had carried out crimes of torture, murder and forced displacement against five Indigenous groups in southeast Colombia. “Today we are delivering justice to the most forgotten peoples of a segregated Colombia,” JEP magistrate Catalina Diaz said. She explained that FARC commanders had ordered subordinates to plant landmines on Indigenous territory and ruin ecosystems the tribes relied on for survival. “These people have had their basic right to exist compromised,” Diaz added. The indictment is the latest example of Colombia’s efforts to reckon with the abuses and violence of a civil conflict that lasted for more than half a century, resulting in severe rights abuses . Since the 1960s, left-wing rebels, government security forces, criminal networks and government-aligned right-wing paramilitaries have clashed over efforts to control territory and shape the country’s power structure. Indigenous communities and activists continue to face violent attacks in Colombia today. Continued fighting has also led to an ever-growing death toll. A 2022 report from Colombia’s Truth Commission found that 450,664 people were killed between 1985 and 2018 as a result of the conflict. An additional 121,768 people were forcibly disappeared. Indigenous activists and community leaders hailed JEP’s decision on Tuesday as an acknowledgement that their communities were targeted. “For the first time, the Colombian state recognises that [armed groups] did not just kill individuals,” said Yhon Jairo Figueroa, a leader of the Koreguaje tribe. “But they attempted to kill the knowledge, the language, the territory.” Three of those accused are also former members of the last secretariat of the FARC, which reached a peace deal with the government in 2016 that included disarmament. Critics of the deal and its implementation say that many of those responsible for abuses have escaped accountability. Some FARC fighters who refused to accept the agreement have since formed splinter groups that continue to fight in the conflict. The 2016 deal ultimately granted the former rebels 10 seats in Colombia’s Congress to address the FARC’s political concerns. One of the suspects indicted Tuesday was Julian Gallo, who served eight years as a senator under that deal. The JEP, for its part, can impose only non-prison penalties. Last year, for instance, it sentenced seven ex-FARC members accused of kidnapping to eight years of reparations, including landmine clearing and helping to find missing persons. Separately, JEP also sentenced former military members to reparation work for their involvement in the killing and disappearances of civilians, who were then tallied as rebels in government records. Those systemic misrepresentations became known as the “false positives” scandal. But critics warn that threats to JEP’s existence loom under Colombia’s newly inaugurated far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella . Allies of de la Espriella have proposed a nearly 17 percent cut to JEP’s funding for fiscal year 2027. Such budget reductions are set to be weighed by Colombia’s Congress this month. Before taking office in August, de la Espriella served as a defence lawyer, in some cases representing right-wing paramilitaries. He has criticised the JEP, accusing it of issuing lenient sentences.

events.title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, D.C. to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
events.summary: Anthropic is asking a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models. The Defense Department labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk in March, and the AI company sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's decision. Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C. to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models. "The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation." The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models . Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional. Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety." In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation. Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed. A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. The U.S. Department of Justice is warning that hackers working for the North Korean regime are increasingly relying on Americans to facilitate the hacking of U.S. companies. In an announcement on Tuesday, prosecutors said they have indicted and arrested at least two people, and conducted searches across dozens of suspected “laptop farms” in Texas. The computers were allegedly used by North Koreans to remotely hack into American companies and steal sensitive data. According to the DOJ, federal authorities seized over 180 computers that they believe American companies had shipped out to their newly hired employees, not realizing that they were sanctioned North Korean spies who had used stolen identities of U.S. citizens to gain employment. The DOJ said that it raided over 40 laptop farms across Texas, the largest disclosed number of homes and residences used for facilitating North Korean hacks, which were owned by at least two American facilitators. CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate and disrupt the latest North Korean operations, said that laptop farms are “vital” to North Korea in helping its hackers overcome physical, financial, and legal challenges of not physically being in the United States. The prosecutors said at least 70 U.S.-based companies had been infiltrated by the hackers, who are believed to have generated around $3 million in stolen funds. The DOJ did not name the affected companies, but described them as healthcare, cyber support, retail, communications, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio and 16 other states, including the District of Columbia. “Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals,” the Justice Department said . Oftentimes, North Korean hackers use real-looking email addresses, spoofed LinkedIn profiles, and extensive online and social media accounts as cover for their activities. In a separate public service announcement , the FBI said that there are “thousands” of North Korean-state controlled IT workers working at Western companies, which “pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.” This is the latest wave of arrests, indictments, and enforcement action targeting North Korean activities in the United States in recent years. The breakaway regime has used this “remote IT workers” scheme to allow North Koreans to gain employment with U.S. and European companies, earn a wage, and then steal sensitive information and intellectual property while as employees. The victim companies are then extorted into paying the hackers further. The remote IT workers’ scheme is one of several strands of illicit revenue that the North Korean regime aims to generate, including hacking crypto exchanges and open-source developer projects , with the aim of funding its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. The regime is thought to have stolen at least $2 billion in crypto during 2025 alone. Experts on North Korea have put the number of hacked companies and the amount of stolen crypto as likely much higher than reported. Earlier this year, CrowdStrike said in a separate report that North Korean hackers were behind around half of all documented “hands-on-keyboard” intrusions over the past year, referring to hacks that are carried out by humans and not automated tools or AI. events.title: China's exports likely grew by double-digits in September
events.summary: Global demand for AI-related goods has helped drive China's exports higher. The world's second-largest economy has struggled to ramp up domestic demand. BEIJING — China's exports likely grew by 25.5% in September from a year ago, picking up modestly from the prior month, according to a Reuters poll ahead of the expected Wednesday data release. Imports for September were forecast to slow to 24.5% year-on-year growth, down from 28.2% in August, the poll showed. Earlier this year, China's exports and imports each grew at their fastest pace in five years. A surge in demand for China-made parts for data centers to power artificial intelligence has helped fuel exports, along with stabilization in tensions with the U.S., China's largest trading partner on a single-country basis. Global scrutiny on the economic impact of China's surging exports has escalated in recent years , amid sluggish domestic demand. AI-related demand and a coinciding rise in prices of core products have also helped support import growth. The U.S. and China last month announced plans to roll back tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, and extend a broader trade truce by two months to January. The European Union last week announced China agreed to halve its exports of hybrid-powered cars to the bloc, following high-level trade talks in Beijing.

events.summary: The second-largest US bank faces record penalties for failing to comply with sanctions and money laundering laws. The US Treasury Department has imposed more than $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America, the second-largest bank in the US, for violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The fines announced on Tuesday include the third-largest penalty in the department’s history, the US Treasury said in a statement. list 1 of 4 Majority in US say Trump prioritises personal wealth over all else: Poll list 2 of 4 US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records list 3 of 4 Trump says Houthis trying to increase oil prices before US elections list 4 of 4 Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. He added that these “actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law”. According to the Treasury Department, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty over the bank’s failure to mitigate and report “priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border”. The failures identified by FinCEN involved deficiencies related to the bank’s suspicious transaction identification and reporting and customer due diligence processes. According to the statement, “the Bank effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations”. “Bank of America failed to timely report to FinCEN over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions”, the Treasury said in the statement. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $750 million fine, the largest in its history, for the bank’s deficient and ineffective anti-money laundering compliance programme. FinCEN’s $1.2 billion penalty includes credit for the OCC fine. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also announced an $11.6 million settlement agreement over apparent violations of numerous sanctions programmes, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics and global terrorism. Bank of America agreed to settle 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programmes, and the settlement includes “significant compliance commitments regarding training, testing and audit, and future communication and cooperation with OFAC”. In the statement, the Treasury said the actions “underscore the importance of effectively complying” with US anti-money laundering and sanctions requirements. In response, Bank of America said in a statement: “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right.” “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.”

events.title: Namibia battles cattle disease outbreak as EU suspends several meat imports
events.summary: Foot-and-mouth disease threatens livestock farmers’ livelihoods and disrupts meat supplies as authorities impose curbs. Windhoek, Namibia – “We had to close the market for several days. It was just before the weekend and month’s end. That’s when we need the money the most,” says Francisco, a vendor at Single Quarter, Windhoek’s largest open meat market. He pours vinegar and cooking oil into a tomato and onion salsa, a traditional accompaniment to kapana, a popular grilled-meat street food. Around him, many stalls and grilling stations sit empty. Instead of the crowds that typically fill the market during business hours, only a handful of customers move between the stalls. Recent closures and concerns about meat supplies have disrupted business. “Our business is slow. We are struggling to buy meat, but without it, we cannot survive,” says another kapana vendor, who asked to remain anonymous. “This is our livelihood. The meat is much more expensive now, so we are making less money altogether. If this continues for three months, it is going to be very bad for us.” In Katutura, Windhoek’s largest township, uncertainty over beef supplies is adding to residents’ financial concerns. “If we don’t eat meat, what are we going to eat? We are Namibians,” one resident says, describing meat as a staple of the local diet. Another worries about rising prices and the wider consequences for Namibia, where livestock exports are an important part of the economy. At a supermarket in the Okuryangava suburb, the butchery has already run out of some premium beef products. Store manager Enrico De Azevedo, 23, says consumer behaviour has also contributed to the pressure. “We saw people panic-buying like they did during the COVID-19 pandemic with toilet paper. Now, they can go and stack their meat next to their toilet paper,” he says. De Azevedo also recognises the wider economic risks. “For those in the export business, this will have grave implications.” Outbreak threatens Namibia’s export market Namibia’s Directorate of Veterinary Services (DVS) confirmed an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) on a commercial farm in the Karasburg State Veterinary District, in the southern //Kharas Region, on September 23, 2026. In an address on October 5, President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said surveillance teams had recorded 127 positive cases across 15 farms. Teams had inspected 29,313 animals across 68 farms. The government had also established 20 surveillance teams and 10 roadblocks in the region as part of its response. In an update covering the situation as of October 6, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform reported that 129 animal samples had tested positive and 17 farms had been confirmed infected. Veterinary teams had inspected 72 of 81 targeted farms. The outbreak was subsequently confirmed in a second region. On October 7, laboratory tests confirmed FMD in cattle at Kalala Island, in the Kabbe constituency of the Zambezi Region, in northern Namibia. Veterinary officials from the Katima Mulilo State Veterinary Office investigated the suspected outbreak on October 5 after observing clinical signs in 20 cattle. Twelve samples were collected and submitted to the Central Veterinary Laboratory in Windhoek on October 6. All 12 tested positive for the virus the following day. In a public notification issued on October 10, the ministry outlined restrictions across the Zambezi Region following confirmation of the outbreak. These include suspending the movement of cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products, cancelling previously issued movement permits, and halting livestock auctions, informal markets and other animal-gathering events. Slaughter at local abattoirs, informal markets and social events has also been suspended. Slaughter at export abattoirs may continue for eligible cattle under the commodity-based trade system, provided the animals meet quarantine requirements and pass traceability checks. Emergency vaccination has begun in the affected area, while roadblocks and intensive surveillance are intended to prevent further spread. FMD is a highly contagious viral disease affecting cloven-hoofed animals, including cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. It can disrupt livestock production and trade, particularly when it affects areas recognised as free of the disease. Following confirmation of the //Kharas outbreak, Namibian authorities notified the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and introduced restrictions on the movement and export of cloven-hoofed animals and their products. The European Union subsequently amended its import rules for Namibia’s previously authorised export zone, known as NA-1, following the outbreak. The Zambezi detection has added to the challenge facing veterinary authorities, who are working to contain the disease and prevent further infections.

events.title: OpenAI says it found a 'hidden' recording device planted in its office
events.summary: OpenAI said it found a recording device "hidden" in one of its offices and reported the matter to the FBI. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI said the device was "concealed in toilet paper" and planted in one of its offices. The company said it then used its own models to determine who planted the device. The Department of Justice said an employee was arrested on October 9. OpenAI said it found a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in one of its offices and used its own AI to identify who planted the device. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," OpenAI wrote in an X post on Tuesday. "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work." A statement from the Justice Department said that the employee in question is allegedly 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national. Alfozan was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan made his first appearance in federal court on Tuesday, the statement said. A complaint filed in the Northern District of California said that an employee found a USB device surreptitiously placed on the back of a television located in an " executive conference room ." The device was concealed in toilet paper, the complaint said. Photos attached to the court documents and DOJ statement showed the device positioned behind what appears to be a television. The complaint said the device consists of a "thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage." An FBI affidavit filed in the Northern District of California included photos of what prosecutors said was a recording device surreptitiously hidden in an executive conference room. Department of Justice The complaint further said that CCTV footage showed Alfozan near the conference room on multiple dates prior to the device's discovery. "According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the DOJ said. An FBI affidavit included an image of what prosecutors said is Abdulrahman Alfozan looking behind a television located in the conference room where the recording device was planted. Department of Justice Prosecutors allege that Alfozan used a productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses and meeting rooms, and used a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse to submit prompts related to building and hiding an audio recording device. Some of the queries to the productivity agent included a list of "today's meetings in this room" and "what meeting was this presented at and when was it recorded," the complaint said. A screenshot of the criminal complaint shows a list of queries federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan made to a "productivity agent." Department of Justice A LinkedIn account with the same name as the defendant in the complaint showed that Alfozan was an engineering lead at OpenAI and is a partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm that invests in early-stage tech startups across the Middle East and North Africa. A contact associated with the LinkedIn account and a spokesperson for Raed did not immediately return a request for comment. Alfozan's attorney did not return a request for comment. OpenAI said that it found no evidence that the employee improperly accessed or manipulated model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was fired, OpenAI said in the social media post. OpenAI told Business Insider that its models were used to help with the technical investigation of the incident, including analyzing forensic images of the device's storage. It also said it has evidence that the employee intended to plant more recording devices throughout OpenAI's offices. OpenAI said in the X post that the case was an example of how AI can help address " sophisticated security threats ." The announcement comes on the heels of a cluster of firings at OpenAI unrelated to the recording device. In the prior case, the company let go of three safety and alignment employees who it alleged had "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." The workers, Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni, and Tomek Korbak, published a letter disputing some of the claims circulating about their conduct. They wrote that they were concerned about the lack of clarity around their firings, as well as the way they might chill transparency at the company. OpenAI stood by the dismissals. The company published an internal note that said, "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." events.title: Singapore third-quarter GDP growth softens from four-year high but beats estimates
events.summary: Singapore's GDP growth softened to 5.4% for the third quarter. This was down from the revised 6.2% in the quarter before, but beat expectations of 5%. The slowdown was due to a decline in the country's manufacturing sector, although this was offset by an expansion in construction. Singapore's economic expansion decelerated in the third quarter of 2026, with GDP growth dropping to 5.4% after hitting a four-year high in the last quarter. However, the GDP print beat expectations of a 5% growth from economists polled by Reuters. Government data showed a decline in the country's manufacturing sector, although this was offset by an expansion in construction. Manufacturing is one of the city-state's largest sectors, contributing about 20% of its GDP. Singapore back in August had lifted its annual economic growth forecast as AI-related sectors and exports powered its economy to beat expectations for the first two quarters of the year. This forecast is still mantain GDP growth for 2026 is expected to come in at 4.5% to 5.5%, more than double the lower end of its previous forecast of 2%-4%. This has been the second time Singapore has upgraded its growth estimates. At the start of the year, the country's ministry of trade and industry had estimated growth at 1%-3% . The GDP numbers come as the Monetary Authority of Singapore held its monetary policy steady, marking a pause after two straight rounds of tightening. The city-state had tightened its policy in back to back in April and July, citing inflation risks due to higher energy prices. The MAS still projects inflation will remain high in the near term due to higher energy and food prices, then ease from mid-2027 "as import costs ebb and domestic price pressures stay subdued." "The Singapore economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, and moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten," the MAS added. Singapore does not use an interest rate to set monetary policy. Instead, it manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies belonging to the country's major trading partners, allowing the exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band. events.title: Court dumps Plibersek heritage decision that halted $1b gold mine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Federal Court declares Commonwealth's blocking of New South Wales gold mine 'invalid' Regis Resources argued the Commonwealth's decision rendered its gold mine unviable in its current form. ( ABC News: Lani Oataway ) A Federal Court judge has found an Aboriginal Protection Order that halted an approved gold mine in NSW is "invalid". Regis Resources launched the legal action in 2024, challenging the Commonwealth's decision relating to its McPhillamys Gold Project Justice James Stellios has ruled that the project must be referred back to the federal minister for redetermination. The Federal Court has overturned a Commonwealth decision that halted a billion-dollar gold mine in New South Wales. Regis Resources launched legal action against then federal minister for environment and water Tanya Plibersek in November 2024, challenging the validity of an Aboriginal Protection Order she granted over part of its McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney. The order applied to 400 hectares of the site, including an area where the company wanted to build a tailings dam, which is used to hold mining waste. It was made after the mining project received approval in 2023 . At the time, Ms Plibersek said the order would protect the headwaters and springs of the Belubula River and that the company could construct its tailings storage elsewhere. But Regis Resources disputed this, saying the decision impacted a critical area of the project development site and meant the project was "no longer financially feasible". The Section 10 Aboriginal Protection Order made (in yellow) over part of the McPhillamys Gold Project site (in grey). ( Supplied: Regis Resources ) Justice James Stellios has presided over the Federal Court challenge and held two days of hearings in December 2025 . He delivered his judgment during a short sitting today, which found that Regis Resources was successful in the judicial review and the minister's "declaration is invalid". The Aboriginal Protection Order was granted after Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds lodged an application to protect the area under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act in 2020. Tanya Plibersek granted the Aboriginal Protection Order over part of the McPhillamys mine site in 2024. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) The court heard the application was supported by the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC) and referred to a Dreaming story called the Blue Banded Bee. Justice Stellios told the court that this information "constituted a new application" and should have been referred to the government reporter for consideration and to carry out a public consultation process. "The court's decision and my reasons say nothing about the merits of the claim ... whether it's a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration ... those are matters within the authority of the minister ... not the jurisdiction of this court." Regis Resources took the office of the federal environment minister, now held by Murray Watt, to the Federal Court. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Justice Stellios said the appropriate remedy was for the proposal to be sent back to the federal minister for environment and water, now held by Murray Watt, for redetermination. He ordered the parties to provide written submissions on costs to be submitted by October 27. Regis Resources said in a statement the company was eager to move forward. "Today's Federal Court judgement is a significant and welcome step forward," the company's managing director Jim Beyer said. "The judgement finding that the Section 10 Declaration is legally invalid vindicates the position we have held since the Declaration was made in August 2024. "We are extremely pleased the court has agreed." The company said it intended to actively participate in any redetermination process. The NSW Minerals Council said it was a win for common sense. "This is a stark example of how seemingly endless opportunities for activists to disrupt and delay projects continue to cost NSW investment, jobs and growth," CEO Stephen Galilee said. "This whole sorry saga should be a warning to governments at all levels that their assessment processes are too complicated, too inconsistent, and too vulnerable to spurious challenges and objections." Speaking before the decision was released, NSW Premier Chris Minns said he wanted the mine to go ahead. "I understand that's not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment," Mr Minns said at a press conference.

events.title: MAS keeps Singdollar appreciation rate unchanged but warns of elevated inflation
events.summary: Unlike most central banks, which target interest rates, MAS uses S$NEER, which is a trade-weighted basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners. MAS kept Singapore dollar policy unchanged, but said the war-linked energy shock will keep inflation elevated until 2027. The bank said the S$NEER band will keep strengthening to curb imported inflation, after two policy tightenings in 2026. Core inflation rose to 2.1% in July to August, and MAS expects growth to stay steady as GDP grew 5.4% in the third quarter. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s central bank maintained its monetary policy stance, but warned that persistent energy price pressures from the Iran war will keep inflation elevated well into 2027. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Oct 14 that it will keep the rate of appreciation of the Singapore dollar’s trade-weighted value unchanged , also called the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) policy band. Unlike most central banks, which target interest rates, MAS uses S$NEER, which is a trade-weighted basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners. This is because, in a small and open economy such as Singapore’s – where gross exports and imports of goods and services are more than 300% of gross domestic product (GDP) and almost 40 cents of every dollar spent domestically is on imports – the exchange rate has a much stronger influence on inflation than interest rates. MAS said: “The current appreciating policy band will allow the S$NEER to continue to strengthen and lean against the anticipated near-term rise in imported inflation, ensuring the gradual easing of inflationary pressures in 2027.” Faced with sticky inflation amid an unresolved energy shock from the Iran war, MAS has already tightened its policy stance twice in 2026 – in April and July – allowing for a stronger S$NEER that helps dampen the impact of rising import costs. Global crude oil benchmark Brent was trading at around US$106 per barrel on Oct 14, up more than 70% since the start of the year, as supplies from the Middle East remained constrained amid the Iran war and the conflict between top oil exporter Saudi Arabia and Yemen. “Since September, energy commodity prices have risen anew and are projected to remain high in the near term,” said the central bank. Global and regional food prices are also expected to pick up as costlier inputs and adverse weather patterns impact food production. Firming imported cost pressures in Singapore will keep core and all-items inflation at the current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead, MAS said. Core inflation, which excludes the costs of accommodation and private transport from all-items inflation, rose to 2.1% on the year in July to August, from 1.5% in the second quarter. For 2026 as a whole, core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0%, while all-items inflation should come in around 2%. MAS said inflation should ease more discernibly in the second half of 2027 as global energy prices gradually moderate, but with inflation running high all the way to mid-2027, both core and all-items inflation are projected to average 1.5% to 2.5%. For now, economic growth is not a worry for the central bank. Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry’s advance estimates released on Oct 14 showed Singapore’s overall GDP grew by 5.4% year on year in the third quarter. MAS said: “The Singapore economy is expected to continue expanding steadily in the quarters ahead.” Ovais Subhani is senior business correspondent at The Straits Times. He writes stories that demystify the latest economics, trade and finance news.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts First round of redundancies to exit Whyalla steelworks by end of week More than 250 Whyalla steelworks employees have accepted redundancies since the permanent closure of the blast furnace. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) The first of more than 250 Whyalla steelworks employees to accept redundancies will leave on Friday. The plant's direct workforce will be reduced due to the permanent closure of the blast furnace last month. Workers have told the ABC they feel uncertain about their future in the steelmaking town. The first of more than 250 workers to accept redundancies at the Whyalla steelworks will finish up this week — but those who want to stay are still facing an anxious wait. The permanent closure of the blast furnace last month will reduce the plant's direct workforce from 1,700 to 1,200, while at least another 300 contractor roles will also be affected. Australian Workers' Union organiser Shane Karger said he expected about 270 direct employees to accept "genuine redundancies" by the end of this month. The first group of those will exit by this Friday. Mr Karger said following that, voluntary redundancies and early retirement scheme applications would be processed. Genuine redundancy occurs when a worker's role is no longer required, for example, those who were working at the blast furnace. He said voluntary redundancies would go to workers in departments that would reduce their numbers but not shut down entirely. Shane Karger said it's been a emotional time for workers in Whyalla. ( ABC News ) Mr Karger said the final number of redundancies should be known by November. "[That] will then sort out how many positions are up for redeployment," he said. Even for those who stay on, it is unclear what the future will look like. The steelworks has been in administration since early last year, with the announcement of a buyer expected by the end of 2026. Mr Karger said unions have been working with administrators KordaMentha to make the process as fast and smooth as possible. "There's been a lot of emotion," he said. "You've got other workers that are looking forward to a well-earned rest after a very long career at the steelworks." The steelworks was forced into administration in February last year. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Several contractors have confirmed to the ABC that they have already laid off staff, with more than one closing down entirely. Jack Taylor, 30, has done manual labour at the steelworks for 10 years but will clock off for the final time this week. His was one of the roles being cut and he has opted not to apply for redeployment, instead accepting a redundancy. "It was a big decision to make," he said. "I own my house here in Whyalla so going for redeployment [would have] meant I'd have a chance of keeping a job, having income coming in." Jack Taylor accepted a redundancy. ( ABC News ) Mr Taylor said years of uncertainty over the future of the steelworks had taken a toll. "We've been through administration two times. "I'm just a bit over all of it, to be honest." He plans to apply for fly-in-fly-out jobs in the mining sector, and hopes to stay in Whyalla. "I've got my family, the footy club, all my friends and that here," he said. events.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI employee who allegedly planted recording device in conference room
events.summary: An OpenAI employee was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found hidden inside the executive conference room. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested in connection with the matter, the DOJ said. Alfozan was fired from OpenAI after the incident, the company said. An OpenAI employee was arrested after a " sophisticated recording device " was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday. The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology." Alfozan is also listed as a partner at Raed Ventures , a venture capital firm that focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, according to its website. The firm announced on Feb. 6, 2025, that H.H. Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, had joined the firm as a venture partner. Alfozan was announced as a venture partner two days later. The Raed announcement for Alfozan lists Meta , Microsoft and SAP as previous roles and said he studied computer science and engineering at MIT. Raed, which is headquartered in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance." Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room. The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room. The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device." The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ. This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems. Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI." —CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this article. events.title: FBI arrests OpenAI employee accused of planting secret recording device in conference room
events.summary: In a stunning disclosure, the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) announced Tuesday that it has arrested an OpenAI employee who is a Saudi citizen, charging him with secretly recording conversations in a conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. A specialized OpenAI security team—the technical surveillance countermeasures team—first found a recording device on Sept. 30 during a sweep of the conference room, OpenAI told Fortune . The listening device was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television, concealed by a small piece of toilet paper, according to the FBI. OpenAI contacted the FBI after discovering the listening device, which the company says was sophisticated and designed to evade detection. It had advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring. In that conference room, executives frequently held “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information,” the FBI said. That includes “proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.” The suspect is Abdurahman Alfozan, 35, a citizen of Saudi Arabia, the FBI said, without specifying the nature of his status as a U.S. resident. He was an engineering lead, according to his LinkedIn, who worked on OpenAI’s “Agents Platform,” according to his X bio. He formerly worked at Meta for five years, and is a graduate of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (2016) and UC Berkeley (2025). The FBI did not immediately arrest Alfozan upon learning of the device, nor did OpenAI immediately fire him, both of which eventually happened on Oct. 9. He is currently in federal custody and appeared in federal court today, and will appear again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing. He faces a maximum sentence of 5 years in prison, plus three years supervised release, if convicted. Between Sept. 30 and Oct. 9, OpenAI worked with the FBI on the timing of Alfozan’s termination, so as to not disrupt their investigation, the company said. OpenAI said it restricted Alfozan’s access to systems and parts of the office, suspended his network access, placed him on leave, and took his company-issued equipment. However, there was clearly a continued breakdown in security, as Alfozan was allegedly able to enter the conference room again on Oct. 5. He checked behind the TV for the device, which was no longer there, but was captured on closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office, according to the FBI. Also “on or about” Oct. 5, Alfozan allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room at OpenAI, which contained his wallet, identification, and another similar recording device. The device pictured in the FBI’s release bears the brand “seeed studio” from seeedstudio.com. It’s unclear what Alfozan planned to do with the data, and at this time neither OpenAI nor the FBI has found evidence that anything leaked. A few days before implanting the device, from Sept. 24 to Sept. 30, Alfozan began consulting an unnamed chatbot, using his spouse’s account, about building, installing, and encrypting audio recordings, among other things, the FBI claimed. He also used a “productivity tool”—presumably internal to OpenAI—to inquire aboutOpenAI’s “building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of ‘leadership and exec’ and external partner meetings, according to the FBI. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a post on X on Tuesday. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.” However, the investigation remains ongoing. OpenAI is using the event to showcase how its technology can help combat these types of threats. The company said it used its models “to understand the device” and figure out which employee had planted it.  FBI Director Kash Patel called the incident a matter of national security. “Protecting American SI [Super Intelligence] is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” he said. It was not immediately possible to reach Alfozan. Timeline of alleged events, as disclosed by the FBI and OpenAI: Sept. 24: Alfozan allegedly begins consulting an unnamed chatbot about building, installing, and encrypting audio recordings, among other things Sept. 28: Alfozan allegedly plants the device in the conference room Sept. 30: OpenAI finds the device, informs the FBI Oct. 5: Alfozan allegedly enters the conference room to check the device behind the television, leaves unattended bag with another recording device in another room Oct. 9: FBI arrests Alfozan, OpenAI terminates him Oct. 13: FBI and OpenAI announce the arrest  Oct 19: Alfozan will appear again in federal court This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: SoftBank junk bond sale raises stakes for CEO Son’s all-in AI bet
events.summary: The scale of Masayoshi Son’s investments, which include backing of about US$64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. SoftBank’s record US$11 billion junk-bond sale shows pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to prove his huge AI bet will pay off, especially through OpenAI. The company is borrowing at up to 9.75% to keep assets it expects to rise in value, while investors worry about concentration risk and possible AI market overheating. Analysts say SoftBank’s AI bets are far bigger and riskier than before, with mixed past results, but supporters believe AI could still bring major financial gains. TOKYO – SoftBank’s promise to pay its highest-ever yields in a record US$11 billion (S$14.1 billion) junk-bond offering highlights the pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to secure returns on his all-in bet on AI amid concerns about possible overheating in the market. The SoftBank debt issuance in September added to a sharp surge in corporate borrowing in 2026, including major bond sales from Amazon.com, Alphabet and Tencent. The scale of Son’s investments, which include backing totalling US$64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. Those fresh investments are now coming under sharper scrutiny by analysts and investors amid worries about the degree of concentration in SoftBank’s portfolio and whether a payoff from the expenditures by AI companies will come soon enough. SoftBank previously sold shares in Nvidia and T-Mobile US to fund its investments, but it is now borrowing at record yields of up to 9.75% to retain assets that it believes will appreciate, a senior SoftBank executive told Reuters. “We’ve borrowed money in large part because we don’t want to sell assets that we believe will keep rising in value,” said Alex Clavel, CEO of SoftBank Investment Advisers, which manages the Vision Funds. Sam Altman’s OpenAI is the core investment in the latest iteration of Son’s investment strategy, following lucrative bets on Chinese tech giant Alibaba and chip designer Arm. “Given OpenAI’s appreciation to date, 9.75% is still very reasonable,” Clavel said. Arm’s valuation has grown fivefold since it floated in 2023 and further listings from SoftBank’s private AI portfolio would clarify their value and more easily allow the assets to be monetised for additional investment activity. Altman has said OpenAI will not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns about artificial intelligence. It also faces competition from rival Anthropic and hyperscalers, as well as low-cost Chinese labs. SoftBank was previously “betting on a bunch of numbers at the roulette table. Now it’s red or black, either lose everything or gain everything”, said analyst David Gibson of MST Financial. Increased scrutiny of AI-related fundraising SoftBank will pay its highest-ever coupon of 9.75% on a bond issued in September that matures in 2034. That return compares with Alphabet offering 5.2% for a bond issued in August that matures in 2033. SoftBank’s shares surged to a record high of 8,632 yen in June, though they have fallen 38% since then, while its credit default swap spreads – the cost to insure its debt against a default or other credit event – jumped 24% over the same period. SoftBank’s higher yields reflect investor perceptions of their risk and concentration in large positions, analysts say. “The bets are much bigger than we’ve ever seen,” said Amir Anvarzadeh of Asymmetric Advisors, who recommends shorting the stock. James Athey, a fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough, said the fund was not allocating to high-yield bonds at this stage of the credit cycle, given current tight spread levels. “SoftBank is so aggressive, so concentrated and so all-in, I don’t think we’d be looking there first anyway,” he said. Clavel, however, says SoftBank’s OpenAI backing reflects their deep business ties. “We see OpenAI as a partner, building a relationship that can deliver strategic value as well as financial returns,” he said. OpenAI is also an investor in and customer of data centre company SB Energy, which SoftBank is looking to list and may seek a valuation of US$50 billion, Reuters has reported. “SoftBank is taking advantage of hyper-excitement around AI-driven businesses, applying very high valuations for relatively low revenues, and they are looking to capitalise,” said MST’s Gibson of the potential valuation. Son’s bets have a mixed track record – his investment in Chinese tech giant Alibaba was a major success, but Son also directed US$16 billion to Adam Neumann’s WeWork, which ultimately went bankrupt. Other setbacks included a crash in the value of its investments as central banks moved to hike rates in 2022. “OpenAI’s value appreciation to date far exceeds the losses in our 2021 vintage investments,” Clavel said.

events.title: Singapore’s GDP grew by 5.4% in third quarter of 2026
events.summary: On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the Singapore economy expanded by 1.1%, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter. Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter of 2026, slower than 6.2% in the previous quarter, said METI on Oct 14. Manufacturing rose 7.5%, while construction grew 8.8% as public and private projects increased. Services also grew, led by wholesale trade, transport, IT, finance and hotels. METI said fuller third-quarter GDP data, including inflation, jobs and productivity, will be released in the Economic Survey of Singapore in November 2026. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter, moderating from 6.2% in the previous quarter. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the economy expanded by 1.1%, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter, said the Ministry of Energy Trade and Industry (METI) on Oct 14. The manufacturing sector grew by 7.5% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, slower than the 12.9% growth in the previous quarter. The construction sector expanded by 8.8% year on year in the third quarter, faster than the 6.1% growth in the preceding quarter, as both public and private sector construction output increased. Among the services sectors, the wholesale and retail trade, and transportation and storage sectors collectively grew by 8% year on year in the third quarter, extending the 6.9% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the retail trade sector. Growth in the wholesale trade sector was led by the machinery, equipment and supplies segment, which saw strong growth in tandem with the robust increase in electronics exports over the same period. Meanwhile, growth in the transportation and storage sector was largely supported by the water and air transport segments. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the wholesale and retail trade, and transportation and storage sectors as a whole grew by 2.2%, improving from zero growth in the second quarter. The group of sectors comprising the information and communications, finance and insurance and professional services sectors expanded by 4.3% year on year in the third quarter, easing from the 5.1% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group grew during the quarter. Growth in the information and communications sector was driven by the IT and information services segment, while that in the professional services sector was largely supported by the architectural and engineering, as well as the technical testing and analysis services segment. Growth in the finance and insurance sector was led by the fund management and banking services segments. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, this group of sectors expanded by 0.4%, moderating from the 2.8% growth in the second quarter. Growth in the remaining group of services sectors, comprising accommodation and food services, real estate, administrative and support services, and other services industries, came in at 2.1% year on year in the third quarter, extending the 2.4% growth in the preceding quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the food and beverage services sector. In particular, the accommodation sector grew on the back of an increase in gross lettings in the higher value-added hotel segments. A Saudi national who worked as an engineer at the artificial intelligence firm OpenAI has been arrested after a listening device was found in the company’s conference room, according to United States authorities. In a statement on Tuesday, the Department of Justice said that the employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi engineer named Abdulrahman Alfozan, had worked at the company since July 2025. list 1 of 3 AI deepfake ads grow more popular in US midterm campaigns, blurring truth list 2 of 3 AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says list 3 of 3 Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks Prosecutors accused Alfozan of using the listening device to illegally obtain sensitive information. Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. “Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Kash Patel, the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in response to the arrest. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the case was “taken extremely seriously”, adding “theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security.” A Justice Department complaint said that the device, concealed in toilet paper, was installed around September 28 and discovered on September 30. Prosecutors explained that video surveillance from OpenAI’s offices showed Alfozan appearing near the executive conference room on multiple dates before the device was discovered, despite having no authority to access the room or participate in its meetings. Such meetings, they added, were highly confidential. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.” Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.
