events.title: AI agent company Decagon has held early M&A talks and hired a banker
events.summary: Lisbon , Portugal - 12 November 2025; Jesse Zhang, Co-founder & CEO, Decagon AI on Centre Stage during day two of Web Summit 2025 at the MEO Arena in Lisbon, Portugal. (Photo By Shauna Clinton/Sportsfile for Web Summit via Getty Images) Shauna Clinton/Sportsfile for Web Summit via Getty Images AI startup Decagon builds AI agents to automate customer support for enterprise customers. The company has hired an investment bank to evaluate M&A interest. There have been early talks with potential buyers. Update: This story has been updated to reflect that ServiceNow says it is no longer in talks with Decagon. Buzzy AI agent startup Decagon could be the latest company swept up in a growing wave of AI dealmaking. The company, which was last valued at $4.5 billion earlier this year, has hired a bank to evaluate acquisition interest, according to people familiar with the matter. Decagon held early discussions with cloud software giant ServiceNow, but a spokesperson for ServiceNow says they're not ongoing. People familiar with the matter told Business Insider there have also been early talks with other companies; if a deal does not materialize, Decagon could instead raise a new funding round. "Our approach to M&A has not changed: we remain an organic growth company first. M&A is a tool to accelerate our roadmap or open meaningful new innovation," said Amit Zavery, president, chief product officer, and chief operating officer of ServiceNow. The interest in Decagon represents a new shift in the AI boom: after years of huge venture rounds and soaring valuations, tech companies are increasingly looking to buy their way into promising AI markets. Hugging Face was recently acquired by Nvidia for 12.9 billion, and OpenRouter was snapped up by Stripe for around $8 billion. Growing AI-related businesses are often getting offers at a significant premium to their last valuation, so if Decagon were to accept an offer, it could be considerably higher than its previous $4.5 billion value. Founded in July 2023 by Jesse Zhang and Ashwin Sreenivas, Decagon uses generative AI to automate customer support for enterprise customers , including Delta, Snapchat, and Ticketmaster. The company has raised over $400 million from a roster of well-known Silicon Valley investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Index Ventures, Bain Capital Ventures, and Accel. It competes with industry veteran Bret Taylor's Sierra, which was valued at $15.8 billion earlier this year. ServiceNow's previous interest in Decagon came as it looked to reassure investors that it can adapt to AI’s threat to traditional software businesses. Its shares tumbled earlier this year during the so-called SaaS-pocalypse , when investors feared AI could erode software companies’ profit margins. It was also punished for making a $7 billion acquisition of the security business Armis, a deal announced late last year. The stock has since rebounded by 55% in the past six months as ServiceNow continues to invest heavily in AI and reshape parts of its business. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ex-gang leader gets 40 years to life for rapper Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
events.summary: A 30-year hunt for justice ends with the sentencing of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, who has written about his role in Shakur’s shooting death. A former gang leader accused of masterminding the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison. Tuesday’s sentencing capped a 30-year-long cold case that rattled the golden era of rap music in the United States. list 1 of 3 Former gang leader found guilty of Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder list 2 of 3 Tupac Shakur killer sentenced to 40 years in prison In August, Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, had been found guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. Davis, 63, is the sole person charged in the death of Shakur, who died at the peak of his fame at age 25. Judge Carli Kierny announced Davis’s sentence at a hearing in Las Vegas, Nevada, where she chided him for the murder. “You don’t get to take a man from his family, you don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it, especially when that man is Tupac Shakur,” Kierny said. “The world never forgot about him and his death, and neither did Las Vegas.” During the hearing, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars. For nearly three decades, Shakur’s death remained one of the music industry’s most notorious unsolved mysteries, prompting endless debate over who did it and why. Davis had long been a suspect, but investigators lacked evidence to pursue an indictment. The investigative deadlock shattered after Davis publicly boasted about his involvement in media interviews. He also recounted his role in the murder in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend . Previously, Davis entered into a 2008 proffer agreement with federal law enforcement officers, granting him limited immunity for statements he made privately to investigators. But by repeating his statements outside his meetings with investigators, prosecutors said Davis had effectively voided the agreement’s protections. DiGiacomo said that Davis was trying to profit from a killing that he committed, and for that, he deserves the maximum possible sentence. Shakur had been in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight on the night of September 7, 1996, when he was shot. Investigators said the shooting took place roughly two hours after a confrontation between Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson, and Shakur’s entourage. In his memoir, Davis accused Shakur and his friends of assaulting his nephew. He explained he then sought to retaliate, and he admitted to handing the murder weapon to two alleged accomplices, seated in the backseat of a white Cadillac, who then fired the fatal shots. Shakur had been in the passenger seat of a black BMW, stopped at a red light, when his vehicle came under fire. He died six days later. Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive. Members of Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur. “This man’s life mattered,” Sekyiwa Shakur told the court, while her brother called the murder “devastating, heartbreaking and sad”. Following the verdict, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal described the Shakur family as having to endure years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved”. “They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said. The ex-gang leader briefly addressed the court on Tuesday, asking the judge to order the return of property seized from his residence, including personal photographs. When the judge asked if he wished to make any additional statements, Davis declined, stating, “No, I’m good.” He added that he would “appeal this case for sure”.

events.title: Mike Johnson's Latino voter problem keeps getting worse
events.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years. Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018. The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research. In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%. That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis , a leading authority on Latino voting behavior. Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP. In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown. The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters. Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys. Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living. 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue. 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans. That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February. The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. The Equis survey is the latest indication they could help Democrats take back Congress. Note: The Equis survey was conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2 via phone and text-to-web with 1,800 registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino nationally. The sample was weighted to match the composition of registered voters modeled as Latino by state, gender, age, education, vote history, voter registration date, VCH score and 2024 vote recall.

Omar's office and Democratic House leadership quickly denounced the action as an "abuse of power," with a spokesperson for Omar saying she "has done nothing wrong." What we're hearing: "People are outraged. ... [This is] what authoritarian tyrants and dictators do," said the senior House Democrat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to relay colleagues' private conversations. Another House Democrat told Axios "the chatter on texts" is that "folks are irate." Zoom out: Democrats allege the raid fits into a broader pattern of Trump using federal resources to boost Republicans and target his political opponents. DHS became embroiled in controversy just last week after a statement targeting Pennsylvania Democrat Janelle Stelson, which critics said violates federal laws restricting partisan activities by federal officials. Trump has also come under fire for using taxpayer funds to run campaign-style television ads touting him and his administration in the run-up to the midterms. What they're saying: "President Trump will keep trying to intimidate and bully Americans ahead of the midterms," said Balint, adding, "We suspect he will try anything to stay in power and in control." Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) said that "of course there will" be more like the Omar raid, saying Trump is "the pettiest, worst human being" and "can't help himself." Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios: "This is some serious hate-baiting bullshit. This administration is just despicable." Asked whether he expects more, Huffman said, "Of course." The other side: One congressional Republican cheered the raid on Omar, who has long been the target of right-wing attacks on her immigration status. The White House, DOJ and DHS did not respond to a request for comment. What to watch: House Democratic leaders are already signaling plans to wrap this into their oversight agenda if they retake the majority. "We will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his deputies said in a statement. events.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
events.summary: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027). At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system. While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework ( CVE-2026-108398 ) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug. Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs. “We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said. Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software. Tyler Reguly , associate director of security research and development at Fortra , notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first. “Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said. Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

events.title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
events.summary: An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room. He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing. OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device that had not been installed in Alfozan’s bag at the office. Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US district court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest. Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X . “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.” OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep. Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview , Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations. The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment. Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies. According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.” The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated. OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted. After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing. According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found. He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

events.title: Applied Materials’ $5 billion AI lab aims to cut chip development time in half—and restore Silicon Valley’s edge
events.summary: Silicon Valley has built some of the world’s most impressive and valuable companies, with names like Apple , Alphabet , and Meta , worth trillions of dollars apiece.  When it comes to building the actual facilities where chips, computers, and other game-changing innovations are created, however, America’s tech capital has much less to show. Most chip facilities are now located overseas or out of state, and the most striking thing about Silicon Valley’s landscape of low-slung buildings and office parks is just how unimposing it is.  That makes what Applied Materials—the world’s largest chipmaking equipment producer—did on Monday so unusual. The 59-year-old company officially unveiled its new EPIC semiconductor research and development facility, a two-year construction project located at Applied Materials’ Sunnyvale, Calif. campus, just down the road from its headquarters. Quite simply: it’s the biggest thing around.  The massive 600,000-square-foot structure of glass, concrete, and steel (two Eiffel Towers’ worth of steel, according to the company), looms over its environment like a spaceship from another world.  The idea behind the facility is equally bold. The $5 billion EPIC center was built in partnership with some of the world’s top chip industry players, including Intel , TSMC , Micron , SK Hynix, and Samsung . The companies will each have teams of researchers on-site, working alongside Applied Materials’ engineers and getting early access to Applied Materials’ newest equipment, to develop advances in microprocessors and memory chips.  Applied Materials described EPIC as the largest-ever U.S. investment in advanced semiconductor equipment R&D, with total capital investment expected to reach $5 billion when all is said and done. The facility’s so-called clean rooms, in which bunny-suit wearing researchers operate machines that etch microscopic circuits into silicon wafers, will occupy the space of three football fields. Within that space, competing companies—like memory chip companies Micron and SK Hynix—will have their own private test facilities, crammed with advanced chipmaking gear, where they will work directly with dedicated teams from Applied Materials. “Having innovators co-located together, having earlier access to the technologies that enable new AI architectures, is a complete game changer,” said Applied Materials CEO Gary Dickerson in an interview with Fortune at the event.  According to the company, the collaboration at EPIC will speed up the time it takes to develop each new generation of chip architectures, cutting the typical “concept to commercialization” timeframe from 10 to 12 years to as little as six years.  Applied Materials President and CEO Gary Dickerson Applied Materials The ability to understand what’s technically feasible earlier on in the process increases the chance of breakthroughs and hopefully reduces the number of dead ends that researchers go through. Until companies collaborate in the lab, Dickerson said, “they don’t know what they don’t know.” The EPIC center is purely for research, not for commercial production of chips—so it’s not, in itself, likely to bring chip manufacturing back to the U.S. But it represents an important step in keeping Silicon Valley—and Applied Materials—at the forefront of cutting-edge chip technologies, a critical weapon in the race to develop ever more powerful AI models. A reminder of the stakes was on display Monday as CXMT, a memory maker in China, announced a breakthrough in memory chip density. The breakthrough, if substantiated, could allow CXMT to produce more power-efficient memory chips, beating Samsung and SK Hynix to the milestone. The news sent shares of both companies down roughly 7% and 10% respectively in South Korea, according to Bloomberg .  The U.S. government has barred the sales of advanced GPU chips and advanced chipmaking equipment to China, in an effort to deprive the country of the computing brawn necessary to create AI models capable of outperforming models made by U.S. companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Dickerson repeatedly invoked “winning the AI race” at Monday’s event, though he would not comment specifically on his views about U.S. regulations on sales to China. (In February, Applied Materials paid $252 million to settle a case with the U.S. Department of Commerce that accused the company of shipping equipment to China that did not comply with U.S. export restrictions.) Founded in 1967 as a chemistry supply company to serve the then nascent semiconductor industry, Applied Materials has grown into the world’s largest provider of chip making equipment. The company has been a major beneficiary of the AI boom and the resulting shortage of memory chips , with its shares up more than 110% over the past 12 months. In August, the company reported $9.12 billion in quarterly revenue, up 25% year-over-year, and the company has said it has visibility into customer demand as far as 2030. Given the memory chip industry’s history of boom and bust cycles, some industry observers worry that overinvesting by both chipmakers and chip equipment makers could pose a risk if demand drops. Visibility into customers’ future demand, they say, is not the same as signed contracts. Dickerson said the new products and services that companies are developing to take advantage of AI give him confidence that demand for chips, and for improvement in the performance and the power efficiency of chips, is only going to increase.   “This is moving so quick,” he said. “There’s never been an inflection like this in our lifetimes.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip , PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI). “The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.” Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers. While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable. Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease. “One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.” The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word. To use the device, patients undergo an hour-long procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors. “The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed under the in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where . . .it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.” He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a there’s a next ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.” When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired. As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue. The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors. “In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.” Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI.

events.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
events.summary: Google's translation service handles one trillion words per month "Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard. "It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator. "You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS. He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs". "But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon. A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather. In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate. That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems. Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year. AI translation is the "right call" in many cases says John Zimmerman "For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages. "For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says. With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia. Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI. "Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains. But that human input is required less and less. "The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft. "Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman. Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French. She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them. "There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said. The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié. When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y". In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase. The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees. Ariella Baltié specialises in legal translation work Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field. "The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations. She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth). "That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter. She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult. "Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot." Carol Bereuter is a specialist in medical translations "If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon. Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

events.title: Goldman says investors are looking for 'profitable' Chinese business growth overseas
events.summary: Goldman Sachs predicts Chinese companies will only expand their overseas market share. Stock investors are "ruthless" in punishing stocks of incumbents that lose market share, Goldman said. But it noted the market is far more skeptical about Chinese companies' global opportunities. BEIJING — Equity investors are skeptical of Chinese companies' rapid expansion overseas, according to Goldman Sachs. The "market wants to look for profitable expansions," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs Research, said on a podcast that the investment bank published Tuesday. Sluggish consumer demand in China has pushed many companies, such as electric car brands, to accelerate plans for entering other countries. Automaker Geely is one of the latest Chinese companies to push further abroad, announcing Friday it plans to enter Canada next year . Chinese companies' overseas market share will likely reach 31% by 2035, up from around 18%, Chen and her team predicted in a Sept. 14 report. Their analysis covered more than 10 sectors, including express delivery, industrial robots and so-called white goods such as air conditioners. Chinese businesses often find higher profit margins abroad than they would at home, enabling the companies to charge lower prices than local competitors. Investors need to be convinced the global expansion "does not end up with something similar to involution, where the price actually gets killed because of competition," Chen said Tuesday, adding that geopolitics and market access restrictions also weighs on stock performance. Involution refers to race-to-the-bottom competition in China, which regulators have attempted to address in recent years. That uncertainty means Chinese companies have very little of their global expansion opportunity priced into their stocks, Chen said. But on the flip side, she noted that investors are "ruthless" when incumbent companies lose their market share: A 10% to 15% loss could shrink market capitalization by 50% to 80%. The Chinese players are not just looking at the U.S. and Europe. Goldman Sachs noted some of the most rapid growth is in emerging markets, as the businesses also pursue areas underserved by competitors. "Chinese brands are no longer simply market challengers," Euromonitor said in a report last month. events.title: US fines Bank of America US$1.2b for anti-money laundering violations
events.summary: The announcement marks a hit to Bank of America just a day before it reports its third-quarter earnings. US regulators fined Bank of America more than US$1.2 billion for anti-money laundering and sanctions breaches, saying it failed to report over US$5 billion in suspicious transactions. The Treasury said some activity involved Chinese money laundering networks, the south-west US border, and sanctions violations linked to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. Bank of America must fix its controls, face independent reviews, and absorb a US$1.2 billion charge, while its shares fell 2.6% after the announcement. WASHINGTON – The US Treasury Department said on Oct 13 that it is imposing penalties of more than US$1.2 billion (S$1.54 billion) on Bank of America, citing “violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws”. The second biggest US bank failed to properly report more than US$5 billion in “suspicious transactions,” the department said. Some of these involved risks related to national security and other concerns, including transactions “indicative of Chinese money laundering networks” and illicit finance around the south-west US border. The overall charge involves US$1.2 billion assessed by the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. This includes a US$750 million civil penalty from a key bank regulator, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced a US$11.6 million settlement with the bank over “apparent violations of numerous sanctions programmes, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism”. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” he said. A Bank of America spokesperson told AFP its results would include a US$1.2 billion charge weighing on net income by around 17 cents per share. They added that the institution is committed to finishing the work needed to address issues that regulators raised. “We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year,” the spokesperson said. US regulators have published a consent order requiring Bank of America to work with a third party to identify and report suspicious transactions that went undetected. The institution will also have to undergo an independent review of its programmes for monitoring suspicious activity, and on other forms of due diligence. The bank is subject to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order as well, calling for it to address issues in its anti-money laundering programme and compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act. But the Treasury noted on Oct 13 that the bank “failed to prioritise” compliance despite agreeing to the 2024 order. Due to Bank of America’s “egregious and continued” violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, the OCC imposed its biggest civil money penalty assessed against a bank, said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould. Bank of America shares were down 2.6% in after-hours trading, following the Treasury’s announcement. AFP

events.title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?
events.summary: Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired? Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job? We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates , external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason. But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating? Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager. He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI. "Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that." Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on. He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates . "That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening." This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI during recruitment "at some stages of the recruitment process". According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions. However, it also found some 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments. On top of this, the tech is also helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". And Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market. EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem. EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but took the decision to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year. Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process. "What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't." Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible. It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates' skills. But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews. "A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script." AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff' Published 25 March 2025 AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts Published 5 March Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI Published 21 May One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews. While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would. "I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?" According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough.

events.title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
events.summary: About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year. The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance. The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases. Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service. Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26. It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds. But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class. "I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out." A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time. Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs Published 6 days ago Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time Published 29 May Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say Published 16 February Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload. We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day. Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare". "We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands. Bryn Dymott says he is speaking out now because he wants people to know what's really happening Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas. "People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered." Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening. He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise." So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices. Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems. The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others. "Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU. The union said most Royal Mail workers leaving the company were believed to be new starters on part-time contracts, but also said there had been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing. Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas. It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses." The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period. The BBC saw returned post that couldn't be delivered so ended up back on the frames in a Royal Mail office Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027. The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out. The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets. But some MPs think it is time for a new approach, and a group of them will meet the regulator later on Wednesday.

events.title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. In most factories, automation is fixed: robots and machines are programmed for one specific task and product. Changing a line means reprogramming and physical retooling, or swapping out equipment, which can take weeks or months. San Francisco-based Industrial Next says it’s changing that. The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor. The company announced on stage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing. Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix. The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills. After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt. “We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing–designing cars and designing self-driving systems–and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.” The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better. “I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.” Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability. Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks. “We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.” In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts. Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones.

events.title: Manchester United’s Martinez blasts board’s lack of investment
events.summary: Manchester United beaten 2-0 at Atletico Madrid, but defender Lisandro Martinez slams club’s failure to invest in team. Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez blasted the club’s board for a perceived lack of investment this summer, after the team were beaten by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday. United are winless in five games across all competitions after the 2-0 defeat in the Spanish capital and have made their worst start to a league season in 40 years. list 1 of 4 Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa list 2 of 4 Michael Jordan’s ‘Last Dance’ NBA Finals jersey sells for record $14m list 3 of 4 Canelo Alvarez ‘will fight in Riyadh’ despite Saudi airport attacks list 4 of 4 Verstappen wins chaotic Singapore GP F1 sprint after Russell crashes “Really poor,” Martinez told Amazon Prime when asked about the team’s performance against Atletico. “I have to control myself a lot but sometimes is a reflection… [or] mirror of how our club is at the moment.” Martinez said he “100 percent” expected more investment in the squad over the summer after United finished third in the Premier League last season and returned to Europe’s top competition. “I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox], I have to be honest, as players we have to do more, but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for these kind of nights,” he continued. Martinez said last season the club had “created the base to create an amazing team”, but they did not follow through. Pressure is mounting on coach Michael Carrick after five games without a win, but Martinez suggested sacking the Englishman was not the way forward. “You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager. What about other areas? I can’t say more,” said Martinez. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach [is to blame], easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas.” Red Devils minority owner Jim Ratcliffe was at the stadium to watch the league-phase defeat by last season’s semi-finalists. Man United spent around 140 million pounds ($185m) this summer on midfielders Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, but fans were upset the club did not reinforce other positions, including left-back and striker. Speaking to reporters after the game, Carrick said he had not heard Martinez’s comments and so could not judge them. “I think it’s a little bit on the emotions of the game as well, of coming here and being disappointed not to get something from the game,” said the coach. events.title: Here's where Jim Cramer stands on this newly public AI infrastructure stock
events.summary: CNBC’s Jim Cramer said investors should hold off on buying newly public AI infrastructure company Accelevation Holdings, citing political uncertainty surrounding data centers ahead of the midterm elections and the presence of well-established competitors. "Accelevation has an exciting story, but after it came public with a whimper, I'm not too eager to jump on this one," he said. "For now, I say let's put Accelevation on our watch list and see if management can deliver before we pull the trigger." There's a new picks-and-shovels play on the artificial intelligence build-out, but CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that investors should keep the stock at arm's length. The " Mad Money " host gave two primary reasons for holding off on Accelevation Holdings : He's becoming more cautious about data center stocks ahead of the midterm elections and prefers established companies with proven track records. That's why Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by the CNBC Investing Club, instead owns shares of AI infrastructure players such as gas turbine maker GE Vernova and electrical equipment supplier Eaton . Accelevation, which makes and installs electric, cooling equipment and support structures inside data centers, priced its offering on Sept. 29 at $18 per share, below its proposed offering range. Shares debuted the next day and closed at $17.95. They have since fallen to just over $15, a disappointing first couple of weeks for a company benefiting from surging demand for AI infrastructure. Cramer's first concern extends beyond Accelevation. With the midterm elections just three weeks away, he expects political opposition to data center construction to remain a headwind for the broader industry. The enormous electricity demands of these facilities and their potential impact on energy costs have become political flashpoints , making Cramer reluctant to recommend buying into the sector before voters head to the polls. "If you're going to buy a data center supplier, I think you should wait three weeks until after the election — that's when I expect some of the political heat to die down," he said. His second concern is specific to Accelevation. While the company's growth has been impressive, Cramer is less confident in its ability to consistently turn that demand into profits, particularly as it competes with larger industrial players. Accelevation's revenue surged 147% in 2025, while sales jumped another 176% year over year in the first half of 2026. However, higher labor costs and project inefficiencies weighed on gross margins during that period. "That tells me some of this work has been much harder to execute profitably than these guys expected," Cramer said. He also expressed concerns about Accelevation's competitive position, citing Vertiv and Eaton as established companies that pursue overlapping segments of the data center infrastructure market. "There are a ton of different ways to play this story," he said. "I'd rather go with the ones that have earned my confidence." events.title: Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman thinks the AI doomer narrative isn’t doing the industry any favors. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , the AI chipmaker exec quipped that “some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn’t be allowed to talk in public.” He’s referencing the negativity now spreading around the dangers of AI, from models breaking containment to AI insiders debating the percentage chance that AI may kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. The argument has become so mainstream that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was recently parodied in a skit on “Saturday Night Live,” where the fictional character summed up the discourse, saying, “We do not condone what we are doing.” Feldman, however, thinks the promise and potential that go hand in hand with AI developments are getting overlooked. He thinks AI leaders should spend more time telling people that AI could lead to a world where your grandkids will “never meet anybody who dies of cancer,” for instance, even if they have concerns about AI risks. Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company’s customers include big names working with the technology, like OpenAI, Block, Figma, pharmaceutical giant GSK, and Lovable. However, he’s pragmatic about weighing the trade-offs between risk and reward. “I don’t think there are powerful technologies that don’t come with the challenge of ‘what happens when powerful technologies are in the hands of bad people?’ I think you can’t make one and not have the other,” Feldman said during his interview at Disrupt. “I think what we have to say is that this technology is powerful,” he added. “We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably,” he added. The chipmaker CEO also suggested that some of the negativity around AI has to do with how the data center industry has approached the new buildouts created by AI demand. “As an industry, we weren’t super good for the past few years at working with local communities, particularly in the U.S. We — the industry — didn’t do what others have done in the power industry in oil and gas. They didn’t work with the community. They didn’t engage the community as they should have, and that was a problem,” Feldman said. He compared the NIMBY-ism — “not in my backyard!” — of what’s going on in the U.S. with other countries, naming Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico, and Sweden as markets where they’re encouraging companies to build data centers. Feldman also wasn’t concerned that efficiency improvements would create less demand for his chips, or those from other companies competing with Nvidia, as Cerebras is. “We can do our job as hardware vendors to make our compute more efficient, and then the model makers can do improved work in making their models more efficient to achieve the same goals. events.title: Art of Play co-owner says Kelly Clarkson's post was 'like she threw a Molotov cocktail at us'
events.summary: Kelly Clarkson's complaint went viral. The store's owner told Business Insider that people in his life are hearing from her fans. Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images - Ben Shimkus/Business Insider Art of Play's co-owner told Business Insider Kelly Clarkson's post was "like a Molotov cocktail." The viral fight placed Adam Rubin's small Brooklyn shop at the center of a massive online drama. Rubin says the store got threats online — and hugs from supportive strangers. Adam Rubin said he wasn't supposed to come into work on Tuesday. The co-owner of Art of Play — a small Brooklyn-based shop with tarot cards, funky home decor, magic trick books, and a wooden bird named Molly — said he was supposed to get some stitches removed. Instead, he came in to answer questions about Kelly Clarkson's viral social-media complaint. "It's like she threw a Molotov cocktail at us," Adam Rubin told Business Insider. "And we're just here to pick up the pieces." On Saturday, Clarkson wrote on X that she had driven to Brooklyn to visit Art of Play and was treated as if she could not afford an item she wanted to buy. She compared the experience to the "Pretty Woman" scene, when Julia Roberts' character is dismissed by salespeople at a luxury store. Art of Play has an altogether different story. The store said Clarkson had asked to buy Molly, a one-of-a-kind bird automaton that was not for sale. Clarkson responded by calling the shop liars. On Tuesday, Rubin told USA Today the bird is now for sale for $15 million. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Art of Play (@artofplay) Internet sleuths have been attempting to sort out the drama, largely to no avail. Investigative journalist Pablo Torre is also on the case — an update Rubin declined to comment on. The back-and-forth has pushed an otherwise sleepy block of Brooklyn into a surprisingly large online drama. Art of Play sits adjacent to a hospital and across from the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, in what Rubin called a " Robert Moses-abandoned " stretch of old buildings that had fallen into decay before businesses like his arrived. On Tuesday, angry Clarkson fans showed up outside the shop, Rubin said. "It's only a matter of time until a person carrying a Samurai sword and an 'American Idol' T-shirt shows up outside our store," he said. Several nearby businesses told Business Insider they didn't see the protests. The neighborhood's older residents were largely unaware of the very online drama, they said. The other businesses said the controversy only came up in conversations with people who worked in the area. They largely talked about the absurdity of their small neck of the woods getting national media attention. The fight, Rubin said, has gotten ugly online — and he said Clarkson's international stardom plays a big role. Her X post, as of publication, has more than 45 million views, while Art of Play is a local retailer with 172,000 Instagram followers. "We had no idea what would happen to us," Rubin said. "She did. She's the superstar." Rubin said the store has received threats and a barrage of online hate. He's also gotten a ton of in-person love, he said, including from frequent customers and strangers who came to visit. A woman he doesn't recognize came by to give him a hug, he said. The dispute is especially strange for Art of Play, Rubin said, because the business is built around in-person interaction. During Business Insider's visit, he noted that shoppers inside were talking rather than scrolling on their phones. Rubin said he would welcome Clarkson back, but he said she should expect the same treatment as anyone else who walks in. "We treated her like any other customer," Rubin said. "She wasn't happy because she wanted to be treated like a star." Clarkson's representatives did not respond to a request for comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tech companies are overhauling company structures to justify AI spending, and it means AI agents could start appearing on org charts, Block CFO says
events.summary: Earlier this year, Block CEO Jack Dorsey laid off 40% of his entire staff , part of a structural overhaul within the company as it ballooned its adoption of AI to automate workflows.  As more companies pour investments into the burgeoning technology, expected to exceed $730 billion this year , they are having to make sweeping changes across their workforce. Amrita Ahuja, Block’s chief financial officer and chief operating officer, predicts many of these changes needed to justify all this spending will take the form of both displacement and in how employees learn to engage with AI. At the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., on Tuesday, Ahuja said she expects more companies to integrate AI agents into their organizational charts, and workers will be responsible for both training and deploying these agents. “Where things are headed—and I’ve already heard about a couple companies doing this, so we’re on the frontier—is you look at your work chart that your company publishes, and it will have not only units, but agents,” she told Fortune senior writer Sheryl Estrada. “Those agents, not too dissimilar to humans, need to be developed over time.” “They need more context. They need more information,” she continued. “They need to understand their goals, and those may change. And so, I do think we’re headed into a new frontier as to what the organization looks like.” At the foundation of workforce changes related to AI is the idea integrating and deploying this technology has to be purposeful in order to be defensible to a company, explained Shelagh Glaser, chief financial officer of Synopsys . She likened AI spending to snacks in the break room, where some customers are in need of premium tiers of products, and others, internal models. “The cost for AI was pretty reasonable until it wasn’t,” Glaser said at the summit. “We are investing in AI. It is an important investment. We want our team to have the latest greatest tools, but just along with everything else, is being super intentional about what that investment is, and that then forms the strategy of how we think about how we get the customer.”  Michelle Zatlyn, cofounder, president, and board of directors co-chair of Cloudflare, said one way AI can offer a return on investment is by unlocking previously unknown talent within a company. On one hand, AI agents have become “an extension of our team,” Zatlyn explained, but thousands of employees now have access to software that allows them to become “builders” and uncover new AI use cases. “It’s been amazing to see where the best builders come from,” she said. “It’s not where you’d expect.” Amazon is able to measure returns on investment in how employees use AI through measuring adoption first, then engagement, and then efficiency through outcomes like time saved, noted Heather Zorn, Amazon’s vice president of customer experience products and services. But above all, the most powerful metric in how useful AI is in the workplace is how much money it brings in, Zorn said. “The ultimate KPI is revenue growth,” she said. “That is the ultimate KPI. We don’t need another KPI.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

After being found guilty of an unprecedented breach of the Premier League’s financial rules, Manchester City turn their focus to the Champions League this week, as they host two-time holders PSG on matchday two. list 1 of 3 Man City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in first game after guilty verdict list 2 of 3 Liverpool vs Man City: Blues remain unscathed, but Premier League in limbo list 3 of 3 ‘Robbed us all’: How Liverpool banners taunted Man City at Anfield Fresh off a defiant league win over Liverpool at a hostile Anfield , City have momentum on their side as they welcome PSG in a clash of two of Europe’s finest teams. An independent commission found City guilty of almost all of the 115 charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, as well as three of four charges relating to failures to cooperate with the investigation. City have denied wrongdoing and lodged an appeal . No sanctions have been decided yet, but if City’s appeal fails, potential punishments include a significant point deduction and expulsion from the Premier League. That keeps PSG fifth and Man City ninth in the league phase of this year’s Champions League. The top eight teams at the end of the league phase qualify directly to the knockout rounds, which begin with the round of 16. events.title: US trial begins for Rwandan-American accused of role in genocide
events.summary: Eric Nshimiye, an American citizen, says the evidence against him consists of unreliable eye witnesses. Boston, Massachusetts, United States – A United States federal court in Boston has begun hearing the case of a Rwandan-American accused of covering up his role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda . Prosecutors say Eric Nshimiye, a 55-year-old father of four and a US citizen, took part in a nationwide outbreak of genocidal violence against ethnic minority Tutsis by majority Hutu extremists in April 1994. More than 800,000 people were killed over about 100 days, in what has been called a genocide by the United Nations. list 1 of 3 Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize? list 2 of 3 African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC list 3 of 3 Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa Investigators from the US Department of Homeland Security arrested Nshimiye at his home in Ohio in 2024, alleging he had lied to them in an interview about his time in Rwanda during the genocide. They also allege he committed perjury in a previous trial in 2019 in Boston when he testified on behalf of a friend who was also accused of perpetrating the genocide. Prosecutors say Nshimiye, a medical student at the time of the genocide in the town of Butare, himself took part in the killing and rape of Tutsis. Hutus who took part in the violence “heeded calls by the government to terminate their neighbours,” Assistant United States Attorney Christopher Looney told the court on Tuesday, including Nshimiye in the group. “He himself attacked Tutsis, and handed Tutsis over to be killed and raped,” Looney said. During his 2019 testimony, Nshimiye denied being part of the genocide, and said he was not part of the pro-Hutu National Revolutionary Movement for Development and the Interahamwe, the paramilitary group blamed for most of the killings during the genocide. Nshimiye faces charges of perjury and obstruction of justice for those denials. If convicted, the Trump administration could try to revoke Nshimiye’s citizenship. Nshimiye, who is an ethnic Hutu, says he had gone to the capital, Kigali, on holiday before violence broke out. He says he never made it back to Butare because of the chaos engulfing the country in April 1994, and instead left the country as a refugee, eventually coming to the US and becoming a citizen in 2009. At the opening of his case on Tuesday, Nshimiye, dressed in a dark blue suit, was calm and occasionally turned to smile at family and friends who came to support him. Since his arrest, authorities have kept Nshimiye without bail in a Boston-area federal jail. Prosecutors plan to put more than a dozen witnesses on the stand, most flown in from Rwanda, who say they recall seeing Nshimiye participate in pro-Hutu political events before the genocide, and some who say they later saw him participate in genocidal violence in Butare. His family says the events of 1994 are more complex than the simple narrative of Hutus killing Tutsis. Simply being an ethnic Hutu, Epa Bizimana, Nshimiye’s nephew, told Al Jazeera, should not be enough to convince a jury someone took part in the genocide. “The jury is going to learn some things for the first time; Americans are going to learn something for the first time,” said Bizimana, who was 10 years old when he fled Rwanda with his family in 1994. Defence lawyers told the court on Tuesday that Nshimiye was not part of the Hutus who participated in the genocide. They say the entire case against him is built on the accounts of eyewitnesses, some of whom were only able to identify him after repeatedly being shown his photo, and some of whom have a history of giving different testimony in trials of alleged genocidaires over the years. Kurt Kerns, one of the defence attorneys, told the court that the prosecution’s case was based on evidence “that only reared its ugly head after Eric came to testify as a character witness, and 25 years after the genocide.” Kerns said Nshimiye had never been implicated in domestic and international tribunals after the genocide, including the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as well as an informal transitional justice system inside Rwanda, called gacaca, which tried more than a million people for their role in the atrocity.
