events.title: Emergency order by US to 'prevent blackouts' could affect data centres
events.summary: The US Department of Energy has issued an emergency order to try to prevent power cuts amid increasing demand. Monday's order prompted PJM Interconnection , a corporation that transmits electricity in parts of the US, to " direct data centres and other large-load customers to switch to back-up generation resources, if necessary". Data centres in the US are commonly blamed for a surge in electricity prices and have driven public opinion on AI to sour, according to polls. In issuing its emergency order, the Energy Department also gave "a high rate of planned generator outages during the autumn maintenance season" as a possible cause of blackouts. PJM has issued a Maximum Generation Alert and Load Management Alert for Oct. 13 ahead of expected tight system conditions caused by unusually warm fall weather and planned equipment outages required for maintenance and construction. This alert does not require any action from… pic.twitter.com/zH8QXo2Jwm — PJM Interconnection (@pjminterconnect) October 12, 2026 The order remains in effect until October 16. Energy Secretary Chris Wright was confident in his decision to order utility companies and others to take emergency measures. "This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including back-up power, available to use as needed," Mr Wright said. The Department of Energy said in a statement that the US had 35 GW of unused back-up generation available nationwide. PJM issued a maximum generation alert for October 13 and 14: "Emergency procedures took place as above-normal temperatures are forecast across much of the PJM region. Additional emergency procedures may be necessary pending system conditions." The company said the alert does not "require any action from customers". The warnings come before the US midterm elections, where energy policy, AI and data centres are key issues. Any blackouts or failure to adequately address them could add to friction between residents in the US and utility companies, as well as AI firms. President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed critics of AI in recent weeks and accused them of "hoaxes". But in February he tried to ease the strain data centres were putting on the grid by signing a non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which technology and data centre companies would provide their own electricity to operate. Meanwhile, the Department of Energy has pushed for the construction of more nuclear reactors to address AI energy needs.

events.title: Jennifer Siebel Newsom on her legacy as California’s First Partner: Equal pay ‘wasn’t enough,’ so she turned to women’s wealth
events.summary: California First Partner and documentary filmmaker Jennifer Siebel Newsom’s time in state office with Gov. Gavin Newsom concludes in January 2027, when the latter’s final term ends after eight years. The former Newsom said she looks back with pride about not standing down on pay equity and other issues that plague women, despite the flack she’s collected along the way. “I’m particularly proud of the work that we’ve done in terms of women’s wealth and closing the women’s wealth gap,” Siebel Newsom said Tuesday at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., in conversation with Ellie Austin, the host of Fortune Daily and editorial director of Most Powerful Women . Asked what metrics she wanted her legacy as first partner to be judged on, Siebel Newsom started with pay. California has “the strongest equal pay laws in the nation,” she said, and “hundreds of companies have signed on to our equal pay pledge .” She launched #EqualPayCA, a statewide campaign aimed at closing the gender pay gap, in 2019. “But that wasn’t enough, which is why we turned to women’s wealth,” she said. Siebel Newsom pointed to the financial literacy requirement in California high schools beginning with the 2030-31 graduating class. She also cited CalKids , a savings program she said was launched before Trump Accounts to incentivize families to invest in their children’s futures. She also highlighted expanded access to capital for female entrepreneurs and broader access to the her husband himself, an issue she notice early on that prompted her to work on making those circles bigger. For Siebel Newsom, the case is economic.  “Women anchor families, communities, and now, as you all know, the economy,” Siebel Newsom said. “One of the reasons we’ve really invested in California for all women … is because we know that if women are not able to thrive, how can their families, their communities, and the economy thrive?” That focus on families runs through her other work. She said investments in universal pre-K, after-school programs, summer school and school meals were meant “to mitigate costs and stress to families in California,” and have saved them thousands of dollars per year. “[I’m a] first partner because I wanted to be a partner to California’s women, children, and families,” she said. Siebel Newsom took the title “first partner” instead of “first lady” to signal inclusivity, recognizing California will one day have a woman or LGBTQ+ governor, and to emphasize the value of partnership in government, according to the governor’s office .  She’s also made an effort to change who gets heard in state government by launching California’s Women’s Wealth Advisory Council.  “I was tired of going into rooms where the majority of the men with access, the majority of the people with access to my husband were men, and a few women,” she said. “I wanted to expand exposure to government.”  A graduate of Stanford University and Stanford’s business school, Siebel Newsom is a documentary filmmaker whose work includes Miss Representation , The Mask You Live In and The Great American Lie . Her latest film, Miss Representation: Rise Up , expands on the original by looking at the backlash against women’s progress and technology used to harass and silence women. It premiered at the Tribeca Festival in June. She said it will premiere in New York City on Oct. 22. She and the governor have four children. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump’s new press secretary was asked where she passed the bar. Her answer raised more questions.
events.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia held her first press briefing Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing questions about her legal credentials. Her answer on Tuesday about where she passed the bar exam added to the confusion. Zacharia earned a law degree from Pepperdine University and has repeatedly called herself an attorney. Newly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as an attorney. The conservative commentator is now facing scrutiny about her legal qualifications after she was pressed to explain them following her first White House briefing with the media. As President Donald Trump spoke to reporters after the briefing on Tuesday, one asked him where Zacharia had passed the bar exam. "What state did she pass the bar exam in? You said she is an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" the reporter asked. Trump then turned to Zacharia, standing behind him, and asked, "Which state?" "When I moved to China," Zacharia answered. Her response added to the confusion over where she may be licensed to practice law in the United States. State bar exams are generally administered in person within the jurisdiction. In a statement, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials." She did not say if she'd passed the bar in any state. "Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," Steven Cheung, White House communications director, said. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary." Zacharia does not appear to be listed in the State Bar of California's attorney database, despite living and working in the state. She also does not appear to be listed in the D.C. Bar's member directory. The Substack publication, Popular Information, reported earlier on Tuesday that it searched records in all 50 states and Washington, DC, and turned up no evidence that Zacharia is licensed to practice law. President Trump on White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia: "I thought she was very good." Q: "You said she's an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" Zacharia: "When I moved to China." Q: "Where did you pass the bar exam?" https://t.co/5xiwyEsVSs — CSPAN (@cspan) October 13, 2026 Zacharia graduated from California's Pepperdine University in 2007 with a bachelor's degree in political science and government. She then received a law degree from the university's Caruso School of Law in 2011, according to the college. The White House said that after she graduated, Zacharia moved to China with her husband for his job at an American private equity firm. She worked on international transaction law, according to the White House. Her LinkedIn page says she served as general counsel for the California-based nonprofit Fix California from January 2024 to March 2025. More than a decade earlier, according to her LinkedIn, Zacharia worked as an associate at the Beijing-headquartered Zhong Lun Law Firm. Trump announced Zacharia's appointment to the White House in a Truth Social post last week, saying she has an "unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." He also referred to her as an attorney in the post. In her own post that followed, Zacharia called serving Trump and the American people the "honor of a lifetime." "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work for him for a very long time," Zacharia said during Tuesday's White House press briefing. events.title: MariBank courts younger customers with child accounts and global stock trading
events.summary: The idea for the child account was mooted by senior management and supported by findings from an internal survey, said MariBank’s head of consumer business Huo Haiyan. MariBank is launching child accounts and global stock trading targeting customers aged 16 to 28 to attract digitally savvy youth and promote financial literacy early. The bank removed its $100,000 deposit cap to improve customer experience and offers high-interest promotions, supported by a strong ShopeeVIP partnership driving deposit growth. MariBank is expanding beyond Sea's ecosystem, addressing underserved banking needs and aiming to build trust as a primary bank over time. SINGAPORE – Sea-owned MariBank is rolling out child accounts and global stock trading targeted at customers aged 16 to 28, as it looks to capture a growing base of digitally savvy youth. The idea for the child account was mooted by the digital bank’s senior management and supported by findings from an internal survey, said its head of consumer business Huo Haiyan. Speaking to The Straits Times at MariBank’s office in Rochester Commons, Huo said several members of the senior management team were heavy users of the bank’s products. One of them, for instance, wanted a more digital and convenient way to give his daughter an allowance, rather than handing her cash. Through an internal study involving parents, the bank found several common concerns, including how to manage children’s transactions and allowances, encourage saving, and build financial literacy from a young age. Targeted for launch i n the first quarter of 2027, the child account will let children make their own transactions within parent-set guardrails, with certain transactions, such as adding a debit card to a mobile wallet on a new device, requiring explicit parental approval. The bank, whose core user base is in its 20s and 30s, is also expanding its investment options to include US and global equities from early 2027. About 30 per cent of MariBank customers have a Mari Invest account, with one in four Mari Invest customers in their 20s – highlighting growing interest in investing among younger customers. Among the investment products it offers, the bank said it is seeing a steady upward trend in take-up for its Mari Invest Singapore Equities product. It declined to share specific adoption or customer numbers. Making investing simple, reliable and rewarding for younger customers who are highly comfortable managing their finances digitally is key, Huo noted. The bank is also no longer subject to an individual deposit cap, allowing it to compete more aggressively with traditional lenders for consumer savings. Mari Savings account holders can now deposit more than $100,000, according to a Reddit thread . MariBank confirmed it lifted the $100,000 individual deposit cap on its Mari Savings accounts in April to address user dissatisfaction and enhance the overall banking experience. Huo said that many users experienced inconvenience when their incoming transactions or payments could not be completed as their account balance had exceeded the cap. There were a few thousand such transactions being rejected monthly due to customers hitting their balance cap. With the cap removed, customers can benefit from MariBank’s high-interest promotions such as new user rates or ShopeeVIP bonuses reaching up to 2.88 per cent per annum. These apply directly to the customer’s full balance and there is no cap on the bonus interest that customers can earn. Huo said the ShopeeVIP partnership was the main driver of the bank’s deposit growth, with 18 per cent of MariBank users being ShopeeVIP users as well. MariBank’s customer deposits rose from $1.54 billion in 2024 to $2.82 billion by 2025. Within one month of the ShopeeVIP partnership launch in July, users who claimed the ShopeeVIP bonus interest rates doubled their balances . While Singapore tech giant Sea’ s ecosystem will remain one of MariBank’s most important and cost-efficient channels, Huo noted that there will always be “a ceiling and a limit”. Sea operates three core businesses through its digital entertainment arm Garena, e-commerce platform Shopee, and digital payments and financial services arm Monee, previously known as SeaMoney. Huo said: “We need to prepare ourselves to reach users outside the ecosystem. We are already trying to scale through other channels such as online marketing and referrals.” Efforts to leverage other channels have been successful, with more than 50 per cent of MariBank customers now coming from outside Shopee, up from the previous 50 per cent. Entering a mature, heavily banked market where consumers already had established banking relationships also presented a significant challenge. MariBank therefore focused on addressing underserved needs among retail consumers and businesses.

events.title: Sam’s Club CEO Latriece Watkins says she feels most powerful watching the people she’s invested in succeed
events.summary: Sam’s Club CEO Latriece Watkins has a career resume that most workers would gawk at, working her way up from an intern at Walmart all the way to leader of one of America’s biggest grocery retailers. But it isn’t the executive titles or career milestones that makes her feel powerful: The greatest source of power comes from watching the peers she’s helped ultimately succeed. “When I feel most powerful is when I see the people I’ve invested in make moves,” Watkins told Most Powerful Women Editor Emma Hinchliffe onstage at Fortune ’s annual MPW Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., on Tuesday. “When I see them get promoted, I see all of their faces running across memory from very early in my career, or very early in their careers, to where they’ve moved now.” Solely focusing on one’s own career could leave opportunities for greater impact on the table, according to the Fortune 500 executive. Watkins has made many strides in her own career, becoming the first woman and person of color to serve as Walmart’s chief merchant back in 2023—one of the most influential roles in retail. And in helping others along her three-decade career at the $890 billion parent company (Walmart), she’s leveraged a symbiotic strategy with her peers so that everyone succeeds. “The contributions we make are more than we could individually do,” she continued. “So power for me is the names of all the people that I can say who [have] benefited from my contributions, and I’ve benefited from being able to either contribute or get feedback from them.” Watkins said that despite being in the top role, business leaders will always need people—and finding the best way to shepherd them can be a challenge for busy executives. In her eight months as CEO, the 51-year-old has found that understanding the power of workers and delivering clarity are required in leadership. Employees will be looking to the top boss for transparency and a clear vision. To get that clarity, Watkins recommends setting aside time to think things through. “People look to you for clarity, which means you have to be clear. You don’t think out loud,” she said. “When you’re the leader, people want to know what you think, and if you haven’t cleared it up for yourself and you’re thinking out loud, you’ll confuse them.” “So take the time—make the time—to create clarity for yourself,” Watkins continued. “It’s one of the hardest things to find this time for yourself. But it’s required, because you can’t get clarity without it.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Character.AI owes Google and Big Law firms nearly $7M, court filings show
events.summary: Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Illustration by Algi Febri Sugita/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Character.AI owes Google and five major law firms nearly $7 million combined, bankruptcy filings show. The AI startup, founded by former Googlers, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection this week. It owes more than $10.6 million to its 20 largest unsecured creditors, court filings show. Court filings show that artificial intelligence startup Character.AI owes nearly $7 million in combined amounts to Google and a group of Big Law firms, shedding some light on the financial strain behind the chatbot's bankruptcy. Character.AI, which lets users create personalized AI bots, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in Delaware on Monday and plans to complete a court-supervised sale of the company by the end of the year. The AI platform's bankruptcy petition shows that it owes its 20 largest unsecured creditors more than $10.6 million, including over $4 million to Google and $2.6 million to a group of five prominent law firms. Hogan Lovells was owed the largest amount among the law firms, at about $2.1 million. White & Case was listed as being owed about $189,000, while the firms Munger, Tolles & Olson; Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom; and Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan were owed roughly $137,000, $126,000, and $64,000, respectively. Representatives for Google and the law firms did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The court filing does not detail the nature of the debts. However, Character.AI, founded by former Google researchers, named Google Cloud its preferred cloud infrastructure in 2023. The startup has also faced a wave of lawsuits alleging its chatbots harmed or encouraged harmful behavior among young users. Character.AI agreed to settle multiple lawsuits earlier this year. The AI company's bankruptcy filings suggest that those legal troubles were part of a broader financial squeeze. Character.AI's bankruptcy petition estimated assets worth $50 million to $100 million and estimated liabilities in the same range. "The burgeoning and evolving field of AI entertainment, however, has proven to be costly to develop and grow," a filing in the case reads. "These high costs, coupled with potential litigation related liabilities and regulatory engagement have contributed to the Debtor's inability to generate sufficient cash flows to support its business in the present form." A Character.AI spokesperson told Business Insider that over the past year, the startup has "taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds." events.title: Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
events.summary: Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee. Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product. Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say. On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said. OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier". According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment. Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'". The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene. That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said. Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation. If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000). events.summary: Topgolf’s VMware costs were going to increase by 400 percent under Broadcom. events.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer after surgery to remove part of lung
events.summary: The 71-year-old is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung. Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican. Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment. list 1 of 3 Pope Leo says AI risk concerns not ‘fake news’ list 2 of 3 Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution list 3 of 3 Pope Leo continues working after lung surgery announcement In a statement released Tuesday, the Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”. The 71-year-old has returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled. The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests. The Holy See’s press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer. Before the procedure, Leo waved to dozens of well-wishers gathered at the hospital’s main entrance. In an unusually transparent update on papal health, Leo first revealed that doctors found a small nodule during his Sunday noon prayer in St Peter’s Square. “The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it,” he said during remarks delivered in Italian. The pope has no reported history of serious illness and is considered physically active, routinely swimming and playing tennis. The surgery comes ahead of an official Latin America tour scheduled for November 6-17, with stops planned across Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is unclear whether his recovery will affect the ambitious itinerary, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and significant altitude changes in Peru. The pope told reporters on Sunday that he intends to make the journey.

Atletico Madrid eased to a 2-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League on Tuesday to pile pressure on Red Devils coach Michael Carrick. Pablo Barrios pounced inside the first minute for Diego Simeone’s side and after Leny Yoro’s 74th minute red card set United back further, Ademola Lookman added another for the hosts in Madrid. list 1 of 4 Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa list 2 of 4 Michael Jordan’s ‘Last Dance’ NBA Finals jersey sells for record $14m list 3 of 4 Canelo Alvarez ‘will fight in Riyadh’ despite Saudi airport attacks list 4 of 4 Verstappen wins chaotic Singapore GP F1 sprint after Russell crashes Man United have made their worst domestic start in 40 years and this league phase defeat in the Spanish capital was another blow, with the team now winless in five games across all competitions. Carrick handed Carlos Baleba his first start for the club since arriving from Brighton this summer, as well as pushing captain Bruno Fernandes out to the right side. Atletico were without their skipper Koke, after the death of his mother, while coach Simeone selected Julian Alvarez from the off for the first time this season at the Metropolitano stadium, after he tried to force a departure this summer. “Defend what we love,” Atletico fans ordered their supporters with a banner display before kick-off. The Rojiblancos were ahead after just 50 seconds. Alex Baena found a way in behind United’s defence and cut the ball across for Barrios, with Ayden Heaven unable to keep the midfielder’s shot from crossing the line. Bryan Mbuemo might have equalised for the visitors, nudging the ball through Cristian Romero’s legs but firing just wide. Alejandro Grimaldo came inches away from extending Atletico’s lead with a free-kick which hit the angle between post and crossbar. The hosts thought they had a second when Johnny Cardoso finished neatly from the edge of the box before half-time but the goal was disallowed after a VAR review showed the ball had struck Marcos Llorente’s hand during the build-up. Alvarez, yet to score this season for Atletico, hit the post early in the second half. United rallied and Fernandes’s lob drifted narrowly wide before the Portuguese playmaker hit the crossbar from the left of the box after a corner routine. However, the three-time European champions suffered a setback when defender Yoro was harshly dismissed after a VAR review for bringing down Canada striker Jonathan David as the last man. It opened the door for Atletico to grab their second, with David foiled by goalkeeper Senne Lammens but London-born Nigeria international Lookman on hand to tuck home the rebound after 79 minutes. Carrick withdrew playmaker Fernandes, looking ahead to the weekend visit to face rivals Leeds in the English top flight, where improvement is badly needed. Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak saved from United substitute Matheus Cunha in the final stages but there was no way back for United. Simeone’s side were able to claim their first points after an opening defeat at Liverpool.

events.title: They're vital community hubs, but regional post offices face uncertain futures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Concerns for future of regional post offices laid out in Senate inquiry Topic: Postal and Delivery Services Tarpeena resident Shirley Little's mother used to run the town's post office. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) An inquiry into Australia Post's retail network has highlighted the challenges facing licensed post offices (LPOs) around the country. LPOs make up about two-thirds of the network, but Australia Post says almost 40 per cent of licensees plan to exit within three years. The committee's report is due to be released on October 22. Advocates say small-town post offices need to be kept alive as aging licensees and changing community needs threaten their future. A Senate inquiry is underway into Australia Post's retail network that will look into, among other factors, the role licensed post offices (LPOs) play "in delivering community services". An inquiry into Australia Post's retail network will report back this month. ( ABC News ) But in Tarpeena, in South Australia's south-east, locals already know what losing the local post office can mean. In 2022, the LPO running out of the local pub, the Pines Hotel, was closed, leaving the closest post office 20 kilometres away. Long-time postie Shirley Little's mother owned and managed the LPO for more than four decades, back when it operated alongside the local general store. Shirley Little at Tarpeena's post office in 2015. ( Danielle Grindlay ) "I think when the post office did eventually close down, the older people missed it because it was somewhere they could go every day and someone would say hello to them," she said. About two-thirds of the Australia Post network is made up of LPOs, with about 2,900 operating across the country. Unlike general post offices, which are run by Australia Post, LPOs are run by licensees either as a standalone post office or alongside another business. The peak body representing LPO licensees, LPO Group, said other post office services, such as banking, were being "run down" as focus shifted towards parcel services. LPOs make up two-thirds of Australia Post's retail network. ( ABC Pilbara: Louise Miolin ) "When you're in the rural and regional parts of Australia, that's one of the most important businesses in your town," LPO Group chair Scott Etherington said. Pines Hotel licensee Lynton Cram said after the post office moved into the hotel, it failed to attract business. Pines Hotel licensee Lynton Cram ran Tarpeena's post office for a few years. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) "During the week I had very little business, apart from delivering the mail and sorting it," he said. "As far as doing any other transactions like parcels or cash transactions, it was very minimal." In its submission to the inquiry, Australia Post said it faced growing challenges in the regions, including declining foot traffic, increasing costs and a lack of workers. It said 38 per cent of LPO owners were aged 60 or older, and 39 per cent in non-major cities intended to exit the network within three years. The post office in Tarpeena closed in 2022. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) An Australia Post spokesperson said it had been engaging with the inquiry, and would review and consider the committee's report. "We have expanded how and where customers can access our services. "We've done this by adding self-service options like parcel lockers, which are in addition to our reported retail outlets. These services complement post offices, not replace them." Australia Post says it's committed to continuing to serve regional communities. ( ABC Radio Brisbane: Anna Levy ) The spokesperson said Australia Post had paid $635 million in commissions to licensees in the previous financial year, and that those payments had increased each year for the past 15 years. "For the past two years, we have been engaging with licensees and their representative associations to update the current LPO model, which is more than 30 years old," they said. More than 140 published submissions have been made to the inquiry, with the committee's report due on October 22.

events.title: ‘We talk ourselves out of it’: Entrepreneur Emma Grede never second-guesses herself
events.summary: Entrepreneur Emma Grede attributed her ability to keep brands relevant to her complete assuredness in her intuition, which was honed in the expanses of her triumphs—and failures. “I don’t second-guess myself,” she said at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara on Tuesday. “I think a lot of us have that skill, but we talk ourselves out of it, and we second-guess ourselves a lot. One of the most expensive habits that we have as women is waiting until we’re ready.” Grede told Most Powerful Women editorial director Ellie Austin that she has fine-tuned the ability to try something out and has failed so many times that “it stopped mattering” and doesn’t hold her back. The 44-year-old entrepreneur, who was raised by a single mother in East London and never went to college, is the cofounder and chief product officer of $5 billion shapewear company Skims , as well as an investor and fashion designer, most recently founding Off Season, a luxury sports-fashion brand, alongside designer Kristin Juszczyk. Grede’s intuition is what led Skims to release a series of unexpected products, including a push-up bra with a raised nipple detail. Initially seen as provocative, the bra actually serves the purpose of affirming women who have gotten breast reconstruction surgery after a mastectomy, Grede said. While some products like black thongs are meant to meet a demand for the many women who don’t possess one, others, like a face sculpt wrap, are meant to create, occupy, and own a new market. “One of my special sauces is to go in and say, ‘Well, how do you take a problem that exists within this and make it make sense for a new generation of customers?’” Grede said. “So much of what I do is not brain surgery,” she added. “It’s about making things 1% better. It’s about taking existing markets, but really paying attention and really being focused on the excellence of products.” Grede has worked to share her insights with other women, including in her book Start With Yourself: A New Vision for Work & Life , warning that too much advice to other women is feel-good, rather than practical and effective. “What I’m not doing is trying to make people feel comfortable,” she said. “I’m talking about the reality of what I do, and so I actually think that so much of what’s out there, specifically in women’s media, is to make women feel better.  “And I’m interested in that because I’m a results-oriented person. I’m an operator, and so I talk about the truth and the quality it is to operate in my life. I’ve never been shy about saying this is what I had to do. These are the sacrifices that I had to make. These are the tradeoffs in my life. These are the things that I don’t do.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn over claimed sanctions breaches
events.summary: Bank of America was ordered to pay more than $1.2 billion in fines after the Treasury Department said the company breached anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, the agency said on Tuesday. The Treasury Department said the fine is the third-largest in its history. Bank of America was also ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comprotroller of the Currency, the largest ever issued by the OCC. The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over 475 “apparent violations” of sanctions against “ Russia , Belarus, Iran , Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism”. Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US, with more than 70 million clients, and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for customers every year. It enables more than $450 trillion of payments in employee payrolls, supplier payments and corporate credit cards. It also processes an average of $1.9 trillion in wire transfers a day globally for clients. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire us financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law." The Treasury Department said Bank of America admitted it wilfully breached the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to assist the Treasury in detecting and preventing money laundering. The department said the US bank failed to report to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with more than $1 billion implicating national security and other risks pointing to Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and other activity “with a substantial nexus to the south-west border”. The OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against the bank in 2024 over deficiencies related to its Bank Secrecy Act and compliance programmes. “The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable,” said Jonathan Gould, Comproller of the Currency. Tuesday's fine followed an action from the OCC last week, in which American Express was fined $350 million after its compliance programme allowed about $13 billion in suspected money laundering activity to go undetected for more than a decade. Bank of America is due to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday.

events.title: Six Flags shares decline following deadly roller coaster incident
events.summary: One person died and several others were injured in the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia, according to the Cobb County government. One person died and several others were injured Monday in an incident at Six Flags Over Georgia, according to a statement from Georgia's Cobb County Board of Commissioners. The board's chairwoman, Lisa N. Cupid, said that county authorities are working with Six Flags and other partners in the investigation. According to reports citing local police, the incident occurred on the Atlanta-area park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster shortly before 4 p.m. Monday. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, according to the report. Witnesses told a local news station that they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. A park spokesperson for Six Flags Over Georgia told CNBC that the park team is cooperating with local authorities and providing support to those affected by the tragedy, and that Six Flags Entertainment is temporarily closing Georgia's Goliath and nine other similar attractions at its parks. "We were deeply saddened by the guest incident at one of our parks yesterday. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones," the spokesperson said. Tuesday's decline was the stock's worst day since August and puts shares at their lowest level since December 2009. At the close, shares had fallen by more than 50% over the past year.

events.title: US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
events.summary: The fines amount to the third-largest amount in Treasury Department history. WASHINGTON -- The U.S. Treasury Department said Tuesday that it’s imposing $1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The fines on America’s second-biggest bank amount to the third-largest in the department’s history. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.” Treasury said Bank of America also reached an $11.6 million settlement with the department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control over “apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism." In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed the $1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.'' The penalty includes $750 million that will go to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by that federal bank regulatory agency. Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated'' the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,’’ Bank of America said in a statement. “We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 (Comptroller of the Currency) Consent Order and FinCEN’s investigation. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says “ We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.’’ The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly $4 billion settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an approximately $3 billion settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year. Both those historic actions happened as part of the Biden administration’s focus on anti-money laundering and efforts to promote compliance with the then-emerging virtual currency industry. Months later, Binance founder and CEO Changpeng Zhao, was sentenced to four months in prison over charges that he looking the other way as criminals used his platform to move money connected to child sex abuse, drug trafficking and terrorism. events.title: Nasdaq ends lower as chipmakers fall and bank earnings roll in
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City. The Nasdaq ended lower on Oct 13 as chip stocks added to recent losses The Nasdaq ended lower on Oct 13, as chip stocks added to recent losses and investors parsed mixed quarterly results from Citigroup and other big US banks. The PHLX chip index fell 0.23%, down for a fifth straight session, after Broadcom CEO Hock ‌Tan on Oct 12 likened some of the investment flow into the sector to “casino gambling.” Additionally, reports of technological advances by Chinese memory chip company CXMT underscored concerns about rising competition. Micron Technology lost 3.6% and Applied Materials dropped almost 7%. Broadcom rose 0.7%. Citigroup dipped 5.6% and Goldman Sachs lost 0.2% after both banks topped profit estimates. Wells Fargo fell 3.1% after its net interest income missed estimates, while JPMorgan Chase ended down 0.9% following a rare profit miss. Apple hit an intraday record high of US$348.15 (S$444) before closing up 0.1% at US$341.27, putting its stock market value at US$4.98 trillion. Analysts on average see S&P 500 third-quarter earnings surging over 30%, fuelled largely by AI-related technology companies, according to LSEG data. Expectations of a strong earnings season have offset worries about the US war with Iran, surging bond yields and inflation related to high oil prices. “A lot of investors are feeling a sense of relief that markets might start looking at earnings and less at the bond market, less at higher-for-longer oil prices and less at high interest rates,” said Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The S&P 500 declined 0.02% to end the session at 7,805.45 points. The Nasdaq declined 0.15% to 27,204.38 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.35% to 51,670.10 points. The S&P 500 has rallied 14% in 2026, lifted by AI-related technology stocks. However, the median stock in the index is up less than 5% and over 200 S&P 500 components are down for the year. Reflecting expectations of strong corporate earnings from AI heavyweights, the S&P 500 is trading at under 19 times expected earnings, its lowest since 2023. The PHLX chip index has lost more than 8% in the past five sessions and it remains up over 70% year-to-date. The S&P 500 healthcare index fell 1.3% on Oct 13, with Johnson & Johnson down 5.7% despite topping profit estimates. Bumble jumped almost 57% after the dating-app operator agreed to go private in a US$1.3 billion deal. Domino’s Pizza declined 4.8% after scaling back its full-year sales outlook. Advancing issues outnumbered falling ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.1-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 18 new highs and five new lows; the Nasdaq recorded 47 new highs and 408 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was relatively light, with 14.8 billion shares traded, compared with an average of 17.6 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions. REUTERS

events.title: Judge says Musk engaged in intimidation of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans, clears her name
events.summary: Ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans' name was cleared by a federal magistrate judge after Elon Musk and other government officials falsely accused her of criminal actions in 2025. President Trump fired Comans after Musk accused her of diverting millions of dollars to house undocumented immigrants in New York hotels. The judge found that Musk and other officials engaged in "state sanctioned intimidation" of Comans, "while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action.'" A federal magistrate judge in Virginia ruled that Elon Musk engaged in "state sanctioned intimidation" of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans when he posted falsehoods on X last year accusing her of "criminal action" and of "funneling $58 million to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan." Musk, the world's richest person, was working for the Trump administration as the head of DOGE when he shared those posts on Feb. 11, 2025. The Department of Homeland Security said the next day it was firing Comans and three colleagues, and labeled them "deep state activists." In Tuesday's order, U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cleared Comans' name. Comans served as FEMA CFO from around January 2018 until February 2025, and was also FEMA's operating chief from 2020 to 2021. Fitzpatrick wrote in the order that, "The facts establish that high-ranking government officials," including Musk, then a special government employee, had "engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans." "Mr. Musk was the head of DOGE, he knew or should have known that any payments made to state or local governments through a FEMA grant in February 2025 were approved by his subordinates," the judge wrote. He added that Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans "to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action,'" an act Fitzpatrick described as "little more than state sanctioned intimidation." CNBC has reached out to Musk and White House attorneys involved in the case for comment. Democracy Defenders Fund, which was involved in Comans' case, said in a statement that it was pleased with the decision. "Mary Comans served in the federal government for 21 years," said Craig Becker, the group's head of affirmative litigation. "Career public servants are people, not pawns, and no one who has devoted their life to serving the American public should have their good name destroyed for partisan, political gain." events.title: Helix Carbon says it can make iron cheaper by recycling blast furnace pollution
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The iron and steel industries are among the biggest polluters in the world. Plenty of startups have tried to cut the industry’s emissions, mostly by developing new ways to make the metals. Helix Carbon thinks those startups have been going about it all wrong. “Any attempt to decarbonize the steel industry without dealing with the blast furnace is not going to work,” David Brown, Helix Carbon’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. A blast furnace is the giant furnace that turns iron ore into the iron used to make steel. Rather than replace blast furnaces, Helix wants to clean them up. Its approach promises to slash the steel industry’s carbon emissions while boosting profit margins for iron producers, a rare win-win for a dirty industrial process. Blast furnaces have made iron for centuries, using coke, a processed form of coal, to help turn raw iron ore (iron bound up with oxygen) into metallic iron. The burning coke supplies heat for the reaction but doesn’t take part in it directly. Instead, carbon monoxide produced from the combustion does the work of reducing the iron, meaning stripping away its oxygen atoms. The process releases tremendous amounts of carbon dioxide, or CO 2 , which is normally dumped straight into the atmosphere. But Helix Carbon has devised a way to turn that waste carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and recycle it back into the blast furnace. Helix Carbon’s process relies on an electrolyzer, a device that uses electricity and a catalyst to break off an oxygen atom from the carbon dioxide. Electrolyzers aren’t new, but Brown said the startup’s design can handle the entire exhaust stream from the blast furnace. Most electrolyzers are too delicate for raw exhaust like that. They work only on purified, concentrated carbon dioxide, so the exhaust typically has to be processed before they can use it. By injecting carbon monoxide into a blast furnace, iron producers can use less coke. How much, exactly, is still debated, Brown said. Some scientific papers suggest as much as 90% of the coke can be eliminated, while other studies suggest it’s more like 30% to 40%. Helix Carbon is proposing that iron producers start by replacing 33% of their coke. The company says using its technology to do so would save them $14 per ton of iron. “That may not seem like a lot, but margins in the iron industry are famously thin,” Brown said. The iron and steel industries are a combined $2 trillion market, according to Grand View Research , which makes the sector an appealing target for a young startup to chase. But it also moves slowly, in part because its equipment lasts so long. “There are blast furnaces that have lived for over 100 years,” Brown said. To bring in revenue earlier, Helix Carbon plans to court the specialty chemicals industry first. “We don’t need to capture the CO 2 first,” Brown said. “We just utilize it, and that opens up the door of making chemicals on-site right out of waste streams.” Helix Carbon presented live onstage on Tuesday in the Startup Battlefield pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, taking place this week from October 13-15. Join us this week to watch as the rest of Startup Battlefield unfolds. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: My friends suggested a GLP-1 for my weight gain. I found my answer on the dance floor.
events.summary: The author (not pictured) said dance has reinvigorated her fitness routine. FG Trade Latin/Getty Images I was working out six days a week but still gaining weight. People urged me to try a GLP-1, but I my doctor said I didn't meet the requirements. I started incorporating dance classes into my routine and the weight started to come off. I'm petite, have a small frame, and have never had to struggle with weight issues . I regularly went to the gym six days a week, and have done so for years taking a combination of strength training and boot camp-style classes in addition to walking. Despite my efforts, I started adding on weight — just over 10 pounds in about 24 months. I didn't know why or what to do about about the weight gain. I was working out almost every day, but I felt exhausted and defeated. Others suggested I turn to medication. "Don't stress, just get on a GLP-1 , and if your doctor won't give it to you, just grab it online," one friend told me. My BMI wasn't high enough for my doctor to prescribe medication , and I didn't want to override my provider's advice. But despite all of my effort, I wasn't seeing the results I wanted. The author said she started getting bored and the gym and washing pushing herself. She returned to dance, which she loved as a child, and transformed her mind and body. Courtesy of Leslie Vooris. I was bored at the gym Then, during a gym class , I realized I had become lazy. I was picking up the easiest weights and would go through the motions, never pushing myself too hard during workouts. The repetitive movements were just so boring. After that class, I tried to think of an activity that might bring me more joy. Wasn't there something else that could be more fun? That's when I decided to take more dance classes , instead of just the one I was already taking on Saturdays. I was hesitant to dance like I used to years ago I was a danced into high school, but I had to leave the program because of difficulties at home. The author, second from left, said she enjoys the sense of community that comes from dancing. Courtesy of Leslie Vooris. I always felt sadness and disappointment about quitting. I had continued dancing on and off as an adult, but I had never really returned to it in a meaningful way. I thought about how much I loved to dance as a little girl, grinning ear to ear even when I forgot all the steps. Research has shown that the surprising benefits of dance extend beyond physical fitness . Now I take four to five dance classes a week, a combination of modern, and West African. It's fun and doesn't feel like the same drag that the gym was to me. And I finally lost those stubborn pounds I had gained. When I take classes every week, I mix up levels to keep challenging myself and track my progress. Dance has also given me a community where we hold one another accountable and empower one another as we cheer one another on. Dance was the true exercise I really needed Returning to dance has helped me shed those few extra pounds, but it has also helped me connect to a part of me that is more accepting of myself and others. I'm happier and healthier than I've been in years, and no longer associate something I love with failure. I've learned that the workout that keeps me coming back is the one I enjoy, and it's never too late to try again. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering allegations
events.summary: The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for years of failures to report suspicious transactions and address shortcomings in its anti-money-laundering program. Why it matters: The action includes the third-largest penalty in Treasury history. What they're saying: "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release . The big picture: The civil action comes less than a week after federal regulators fined American Express $350 million over similar failures to detect and report suspected money laundering. Zoom in: Bank of America admitted to willfully violating federal anti-money-laundering laws — including requirements to maintain adequate safeguards and report suspicious transactions. Regulators said the bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in more than $5 billion in suspicious activity that was either unreported or reported late. More than $1 billion involved potential national security and other high-priority risks — including Chinese money-laundering networks and suspected trade-based money laundering linked to the U.S.-Mexico border, regulators said. Of note: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency also assessed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the agency's history. Treasury also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over hundreds of apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, including those targeting Russia and Iran. Flashback: Bank of America has been working to address deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering program since a December 2024 regulatory order. But regulators said significant problems persisted. Officials said the bank prioritized revenue while limiting compliance resources — at times relying on law enforcement and other outside sources to identify suspicious activity. The other side: In a statement, Bank of America said it has invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to fighting financial crime. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators." What to watch: Bank of America reports third-quarter earnings Wednesday. The bank said it will record a $1.2 billion, non-tax-deductible charge in those results. The bank said costs associated with its ongoing efforts to fix compliance problems are already reflected in its expenses. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

events.title: Anthropic to disclose new revenue numbers as AI lab financials become central to tech trade
events.summary: Anthropic will release updated financials to a group of institutional investors gathering at its headquarters this week, according to sources familiar with the matter. The disclosure comes as the AI giant prepares for what could be the largest IPO in history. Last week, confusion around a report detailing OpenAI's revenue and updated accounting dragged down major semiconductor stocks and the broader Nasdaq. Anthropic plans to disclose its third-quarter financials for the first time at a meeting with potential investors on Wednesday as the artificial intelligence giant prepares for what could be the largest initial public offering in history. San Francisco-based Anthropic will release the numbers to a group of institutional investors, according to two people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. Bloomberg first reported that the meeting was happening. Anthropic declined to comment. The meeting comes as revenue numbers from the private AI giants have proven to have an outsized impact on broader markets. Last week, confusion around a report detailing OpenAI 's revenue and updated accounting dragged down major semiconductor stocks and the broader Nasdaq. OpenAI shared an updated revenue number of $50 billion with current investors as part of an ongoing fundraise , which was lower than the $70 billion that had been widely reported. The updated number stripped out revenue from cloud partners, and wasn't an indication of changing demand, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal information. It's unclear if Anthropic will account for sales in the same manner and include partner revenue, but the numbers this week will give investors a more accurate snapshot of Anthropic's growth and profitability as they look to value the company ahead of an IPO. It will also help Anthropic senior executives and bankers gauge investor interest and weigh the reaction to these updated financials. AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI Anthropic is plowing ahead with what could be a $2 trillion listing based on its latest reported revenue numbers, which could top $100 billion by the end of this year, according to people familiar with the plans. That valuation would put it ahead of SpaceX 's historic debut. Anthropic filed confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this year but has not made its S-1 financials public. The company will list in November, according to Reuters, but people familiar with the plans could not confirm a listing date. If it does go ahead, Anthropic will also be listing at a time when climbing interest rates are shaking parts of the AI trade. Comments from Broadcom CEO Hock Tan this week further rattled AI names. Tan said at a conference on Monday that with rates climbing, access to capital could be the biggest constraint on AI companies. Chip stocks were lower Tuesday, extending an overnight sell-off sparked by worries over the durability of AI financing. Market conditions are one of the biggest factors in Anthropic's upcoming IPO, and bankers are closely watching investor appetite for growth and AI stocks.

The company said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to understand the “sophisticated” device. OpenAI told TechCrunch that the device contained “advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring,” though it is unclear to what degree this device is technically distinct from other recording devices. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” said OpenAI in its post on X. OpenAI’s spokesperson, Nate Evans, confirmed that the employee started with the AI model maker in July 2025 and worked on the product team. Prosecutors with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California said Alfozan was charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications — effectively accusing him of covertly recording people’s voice audio without their permission. Prosecutors said OpenAI caught the device after it was inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in OpenAI’s San Francisco office. Per the prosecutors, Alfozan was caught looking behind the television where the recording device was placed, and where OpenAI had placed a camera that allegedly caught the employee. It’s not clear exactly for what purpose the recording device was used, but FBI director Kash Patel said the scheme was to “capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology.” Neither Alfozan nor his attorney could be immediately reached for comment. He faces five years in prison if convicted. When reached, a spokesperson for the FBI reiterated a statement made by Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel said. events.title: After 20 years at IBM, I changed careers and started a side gig. Now it's a 7-figure company — here’s how I grew it.
events.summary: Becky DeGrossa spent 20 years in Big Tech before opening her business, CounselingWise. Matthew DeFeo for BI Becky DeGrossa, 66, worked at IBM and then became a therapist before opening CounselingWise. The service helps therapists market their businesses through custom websites, SEO, and Google Ads. She works with 40 to 50 contractors who have great people skills, which has helped her scale. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Becky DeGrossa, a 66-year-old who is founder of CounselingWise from Boulder, Colorado. It's been edited for length and clarity. I earned a degree in computer science from Cal Poly and then spent 20 years in total at IBM , leaving the company in 2003. When I left, I was a consultant and managing principal, and I was supposed to be leading the team up the hill — but I just really wasn't passionate about it at all anymore. I spent a year thinking, "I'm going to go do something else. I've been here forever. What do I know how to do? What do I like doing?" When I thought about what I liked about my Big Tech job, it was being a manager. The most meaningful part of my job was meeting one-on-one with employees to help them out with a problem or coach them along. I'd also been in therapy and had found it extremely helpful, so I thought I'd change careers to become a therapist . I earned a Master's degree in psychology from 2003 to 2006 and then worked as a practicing therapist. While doing this, I started a side gig from my therapy office, organizing little groups of therapists to show them what they needed to do to create their own Google business profile and promote their website. This was the beginning of what became my marketing agency CounselingWise, which helps therapists get found by clients through these services as well as custom websites, SEO, and Google Ads. As I spent more and more time on my business, I didn't have time to be a therapist and build my business. So I closed my therapy practice four years after I started it to pursue my business full time, combining my technical, marketing, and psychology backgrounds. DeGrossa said the most meaningful part of her tech career was meeting with employees to help them out with a problem or coach them along. Matthew DeFeo for BI It was hard to stop my therapy practice — I felt honored to walk alongside my clients through some very difficult things in their lives, and I didn't take leaving lightly. I stopped taking new clients right away, but I gave my existing clients six months' notice. We've been a seven-figure company since 2022 and hit $2 million in June 2026. The business has made approximately $300,000 in profit each year for the past five years. About 99% of our revenue is generated from done-for-you services, including content writing, website development, Google business profile optimization, and Google Ads. Here are the key strategies that helped me build it. 1. I helped people do what they didn't want to do themselves When I started working as a therapist , it took me a while to figure out how to make my website visible. I thought it'd be easy to just put up a business site and get my phone to ring, but I found that Google's local algorithm was actually a specific way of marketing I knew nothing about. So I took classes to learn search engine optimization (SEO) and content writing. I first took a course in copywriting, then learned about ranking in Google Places, and later learned about on-page SEO. Once I started implementing what I learned in these classes for my own website, my phone started ringing. At that time, all my friends were therapists since we went to school together, so I started teaching a class to other therapists about online marketing strategies . I held the classes in my therapy office. We brought in chairs and sat in a circle and I taught them what I was doing with my website. She learned about SEO and content writing before launching her business. Matthew DeFeo for BI I thought they'd do it themselves once I taught them, but most of them didn't feel technical enough or like they were good enough writers, and I realized there was a demand for these services. It was literally one step at a time, realizing, "Oh, people don't want to do this — I could do it for them." 2. I systematized what I learned What helped my business's growth was putting my time equally into learning the technical side, and then focusing on management and systematizing techniques to scale. I learned that in a small nimble market like mine, when I find a good idea, I test it out a number of times to see if it works, and then I systematize it and hire people to do it. And then I go back around — wash rinse, repeat — to find the next hopeful thing that I can test. So I have a little business development team that does all this testing on SEO techniques to become visible in Google and AI search. This consists of on-page optimizations to the website, off-page link-building, and optimizations of Google business profiles. If a particular SEO technique works, then we systematize it, scale it, and roll it out. We're constantly changing our strategy to stay up to date. One example of testing a new idea happened in May 2024, when a major Google Search documentation leak occurred. Based on that documentation and our testing, we added schema to our home and specialty pages. We tested this with several of our clients and it helped them rank better, so we rolled it out as a new part of our strategy. 3. I created a culture where my team cares about my clients. The other part of management I focus on is creating a culture where my team — which fluctuates between 40 to 50 contractors who I pay hourly rates depending on their role and experience level — cares about my clients. In my world, our clients are therapists who are extremely sensitive to human interactions, so we don't just hire smart people who can crank out code. "Our clients are therapists who are extremely sensitive to human interactions, so we don't just hire smart people who can crank out code," she says. Matthew DeFeo for BI We hire project managers, for instance, who have very good people skills. They can work alongside a non-technical client to reassure them the whole way that we have their best interest at heart, and we're going to represent them well on their website. Because of my management experience in corporate, I have a perspective of what it takes to be able to build a really good reputation as a therapist . So I insist on this whole client care piece for our clients, because they do wonderful work in the world, and I want to take care of them. The key is making sure that my technical strategy and systematizing go hand-in-hand with client care, to make sure we take care of our clients in the process and make them feel held by us. Those are the three legs of the stool that have allowed us to continue to grow. Subscribe to the Small Business Insider newsletter . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds
events.summary: Many investors are turning to inflation-linked bonds amid concerns over rising prices. TIPS are offering high yields, but investors need to keep an eye on total returns. Commodities, infrastructure and gold are among the other assets investors are turning to for inflation protection. Inflation will be in the crosshairs Wednesday as investors digest the latest Consumer Price Index. The reading may be one more sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away. It's a tricky situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to get it. Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) are one option with "real" yields now at multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices. While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022 — a supply shock due to the Covid pandemic — it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The headline Consumer Price Index is expected to hit 3.6% in September, partly due to rising energy costs stemming from the war with Iran. The Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, was at a 3% core rate in August. Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023. Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF , which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date. Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising interest rates — with the 10-year Treasury note recently hitting multi-year highs around 5.3%. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered. But rising yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS yield is currently at 2.87%, after closing at 2.951% on Oct. 5, levels not seen since November 2008, according to Tradeweb. "Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management. TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag. The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries. TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing). If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case. "TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained. TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said. The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower. One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance. If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures. Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow. "While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added. Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF , iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF . TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go.

events.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar under investigation by Jeanine Pirro's office
events.summary: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home. The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked." Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which her office said cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well." "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe. Catch up quick: Federal agents searched Omar's home before dawn Monday as part of a separate immigration probe, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reported. Omar described the search in an X post as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." Trump has repeatedly lashed out against Somali immigrants, including Omar — who he described in a post last year as "always wrapped in her swaddling hijab" and "the worst 'Congressman/woman'" in our Country." Zoom out: Omar's office pointed Axios to The Wall Street Journal's reporting last month that the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss allegations that she possibly violated House rules or law by reporting false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures. A disclosure filed last year listed Omar and her husband's assets as ranging from $6 million to $30 million. She later amended the form to reflect a much lower range, the Journal first reported, citing what her team said were accounting errors. Pirro's office did not respond to Axios's request for comment. What they're saying: After Pirro's appearance on Fox News, Trump shared a post on Truth Social suggesting, without evidence, that Omar benefited from fraud in Minnesota .
