events.title: I know my mom is getting older. Seeing it is different from knowing it.
events.summary: The author has lived abroad half her life. Courtesy of the author I've lived about half of my adult life either overseas or traveling. It's been more than 13 years since we've lived on the same continent. My perspective on our relationship and the one with my own daughter is shifting in real time. Time is a funny thing, mostly because it's a construct, but it has a way of forcing people to see things differently, even when they might not want to. I hadn't spent long stretches of time with my mom until her recent visit. After she left, I began to reflect on how the years — and distance — have changed us both. The picture I have of her has stayed mostly the same over the years, but this visit shifted something: I'm now more aware of her aging , and of my own. I'm seeing her for who she is It's hard to see your parents one way as a child and then realize, as an adult, that that impression of them was based solely on a child's perspective and only knowing them relationally as a parent, not fully knowing them as an adult from an adult's perspective. The relationship I had with her as a child and teen may be long gone, and the relationship I have with her now has evolved beyond anything my youthful perspective could have imagined. During this most recent visit, I feel like I'm finally seeing the truest version of her from a healed, adult perspective. She's human. I'm human. We all just have to figure out how we relate to one another and engage in one another's lives. I'm in my hinge generation years The phase of life where I am right now as a millennial has sometimes been referred to as the sandwich generation , but I recently read something about it also being called the hinge generation. I'm approaching this thing called "middle age," and I'm reluctant to identify as such. I'm old enough to have aging parents and be a parent myself, but still young enough that middle age simply sounds like a historical time period. Watching my mother's age become more apparent — both as her child and as a parent myself — has me contemplating the reality of standing in the middle as part of the hinge generation . Seeing her differently has also made me profoundly aware that my own daughter is old enough to perceive me differently from how she saw me as a toddler and young child. I'm less infallible and more easily able to be critiqued, as my human nature is more visible to her developing mind. What does this mean for my own daughter, who's watching me age? How does she feel about our relationship, even in her first decade of life? She may be young, but I vividly remember being that age and even recall what I thought about my mom. While I don't know exactly how my daughter sees me, I have to remember that she is her own person, with her own views and perspectives shaped by everything in her life. While my relationship with my mother may never change from what it is now, the memories I have of it from childhood have at least influenced me as a mom. I want to keep the lines of communication open with my daughter and show up — for both her and my son — with emotional availability and empathy." I see myself in my mom and also my daughter Wherever we are in the "line" of time, we can remember all the places we've already been, ages, and experiences survived. We can look at all the people around us and see them as children who have grown up with diverse experiences that have brought them to their current state and status. The author sees herself both in her mom and in her daughter. Courtesy of the author Human beings will never be perfect. Neither will any type of relationship — familial, romantic, friendship, or otherwise. Time changes people, and time changes perspectives. Where we find ourselves in our thoughts and between relationships is only a transitive place, one that is forever changing as we shift across space and time into the future. Who we will be is shaped by our self-talk and how we see ourselves, and further formed by time and life experiences. How we treat ourselves and others actively plays a role in how relationships develop and end — or how they develop and thrive. Looking 30 years into my future, I see both my mom and myself; looking 30 years back, I see myself and my daughter. We're a connected line of women and lives that have interrelated and interdependent on one another. And each new moment of each new day will shape the mutual direction, depth, and desire to continue onwards. As I like to tell my children: They are the final arbiters in their lives, and they can build their reality — and relationships — through their thoughts, behaviors, and actions. What we each build is up to us. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts
events.summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of rogue agents operating at scale and said the bank is building defensive tools. The bank is piloting Smart Cash, an internal tool to forecast cash flow and move funds to maximize yield. Dimon said customers using outside agents must understand the risks and potential transfer of responsibility. JPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call. "You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers. The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers. "Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said. "We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added. That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful. There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added. Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely. In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents. Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer." Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example. Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month. In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts.

events.title: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion over money-laundering violations
events.summary: The Treasury Department announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. Bank of America admits willfully violating Bank Secrecy Act regulations and failing to "timely report" more than $5 billion in "suspicious" transactions, Treasury said. Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency imposed a record $750 million civil money penalty against the bank, which counts toward the $1.2 billion total. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations. Bank of America was hit with more than $1.2 billion in federal penalties Tuesday after regulators said the nation's second-largest bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and fix longstanding anti-money-laundering problems. More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other high-priority risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity tied to the southwest border, Treasury said in a press release . The action also lands less than a day before the bank reports quarterly earnings Wednesday morning. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which enforces anti-money-laundering rules, said the $1.2 billion penalty is the third-largest in Treasury history. Treasury separately announced an $11.6 million settlement over sanctions violations. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money-laundering program, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, according to Treasury. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the press release. Bank of America said in a statement to CNBC that the bank has invested billions in compliance and is "far along" in remediation efforts. The bank said the penalties will result in a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge in its third-quarter results, reducing net income by about 17 cents per share. It said remediation costs are already reflected in its current expense base. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," spokesperson Christa Robinson said. The bank's stock was down about 2% in after-hours trading on the news. The new penalties will put renewed focus on the record of longtime CEO Brian Moynihan , who took over in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure resolving tens of billions of dollars in mortgage-related legal and regulatory matters tied largely to decisions made before he became CEO. For much of the past decade, Moynihan has emphasized what he calls "responsible growth," as Bank of America sought to distance itself from the risk-taking and legal problems that followed the 2008 financial crisis . Moynihan is scheduled to appear on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " at 10:20 a.m. ET Wednesday following the bank's earnings report. Treasury says BofA "prioritized its revenues" Treasury said the bank "prioritized its revenues" while minimizing the impact on compliance resources. The agency said the bank relied so heavily on law-enforcement inquiries and referrals from other financial institutions that regulators said it effectively outsourced part of its responsibility for detecting suspicious activity. The penalty from Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network came in coordination with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, or OCC, an independent bureau within the department, which announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America. That sum, which is credited as part of the $1.21 billion total, is the largest penalty OCC has ever levied , the office said. The office accused the bank of serious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering rules, and of failing to fix its deficiencies in accordance with a cease-and-desist order it signed in 2024. "Despite its obligation to the American people as a national-chartered, global systemically important bank, the bank's BSA/AML compliance program continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens U.S. national and economic security," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said in the OCC press release. "The bank's poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable. The second largest bank's egregious and continued BSA violations warrant the OCC imposing its largest [civil money penalty] ever assessed against a bank," Gould said. "The OCC expects all banks to have an effective BSA/AML compliance program. Those that do not can expect swift and significant action from the OCC.

events.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July. Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device. These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components. The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited. The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data. Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng. The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees. However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI. events.title: Cathay Pacific's $19 billion upgrade includes new premium economy and business-class seats. I got a sneak peek — take a look.
events.summary: I tested out Cathay Pacific's business-class Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Cathay Pacific is rolling out new premium economy and business-class seats on Boeing 777-300ERs. The new premium-economy seats feature a winged, cushioned headrest and a footrest. Cathay's business-class Aria Suite comes with storage bins, lie-flat seats, and an art gallery. As Cathay Pacific marks its 80th anniversary, the airline is investing $19 billion into upgrading its fleet, cabins, lounges, and digital products. This includes new-and-improved premium economy and business-class seats, available on select routes aboard its fleet of retrofitted Boeing 777-300ERs. Cathay Pacific's upgraded offerings arrive as airlines increasingly pursue passengers willing to spend more for extra comfort and amenities. Across the industry, carriers are investing in larger premium-economy sections, lie-flat suites , upgraded dining, and lounge access as high-end fares bring in outsize revenue compared to standard economy seats. Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines , for example, recently unveiled new premium-economy cabins and upgraded business-class suites for long-haul flights. At an event in New York City on Thursday, I got to test out Cathay's new premium cabins for a closer look at the enhancements. Cathay Pacific is rolling out the new premium economy and business-class seats on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet. A Cathay Pacific Boeing 777. ADEK BERRY/AFP via Getty Images The upgraded offerings are available Boeing 777-300ERs flights between Hong Kong and Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Vancouver, and will be available on flights between New York-JFK and Hong Kong in 2027. The upgraded seats come with a steep price tag. Mid-November flights from Los Angeles to Hong Kong aboard a retrofitted Boeing 777-300ER range from $1,500 to $2,900 one-way in premium economy and between $3,700 and nearly $5,000 in business class, per Cathay's website. I started in premium economy, where a Cathay Pacific executive told me that "the entire experience is designed from the customer perspective." Cathay Pacific's premium economy seats. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Jason Li, Cathay Pacific's vice president of sales and marketing for the Americas, said that the airline focused on providing "enough differentiation between the premium economy and the economy seat" to make the upgrade worth the higher price. "From the cabin seat perspective, there's more privacy with the little winglet design," Li said of the headrest, elongated on one side to block its neighbor. "The angle of reclining is also much better compared to the economy for our new premium economy class." After I sat down, a flight attendant cheerfully popped the footrest and tilted the seat back to its reclined position for the full premium economy experience. Testing out Cathay Pacific's premium economy seat. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider I felt like I was sitting in an armchair, not an airplane seat. An added bonus is the leather pillow with foldable sides cushioning the headrest, which felt comfortable enough to render a travel neck pillow obsolete. A headrest in Cathay Pacific's premium economy seats. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The longer side of the headrest also featured a built-in reading light. Other amenities include Bluetooth-capable in-flight entertainment on a 15.6-inch 4K screen and numerous charging ports. Cathay Pacific's premium economy seats. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider In- flight WiFi is complimentary for Cathay members traveling in premium economy. Next, I explored Cathay Pacific's business-class offering, the Aria Suite. The Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The Aria Suite, the first version of which debuted in October 2024, comes with a sliding door and divider for maximum privacy. The seat can also recline all the way back for a lie-flat bed on long-haul flights. The Touch Screen Passenger Control Unit, or TSPCU, allows passengers to control their lights and seating positions. The Touch Screen Passenger Control Unit (TSPCU). Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Travelers can choose from three light settings — reading, mode, and console — and three seating positions — taxi, takeoff, and landing (TTL), lounge, and bed. The Aria Suite has several hidden compartments. Hidden compartments and wireless charging in the Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider A flight attendant told me these are useful for storing headphones or other items during bathroom breaks or walks to get blood flowing. The Aria Suite also has a wireless charging station indicated by subtle markings in the side console's marble design. There's also a mirror that folds out of a small cabinet that holds the in-flight entertainment remote. A cabinet and mirror in the Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider At 24 inches, the Aria Suite's in-flight entertainment screens are the largest ever offered on Cathay Pacific. Aside from the upgraded seats, the Boeing 777-300ER business-class cabins include a new amenity: an in-flight art gallery. A rendering of Cathay Pacific's Gallery in the Skies featuring a painting by Stephen Wong. Cathay Pacific Cathay Pacific partnered with artists who share a connection to Hong Kong to display their original works of art in a "Gallery in the Skies." "It's something that we're very proud of in terms of product differentiation and the experience that we offer in flight, which I think is very unique and also brings us to the next level in terms of customer proposition," Li said. Cathay’s retrofitted 777s aim to win over travelers willing to pay for more space, privacy, and elevated amenities. In the Aria Suite. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider For passengers willing to pay a premium, Cathay's new seats could help make long-haul flights a luxurious experience — more than merely bearable. events.title: Volta’s $5 billion debt deal is a pulse check on the AI-financing boom
events.summary: The Scoop Lenders are feeling maxed out on data-center debt. When Volta, an AI infrastructure company, went out recently to raise $5 billion for a data center in Norway, the deal didn’t seem that different from the more than $450 billion in AI-related debt deals done so far this year. But as Volta’s bankers at JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs went out to sell it, some investors pushed back, saying they’re full up on data-center debt and demanding more security and a higher interest rate. The deal is expected to price later this week with a rate of at least 11%, unusually high for a data-center project, anchored by a $1.5 billion order from Apollo, people familiar with the matter said. Commitments for the deal are due this week and lenders are still in discussion about allocations, so details about the financing could change. Volta’s deal is a pulse check on the AI-financing world. Deals are still getting done, but less smoothly than they were earlier this year, with higher rates and more heavily negotiated terms, investors and bankers say. Volta was founded in February and the Norway data center is its first significant project. Some investors balked at its lack of a track record, while others were unnerved by Volta’s reliance on Anthropic to buy much of the data center’s compute. Anthropic doesn’t share much financial information with lenders and the exact level of its obligations struck some investors as unsettled. The deal includes an unusual provision to overcome that skittishness: The interest rate charged to Volta will decrease if Anthropic can get an investment-grade credit rating, some of the people said. The Financial Times reported last month that Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPO advisers were lobbying credit-rating agencies for blue-chip status, which would be almost unheard-of for companies as unprofitable as both AI labs are. JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs have also underwritten a $1.3 billion term loan to Volta. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Apollo declined to comment. Volta didn’t respond to a request for comment. Anthropic didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More September has been the second-lowest month this year for issuance for AI financings, as regulatory and political challenges weigh on data center construction, according to a report from Morgan Stanley. The fourth quarter is expected to slow down further, the analysts said.

events.title: Walmart to cover some GLP-1s, inhalers and insulin for employees at no cost as it expands benefits
events.summary: Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees, in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers ahead of open enrollment. Walmart will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday. The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6. Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization. But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs. The latest benefit changes build on Walmart's yearslong effort to boost employee compensation after previously receiving criticism for the healthcare benefits and wages it offers. Walmart employs roughly 2.1 million associates worldwide, with about 1.6 million of those workers based in the U.S., as of the end of fiscal year 2026. In a statement, the company said it's minimizing premium increases for its employees, raising rates for its starting plan by $1.50 per pay period to $39.80. Walmart told CNBC that's a smaller increase than the company made last year. The company is also expanding an existing benefit that pays for employees to see cancer specialists at the Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic, according to a Tuesday letter to workers from Donna Morris, Walmart's chief people officer. Starting next year, employees under most plans can use that benefit to get a second opinion from a specialist for rare conditions such as ALS, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's. Among the other added benefits is up to 12 weeks of neonatal intensive care unit leave for parents, which can be added on top of regular parental and maternity leave, the letter said. "The steps we're taking are based on years of planning and trying new things, which is allowing us to make meaningful improvements for associates without slashing benefits or significantly raising premiums," Walmart said in its statement to CNBC.

events.title: The GOP billionaire behind the biggest political gift in U.S. history could be sued for allegedly fueling a Chicago rat infestation
events.summary: Chicago officials are weighing legal action against Barre Seid, the 94-year-old industrialist behind the largest known political advocacy donation in U.S. history, over claims that workers he hires to scatter nuts in Lincoln Park are fueling a rat infestation. Alderman Timmy Knudsen told Axios he is pushing the Chicago Park District to sue Seid for damage to the park, while Park District officials told the publication they are still weighing their options. In an Aug. 25 letter to Seid, Knudsen called the matter a final warning and said city staff had received photos and video documenting Seid or his staff putting out food daily for squirrels and other wildlife, according to WGN . The letter said the feeding created a public health hazard because it drew in not only squirrels but also pigeons and rats. Knudsen cited repeated violations of a city code provision barring the buildup of garbage or food that could feed or shelter rats, according to Block Club Chicago , and gave Seid 15 days to stop. While the city has issued citations, that allegedly did little to end the feeding of Chicago’s wildlife. The letter states that Streets and Sanitation has inspected the property multiple times over several years and issued multiple warnings and citations, and that the violations continued despite the fines being paid. Seid paid all fines and tickets without contesting them, Axios reported. “Typically, when you ticket somebody, it stops their bad behavior,” Knudsen told WGN . He said the feeding has increased since the city began ticketing. Neither Knudsen nor Seid responded to Fortune’ s requests for comment. Shells from Brazil nuts, hazelnuts, peanuts, and walnuts were seen at the base of trees near rat burrows in the park, Axios reported. Knudsen told the publication the burrows have grown where the nuts are left, and that Green City Market vendors have seen rats while setting up. Meanwhile, city documents say taxpayers could end up paying for repairs. According to neighbors and Knudsen, Seid and his wife, Barbara, have hired people for years to carry bags of nuts through the neighborhood and the park to feed squirrels, Block Club reported. Knudsen said the workers have been distributing nuts in the park, two or three blocks from the Seids’ home, since early spring. Who is Barre Seid? Seid made his fortune as the owner of Tripp Lite, a Chicago maker of surge protectors and power equipment. ProPublica reported that he transferred the company to a dark-money group run by conservative legal activist Leonard Leo, created in April 2020. It was then sold to Eaton in March 2021 for $1.65 billion, according to the company’s SEC filing , and thanks to that structure, tax experts told ProPublica Seid was able to avoid as much as $400 million in taxes. As Tripp Lite grew, Seid wrote checks to the Republican National Committee, ProPublica reported, and a longtime adviser described him as the Heartland Institute’s major patron, a Chicago-area think tank that disputes mainstream climate science. Tax records obtained by ProPublica show at least $775 million in donations to nonprofits between 1996 and 2018, almost all of it anonymous. In one email obtained by ProPublica and The Lever, Seid described himself as prone to “ anonymity paranoia .” He sometimes used a fake name, Ebert or Elbert Howell, which Tripp Lite staff gave to salesmen and business registries as the CEO’s name, according to his testimony in a federal lawsuit. Chicago has ranked first on Orkin’s list of America’s rattiest cities every year since the list began, 10 straight years as of 2024. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: More than a third of Americans earning over $500,000 say they’re living paycheck to paycheck, Goldman Sachs finds
events.summary: Would you feel financially secure earning $500,000 a year? A surprising share of Americans who actually make that much say they’re struggling to get ahead. More than a third (36.6%) of respondents with household incomes above $500,000 say they primarily live paycheck to paycheck, according to Goldman Sachs Asset Management’s Retirement Survey and Insights Report 2026 . That’s a higher share than any other income group except households earning less than $50,000, where 60.8% said the same. The report’s first key finding sums up the broader problem: Housing, health care, education, caregiving, and everyday costs have outpaced wage growth for decades, leaving households with less room to save. “The challenge is no longer participation,” Goldman wrote. “It is competing needs.” Prices are up, and paychecks haven’t kept pace That won’t surprise most Americans. Consumer prices have climbed roughly 22% over the past five years, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index . Households are paying more for everything from groceries to health care to rent and mortgages. Fuel has added to the pain: Gasoline prices were up 27.4% year over year in August. The typical household has more income to absorb those costs than it used to. Median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025, according to the Census Bureau . But many families still say rising costs are squeezing both their monthly budgets and their long-term savings. The strain is showing up even though the broader economy looks solid. Unemployment was 4.2% in September , and consumer spending rose by $190.8 billion in August, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis . Goldman’s report notes that beneath strong employment and resilient spending lie “growing financial pressures that threaten long-term retirement readiness.” Retirement saving momentum has also stalled. The share of working respondents who increased their retirement savings fell from 55% in 2025 to 39% this year—a drop of more than 16 percentage points. Goldman called it the largest single-year decline since 2020. Younger workers are feeling it, too: Fortune previously reported that many are taking on extra work to make ends meet. A U-shaped curve The more striking finding is how many households earning roughly 5.7 times the national median say they’re barely keeping up. The survey drew on responses from 5,106 people, including 3,612 workers and 1,494 retirees ages 45 to 75. Respondents chose one of three descriptions of their finances: primarily living paycheck to paycheck and struggling to make progress on long-term goals; making moderate progress; or making significant progress on both short- and long-term goals. Goldman grouped respondents into six income bands: under $50,000; $50,000 to $100,000; $100,000 to $200,000; $200,000 to $300,000; $300,000 to $500,000; and above $500,000. The paycheck-to-paycheck share fell from 60.8% in the lowest band to 22.2% among households earning $100,000 to $200,000. It then climbed to 34.2% for the $300,000 to $500,000 band and 36.6% for the top band. Households earning $200,000 to $300,000 were most likely to report significant progress. In that band, 42.2% said they were making meaningful headway on both short- and long-term financial goals. Credit card habits follow the same curve. Some 46% of households earning more than $500,000 say they typically pay only the minimum on their credit card balances each month, or less. That’s nearly identical to the 47% of households earning under $50,000, and well above the 30% of households earning $200,000 to $300,000. Top earners are also putting off their plans. Eighty percent of respondents earning more than $500,000 say they’ve had to delay a major financial goal despite being employed, the highest share of any income group. Forty-five percent say they’ve delayed retirement savings specifically, also the highest of any income group. Why big paychecks don’t always feel big Goldman says the strain at the top looks different from the struggle at the bottom. Lower-income households are trying to cover essentials. Higher earners point to more complex financial lives, higher lifestyle expectations, larger fixed commitments, and a gap between the retirement they envision and what they’ve actually secured. In practice, that can mean a bigger mortgage, pricier cars, private school tuition, and frequent travel—the kind of lifestyle inflation that can quietly absorb a raise. It’s a familiar pattern for so-called HENRYs , or “high earners, not rich yet.” Family obligations play a role at every income level. “Higher-income individuals may be the financial anchors for their extended families,” a Goldman Sachs spokesperson told Fortune . The report also notes that two households can report the same strain for very different reasons. For one, it may mean struggling to cover the bills. For the other, it may mean expenses and expectations that have grown faster than income. The results are self-reported, and most top earners still feel secure in their jobs: 87% of respondents earning more than $500,000 say their work provides a stable path toward long-term financial security. Still, the data challenges a common assumption, Goldman wrote: More income doesn’t automatically buy more financial security. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
events.summary: Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday. Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung . What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday. The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect. Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery. "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said. The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement. Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center. It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things. Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer. The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups. Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized." He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers. Go deeper: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about Leo's diagnosis.

events.title: Trump crosses country in bid to save midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump is ramping up his midterm travel this week, hitting five states as he looks to boost GOP base turnout ahead of a likely tough election night for Republicans. The president has hit the road almost daily this month, holding rallies in a host of states — including Alaska, Arizona, Montana, Georgia, and Kentucky this week alone. All of his stops were targeted to reach media markets in races that Republicans view as competitive, per a GOP official, including an Ohio House race near the Kentucky border. Trump’s goal remains persuading his loyalists to turn out in an election where he isn’t on the ballot. He’s not alone in the turbocharged itinerary; Vice President JD Vance stopped in Texas earlier today to tout GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who’s in a neck-and-neck battle against Democrat James Talarico. Vance used his visit to tout new Defense Production Act-related spending by the administration on a Texas refinery. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: How tech icon Meg Whitman is already leaving her mark on grocery giant Albertsons
events.summary: It’s never a good sign when a company pulls its financial forecasts mid-turnaround. But Albertsons did just that on Tuesday in the first clear sign of how deeply newly appointed executive chair Meg Whitman plans to overhaul the struggling grocery chain. Albertsons—which, in addition to its namesake stores, operates another 21 chains including Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Tom Thumb, and Randalls—said that net sales slipped to $18.9 billion in its second fiscal quarter, led by a 0.8% drop in identical sales, a metric that strips out newly closed or open stores. It was the second quarterly drop in a row, following shrinking growth in the preceding quarter. Albertsons CEO Susan Morris announced a plan in July called “ACI Edge,” aimed at improving the company’s competitiveness by reviewing its strategy, cost structure, operations, and portfolio of brands. On Tuesday, the company said it was pulling its financial forecasts until that review is over. That suggests that Albertsons may be eyeing a deeper turnaround than initially planned under Whitman, the longtime tech executive who joined Albertsons last month. “Everything should be on the table,” Whitman told Wall Street analysts on Albertsons’ quarterly conference call. “Dramatic improvement is needed now. Albertsons must move faster to change the trajectory of the business.” Like all grocers, Albertsons has been struggling with cash-strapped shoppers burdened by food inflation and higher gas prices cutting into their spending on nonessentials. But Albertsons also has a cost structure higher than that of its rivals, leaving less room to maneuver and shield consumers from higher prices than discount grocers like Walmart and Kroger or bulk operators like Sam’s Club and Costco. While Whitman has no grocery experience and little retail experience (from her time as CEO of eBay), she was brought in by Albertsons for her turnaround chops and decisiveness.  After taking the reins at Hewlett-Packard in 2011, she would go on to simplify the structure and product portfolio of a company that had been damaged by its acquisition of Autonomy Corp.; was doing strategy flip-flops; and had suffered from declining revenue and margins. She oversaw the split of the company into two. Before that, she had been CEO of eBay, where she professionalized the management structure and operations of a hot tech startup, setting it up for a period of fast growth under her decade of management. The current period of food inflation has been particularly bruising for Albertsons. Its lower-income customers are trading down to less expensive items and store brands, which either pinches Albertsons’ margins or sends shoppers to Walmart and Kroger. “The reality right now is that the economy is tough for many of our customers,” Morris said. But Albertsons’ sprawling empire of store chains has led to complex operations and the higher costs that come with them, making it harder to be more flexible on pricing.  Calling Albertsons’ prices “ridiculously high compared to rivals,” GlobalData managing director Neil Saunders said that would “be partly justifiable if other dimensions—store experience, service, private label, and so forth—were above par, but they’re not.” To remedy that, he added, Albertsons would need to “invest in prices”—retail speak for “lower them.” And that in turn adds pressure to find cost savings. Whitman’s comments to analysts suggest there will be no sacred cows under her aegis. She hinted that Albertsons could shed some brands through “potential strategic actions.” Morris became CEO in 2025 after the collapse a few months earlier of the planned $24 billion Albertsons and Kroger merger was followed by the exit of both companies’ chiefs. (Albertsons is currently suing Kroger for $9 billion over the failure of the merger.) She had been operations chief for seven years. Before Whitman’s appointment, Morris had already made some moves to make Albertsons more flexible, including lowering the number of operating regions to four from 11 to generate economies of scale and speed up decision-making. She also centralized much of Albertsons’ merchandising decisions under one team. As executive chair rather than simply chair, Whitman’s role is much more hands-on, acting as a close operations and strategic advisor to Morris and helping leadership sharpen strategy, improve execution, and act with celerity. “The company has greater potential than its results have reflected,” Whitman said. “But dramatic improvement is needed now. I believe we will turn the corner.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Agentic AI Automates RTL Waveform Analysis And Debugging (Columbia, Google)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind , and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” “The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.” Find the technical paper here . October 2026. events.title: Congress battle drifts deeper into red territory
events.summary: The battle for Congress is shifting deeper into red territory as both parties deem some races essentially over. The Democratic group Senate Majority PAC is scaling back ads in Georgia and North Carolina as Republican spending there slows, signs both parties see the Democratic candidates — Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper — as increasingly favored to win. The GOP Senate Leadership Fund is spending more to assist Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, after boosting spending in Kansas and South Carolina. And the Congressional Leadership Fund, a House GOP leadership-aligned PAC, is redirecting resources from candidates in purple districts, like those represented by Reps. Tom Kean of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, toward GOP incumbents in districts more handily won by President Donald Trump in 2024, like Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas and Rob Wittman of Virginia. Republicans still have some bright spots on the map. Democrats pulled back on some ad spending in another red district in Arizona, and Republicans are still spending heavily to try to flip outgoing Rep. Jared Golden’s seat in Maine. — Burgess Everett and Nicholas Wu

events.title: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Fusion power usually conjures images of massive industrial facilities laced with large lasers or magnets, but a startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been quietly building a device that can fit on a tabletop. The optics of the device were on display behind Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries , while he chatted with me on a video call. The company has been operating in stealth out of a small lab near MIT, and Kai gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at the technology it has been developing. “We purposely built a small modular reactor. It’s tiny, it’s benchtop,” he told me. “Because it’s small, it makes everything easier.” The small size has allowed Cambridge Heavy to experiment and iterate quickly. “The small module nature can enable 50 to 80 experiments, 50 to 80 shots per day,” he said. Data from those experiments will feed simulations that use AI to optimize the design. That nimble approach has attracted investor attention. The startup recently raised a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures with participation from Overlay, Neta Foundation, P3A, MassCEC, and the Rothrock family. Cambridge Heavy’s fusion reactor uses lasers to compress a fuel target, similar to the groundbreaking experiment that proved controlled fusion reactions could produce more power than they consume. But unlike other inertial confinement designs, Cambridge Heavy’s minimizes the number of lasers required to spark fusion. The system uses two main lasers to drive ignition. One laser is split into multiple beam lines that deliver light in concentric rings. Those rings of laser light are timed to hit the flat, round fuel target successively, starting from the outside and working in. The first ring starts a compression wave within the target that starts traveling inward. The subsequent laser rings are timed to boost the wave at just the right moment to further compress the fuel. As the shock wave reaches the center of the target, a laser fires on the target, generating heat and producing a magnetic field. With the right amount of pressure and heat, fusion occurs. Cambridge Heavy’s design generates high pressures with relatively low laser power, Kai said. The concept emerged from the lab of Keith Nelson, a chemist at MIT. There, researchers used the laser pulses to study materials under extreme conditions. As they ramped up pressures, they realized they were approaching fusion-ready conditions. In about a decade, Cambridge Heavy plans to develop a power plant from the concept, though that’ll require scaling up the design. It will be larger than the current benchtop prototype, though not quite as large as other fusion power plants. Kai said it should be about the size of two basketball courts, and it will test whether the approach can generate enough energy to support a power plant. Before that happens, though, Cambridge Heavy plans to use its smaller-scale devices to make tritium, a rare isotope of hydrogen that will be used by nearly all fusion power plants in the works today. Tritium sells for around $30,000 per gram today. Each power plant won’t need a lot of tritium — on the order of grams per year — but the substance is so rare that only about 40 kilograms exist today. One recent study predicts that without new sources, the fusion power industry will be short by about 28 kilograms in 2054. At current prices, that’s about $840 million worth of tritium. Fusion startups are in the process of designing fuel systems that will help the reactors be largely self-sufficient when it comes to tritium supplies, though they may need occasional top-ups. But that process could take up to 10 years, Kai said, giving Cambridge Heavy years of potential revenue as it pursues its power plant. events.title: Micron sinks, other memory-linked names dip for a second day
events.summary: Memory-linked stocks fell on Tuesday after Asian and European markets were roiled. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress on a new chip structure, intensifying chip competition. Intel and Broadcom CEOs have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom. Memory-linked stocks fell on Tuesday, extending a sell-off sparked by worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition. Memory chip giant Micron slipped 3.62% while other memory-related names such as SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital also dipped. The slide, which followed declines on Wall Street on Monday, comes as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT . Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to the likes of Micron and South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics . Analysts broadly see CXMT as trailing the U.S. and South Korean memory leaders, which means any advancement from the Chinese firm could add more competition to the market leaders. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares closed 2.8% lower in Shanghai. Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks. Adding fuel to the sell-off was a post by Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, who said China has the ability to scale production once it figures out how to manufacture something. "When China figures out how to manufacture a product, their ability to scale is often greater than the rest of the world combined," Musk said on Monday. European chip stocks also sank in early morning trade, with semiconductor equipment maker ASML down 3.3%, and STMicroelectronics and German chip maker Infineon both down 5%. Dutch firms BE Semiconductor and ASM International were both around 4% lower at the open. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.5%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry through its huge investment in OpenAI, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 7.2%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 2.9%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell over 5%, Disco lost 4.7% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.9%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. events.title: Yes, Grimes' new music video used AI — and lots of humans
events.summary: Grimes released the music video for "Accelerando," which includes a long list of credits for dancers, choreographers, and makeup and hair, along with multiple "AI artists." Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Coachella Grimes' new "Accelerando" music video includes some AI-generated elements, her representative confirmed to BI. Grimes said 70 artists and production professionals made the video and deserve credit. The video shows footage of the shoot. No AI was used to record the song or its vocals, a spokesperson for the singer said. Grimes ' fans have debating one question this week: How much — if any — AI did the pop artist use in her new music video? "Are we tripping or does this look like AI CGI for you too?" a Redditor posted on a subreddit dedicated to the singer, whose real name is Claire Boucher. Several people were quick to point to the music video's credits: "Why do you assume AI wasn't used? AI artists are listed in the credits," the thread's top comment reply reads. Similar questions have been circling on X and in the video's YouTube comments. A spokesperson for Grimes told Business Insider the answer is different for the music itself and the visuals. No AI was used to record "Accelerando" or its vocals, the spokesperson said. The video includes "AI-generated elements" that were selectively incorporated into a wider VFX process involving more than 70 artists and production professionals. "Accelerando" is a song that describes our world careening into a tech-forward, apocalyptic state. Its video puts that unease on screen. The camera circles Grimes as she moves through fantastical landscapes, including war-torn scenes and forests with mythical creatures, before landing on the singer and several dancers in a blue-screen studio. Then, a long credit sequence rolls, highlighting how many humans were involved in the creation of the music video. More than 70 professionals — makeup artists, dancers, a choreographer, and production team members — contributed to the production over two to three months, a spokesperson for Grimes told Business Insider. That includes multiple "AI artists," according to the credits. To make the music video, production used AI as a "minor complementary production tool," her spokesperson told Business Insider. The music video included at least three 'AI Artists,' according to the credits. Grimes/YouTube "Reducing months of work by such a talented group of creatives to a minor complementary production tool that still required substantial human creativity to bring to fruition not only discredits the artists behind it, but creates a trivial narrative that misses the real story entirely," the spokesperson said when asked for more detail about the contributions from the credited AI artists. AI has become highly controversial in the US — and a potential minefield for music artists and other creators who use it. Business Insider has reported on several content creators whose followers revolted in the comment sections when they acknowledged their use of AI. Grimes' music video is notable for its emphasis on the human talent involved, including AI artists, and the extent it goes to remind viewers of that. Grimes has expressed complicated feelings about AI. In 2023, she said she'd split royalties for AI art generated with her voice. The same year, the artist partnered with AI toy company Curio to make an interactive, spaceship-shaped plushie called Grok (which was not affiliated with the AI chatbot from her former partner, Elon Musk, that bears the same name). In a conversation with Interview Magazine , published in April, she said she's been writing poetry about AI's creation. "I was thinking about how everyone is like, 'We're building gods,'" she said. "I'm like, 'Why do you automatically assume you're so much lesser? You're literally responsible for creating AI.'" "Human life is very frail and time is very long. But I'd hope, if we had good relations with AI, they would take our DNA and make more of us when things get more hospitable." Grimes has been adamant that the human team behind her new music video should be credited with the work. A recent Grimes post on X about her new music video. X.com/@Grimezsz "For 'Accelerando,' the live-action sequences were filmed entirely against a blue screen, featuring real performers, physical elements, and practical ground textures," her spokesperson said, while saying the video used other standard video-editing tech, like CGI. "AI was selectively incorporated as a supplementary tool within this much larger, artist-driven VFX pipeline, rather than serving as a replacement for the creative or technical work," the spokesperson said. "The production process was intricate, labor-intensive, and fundamentally dependent on the creative judgment, technical expertise, and craftsmanship of the artists involved," they added. During an onstage interview with Fortune in June, Grimes said that AI didn't create music for the coming album. On Friday, the singer posted on X , saying that she did use some AI lyrics for the song "Deepseek." It "contains opinions and lyrics from Deepseek," she wrote, in reference to the popular Chinese AI model. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I've been to Iguazú Falls countless times. Seeing them under a full moon was something else.
events.summary: The author went on a full-moon walk at Iguazú Falls at night. Courtesy of the author My husband and I booked a nighttime tour of Iguazú Falls during the full moon. We walked through the forest in darkness, listening to wildlife and rushing water. The moonlit waterfalls were unlike anything I'd seen during my many daytime visits. I'm originally from Argentina and grew up in Brazil, so I've been to the Iguazú Falls — which sit between the two countries — plenty of times. This year, I decided to take my husband and kids to see the world's largest waterfall system , since they had never been before. And while their minds were blown during our daytime visit, it was the night walk I took with my husband through the falls that, honestly, took my breath away. The full moon tour is small and private The night tour is only available during a full moon , and you can choose different time slots. We were there with friends for a wedding and chose the 9:25 p.m. slot to guarantee it'd be really dark out. While kids are allowed on the full-moon tour, we decided to leave ours at the hotel with my mom so we could fully enjoy the experience. The author walked in the dark through the Iguazú Falls. Courtesy of the author Our tour had 120 people, which is relatively small compared to the thousands you can encounter walking along the metal walkway leading to the falls during the day. The experience felt intimate because we were such a small group, which gave us space and time at every stop. The walk starts right before the falls, with a small performance by the Guaraní, the indigenous people of that part of Argentina . There, our guide also explained what certain words meant, for example, Iguazú means "big water" in Guaraní. The moon guided our way After the performance, we started walking through a thick forest in the dark. The guides told us to use all our senses to experience the national park in a way very few ever do, and they were right. We started noticing different chirps and squawks from insects, birds, and monkeys. There were also different smells coming from the forest. But one sound was undeniable. Even before we reached the falls, the sound they made was so loud that it was hard to ignore, and it grew even louder as we approached. The author heard the waterfalls before she saw them. Courtesy of the author Throughout the tour, we weren't allowed to use flashlights or flash photography . The whole point was to let your eyes adjust to walking in the dark and to let the moon guide you. It was pretty mind-blowing to see how your vision changed the further we went into the park; it didn't feel like nighttime. The waterfalls are breathtaking As soon as we approached the first fall, you could hear everyone gasp and stop to take photos. The enormity of the falls is pretty breathtaking, but also feeling their power at night is indescribable. Even as a writer, I lack the words to explain how powerful it felt. There are two circuits to the falls: top and bottom. Because the water levels are currently so high because of El Niño (so much so that Argentina had to close some parts of the park ), we were only able to experience the top circuit during our visit. We missed out on the Devil's Throat , which gets you incredibly close to the falls. Our route let us see the waterfalls from above and the high jumps the water makes before it reaches the ground again. Argentina had to recently close parts of the tour the author took because the water is so high. Courtesy of the author At times, I just stood there, mesmerized by the sounds of the water splashing with all its intensity, surrounded by mist, under a sky covered in stars. My husband, who was experiencing it all for the first time, kept saying "wow" over and over. At one point, it was just him and me on a long metal structure overlooking the river right before the falls. It felt like we had the whole park to ourselves, and it was the most romantic thing we've done after many years of parenting little kids. We made it back to the entrance of the park around midnight. We brought our kids during the day The next day, we took a trip to the Brazilian side of the falls, which offers a panoramic view of this natural beauty. We rode a boat with our kids and friends close to the falls, where we got soaked and saw plenty of rainbows. On the way back to our car, we saw coatís and monkeys. After that, we took our kids to experience the same walk we had taken under the bright full moon, but during the day. Seeing the difference between what a daytime and a nighttime tour offers, I was left wishing we had taken the kids on the full-moon trip. Before we even left Iguazú, my oldest was already asking us when we were coming back. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Judge says Elon Musk engaged in 'little more than state sanctioned intimidation' when he accused a DHS official of a crime
events.summary: A federal magistrate judge took Elon Musk to task over a statement he made about a fired federal employee. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images A federal judge tore into a February 2025 post Elon Musk made on Twitter about a fired official. The judge wrote that Musk "clearly intended" to make the official feel "afraid." Judge William Fitzpatrick took issue with what federal officials said about the firing of FEMA CFO Mary Comans. A federal judge tore into Elon Musk for reposting a photo of a former Federal Emergency Management Agency official and accusing her of "criminal" conduct. "The fact that Mr. Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action' was clearly intended to make her afraid," Federal Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick wrote in a ruling published on Tuesday. In a blistering eight-page ruling, Fitzpatrick addressed what he described as the reputational damage to Mary Comans, a longtime federal government employee who was fired from her post as chief financial officer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency in February 2025. Musk's February 11, 2025, post, which was made when he was de facto leader of the White House DOGE Office , "served no legitimate governmental interest and was little more than state sanctioned intimidation," Fitzpatrick wrote. Fitzpatrick wrote that federal officials knew at the time that it was false to accuse Comans of trying to circumvent President Donald Trump 's executive order that paused federal funding to non-governmental organizations assisting migrants. Nonetheless, Musk and then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, among others, made statements that Fitzpatrick wrote impugned "the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans," Fitzpatrick wrote. "For reasons unfathomable to this Court, officials chose to turn the power of the federal government against a singular employee with an impeccable record of public service," Fitzpatrick wrote. "In short, Ms. Comans was professionally targeted and personally attacked by government officials for no legitimate reason." Musk's post on X was one of seven statements Fitzpatrick addressed in the ruling. Musk quote-tweeted a post that posted a picture of Comans and Trump with the text, "FEMA CFO Mary Comans was just fired for funneling $58M to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan. FA, FO." In his post, Musk added, "A criminal action." Fitzpatrick wrote that it was clear to other federal officials that Comans had no authority to stop specific grants, and that others had decided to continue funding state and local programs like the ones Musk took issue with. Musk and Noem have since left the Trump administration. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Fitzpatrick wrote that the federal government did not dispute a list of facts about the case, including that federal officials at DHS and FEMA knew that statements about Comans' firing were false when they were made. Tuesday's ruling is just one part of the broader legal fight over Comans' firing. In July, US District Judge Michael Nachmanoff ruled that Comans was unlawfully fired. The Trump administration is appealing that ruling. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If fusion power pans out, and there are signs that it will , the world will need a lot more lithium. That’s the bet behind Licube , a startup that has licensed technology from Hirosaki University in Japan, to purify lithium-6, the form of lithium that fusion plants need to make their own fuel, out of naturally occurring lithium. The reason comes down to the fuel supply. A lot of things have to go right for fusion power to hit the grid, and one of them is the fuel. Most planned plants would run on a mix of two fuels, deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is easy to come by, but tritium is extremely rare in nature, and it’s an open secret in the fusion world that there isn’t enough of it to power every planned plant. The proposed workaround is to make tritium on site, inside the power plant itself. A fusion reaction gives off a stream of fast-moving particles called neutrons. Startups plan to surround the reactor with a blanket of lithium, so that when a neutron strikes a lithium atom, the atom splits into helium and tritium. The tritium can then be collected, purified, and fed back into the reactor as fuel. Not all lithium does this job equally well. It comes in two slightly different forms, lithium-6 and lithium-7, named for their weights. Lithium-6 is far better at capturing neutrons and producing tritium, but it makes up only about 7.5% of natural lithium, and the rest is the heavier lithium-7. Separating the two is difficult, and there is little capacity to do it today, so the world doesn’t have enough lithium-6 either. Licube sees a big market in solving that problem. “If fusion comes online, it should be a $50 billion market by 2040,” Yohei Kiguchi, co-founder and CEO of Licube, told TechCrunch. Licube is one of 20 startups that are presenting onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco as part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition. While fusion has the potential to capture a significant chunk of the multitrillion-dollar energy market, fusion startups are still years away from building their first power plants. “Fusion is the biggest market in the future, but we also understand the future might be late by a few years,” Kiguchi said. Until fusion becomes a major market, Licube plans to use the same technology to purify lithium for use in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission reactors, and spacecraft industries. The core technology is based on the electrolyzer, a device that uses electrical current to drive chemical reactions. In Licube’s case, lithium is dissolved in a liquid on one side of a ceramic membrane. As electrical current flows from one side of the membrane to the other, lithium-6 moves faster. Licube can then draw off that liquid and separate the lithium-6. The goal is to enrich the lithium to at least 99.995% lithium-6. Fusion companies can feed that highly enriched lithium into their fuel breeding systems. Kiguchi was inspired to start Licube after visiting ITER, the experimental fusion reactor being built in the south of France. He said he was living a couple of hours’ drive away in Monaco after retiring from his previous company, Enechange, an energy-switching platform network in Japan. “I found out that I was too young to retire,” he said. “I’m an energy guy. I want to do something bigger.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Real estate agents urged to 'enhance responsibly' as AI use rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Real estate AI use grows with furniture and families altered in advertisements It has become a growing trend for the real estate industry to use AI-generated content to market homes. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The ABC has found several examples of AI being used in real estate advertising around the country. Experts say AI use is common in the industry and support its use as long as it is not misleading. Queensland's Office of Fair Trading encourages the industry to "enhance responsibly". Digitally altered furniture, families and songs about floor plans are some of the ways real estate agents use artificial intelligence (AI) to sell and rent homes. Marketing and consumer behaviour academic Sara Thaichon said the property industry was "one of the fastest adopters of AI in Australia". It has prompted one state regulator to issue a best practice guide to help the sector avoid misrepresentations. This image of a lounge room from a real estate website was generated using OpenAI tools. ( Supplied ) Ms Thaichon said "virtual staging" was common in real estate to help prospective buyers imagine the home's potential. "There's nothing wrong about that if it's done correctly, if the use of AI is disclosed," the Griffith University associate professor said. But she said using AI to enhance and create a false perception of a property can be considered "house-fishing". Sara Thaichon is an associate professor in the marketing department at Griffith University. ( ABC News: Glenn Mullane ) The ABC had found several examples of the technology being used in images on real estate websites around the country. When run through a SynthID detector, those images returned a positive result for OpenAI's invisible watermark, confirming the content had been generated with that tool. SynthID watermark result of an image of a bathroom from real estate website. ( Supplied ) Some real estate websites also feature AI-generated families in property listings. A Western Australia advertisement featured a digitally altered family of four and their dog having a picnic, with one child holding a wine glass. The image was tested with SynthID detectors, but none found a watermark. This image of a family outside a house featured in a Western Australia real estate advertisement. ( Supplied ) Google AI's tool determined the image showed "strong signs of digital manipulation or artificial generation," citing inconsistent lighting, the picnic mat's haloing, and the dad's slightly distorted grip on the bottle. A New South Wales agent used AI to turn several properties' floor plans into acoustic songs featuring lyrics such as "stone-top kitchen, gas and grace" and "four rooms full of little dreams". In one video, a female voice sang "this is where our future breathes" as the vision cut to the home's bathroom. Google's tool found these songs were created using AI music tools. It said the songs followed a standard "generative prompt structure" of address, features, and amenities, with vocals exhibiting synthetic processing and uniform pitch modulation common in AI music. Ms Thaichon said AI songs weren't "a big problem" if the lyrics were factually correct. Parents warned of lifelong risks as students 'subcontracting learning' to AI Data centre companies to pay into new Tasmanian local community fund Hundreds of scientists call for greater AI security in new open letter Are cracks beginning to emerge in the glittery AI facade? Real Estate Institute of Australia president Jacob Caine supported using AI to show a property's potential as long as it was stipulated. Mr Caine said he was aware of incidents where the technology was used to remove "less attractive" features of a place. REIA president Jacob Caine says the use of AI in real estate advertisements was a grey area. ( ABC News: Peter Drought ) He said if it was a deliberate cover-up, that was "misleading" and "frustrating for people". "If you're going to alter the property, be absolutely explicit that you have done and why you've done that." Under Australian consumer law, businesses are prohibited from engaging in misleading or deceptive conduct or making false or misleading representations about products or services. An Australian Competition and Consumer Commission spokesperson said businesses should ensure AI-generated images do not create an "overall false impression".
