events.title: Williams says Fed may not have to hike rates in 2027, at odds with traders
events.summary: New York Federal Reserve President John Williams doesn't see reason for additional rate hikes in 2027 after one more increase this year. Williams' comments place him at odds with the market. The Fed should look at "underlying trends" in inflation amid price shocks connected to energy and artificial intelligence, according to Williams' interview with Bloomberg News. New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Tuesday that he doesn't see additional rate hikes in 2027 after one more increase this year. "I haven't changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike," Williams said in an interview with Bloomberg News. "I don't think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more." Williams' comments place him at odds with the market and some other members of the central bank. Fed funds futures traders are largely betting that the central bank will raise rates at least once in 2027, according to CME's FedWatch data as of Tuesday. Latest trading gave about 90% odds that the Fed overnight rate would end 2027 at least a half percentage point higher than where it is today. The New York Fed head is also at odds with many Federal Open Market Committee members, though he is still in-line with the majority. Eight of the 18 who gave a rate forecast for 2027 see one more increase after an additional hike this year. Williams is a permanent voting member of FOMC, the body that decides where interest rates should be set at each Fed policy gathering. The Fed in September issued its first rate increase since 2023 . Fed officials indicated plans for another hike in meeting minutes, but did not clarify when. The central bank meets at the end of this month and then one more time in December. To be sure, Williams told Bloomberg that "we'll have to see" when it comes to forecasting into the new year. "This economy is being affected by lots of different influences, and we just have to keep watching the data," Williams said. Williams said the Fed should look at "underlying trends" in inflation amid price shocks tied to energy and artificial intelligence. While the former San Francisco Fed chief cautioned that energy prices continue to put upward pressure on overall inflation, he said they could provide relief on an annual basis in the future. Williams also said that effects of tariffs on price growth have mostly been seen. He said overall inflation for 2027 should be "near" the Fed's target of 2% on an annual basis. The personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's favored inflation gauge, in August showed a 12-month increase of 3.4% or 3% if stripping out food and energy prices. "I still believe there's disinflationary forces at play. Those I don't think have fundamentally changed," Williams said. "In fact, my forecast for inflation for next year is inflation to come down quite a bit." — CNBC's Matt Peterson contributed to this report.

events.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
events.summary: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta , both of which declined to back new legislation. The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework . The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.” OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said. However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.” The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.” While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI. MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said. Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.” In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over. Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said. When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so. “What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.” The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government , we will continue to do it.” The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access . The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.

events.title: Social Security benefits are rising again, but probably not enough to offset healthcare costs
events.summary: Increasing Social Security benefits annually helps millions of older Americans afford necessities. Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits are slated to find out on Oct. 14, 2026, how much their monthly check will rise. This cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities. I am a finance professor , and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices . And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face. The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026 , which the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, will also release on Oct. 14. It stood at 3.4% in August , according to the BLS. Experts have no doubt that the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 will be far above the 2.8% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2025 . Many forecasts range from 3.4% to 3.6% . But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured. Calculating the COLA The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices. The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers , known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index. The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January. If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same . That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015. Spending much of the bump on premiums One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation. Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College . For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA. More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are , helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation. Finding other options Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare , say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs. There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older , known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch. The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates. Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W. But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years . What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose. events.title: It pays to switch jobs again, but not everyone has that luxury
events.summary: Job switchers are getting bigger raises than job stayers again. Joe Raedle/Getty Images Job switchers are experiencing better wage growth than job stayers. Last year, both groups saw similar increases, defying historical trends. Still, not everyone can leave their job or find a new opportunity right now. It's once again better to switch jobs than stay in your current gig if you want a raise. "Wage growth for workers who change jobs is picking up again in 2026, even as raises for those who stay put keep slowing," Nicolas Petrosky-Nadeau, vice president for macroeconomic research at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, said in a LinkedIn post. That's based on 12-month moving averages of median wage growth for job switchers and stayers tracked by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta using Current Population Survey data. Year-over-year wage growth for job switchers has been 4.4% for four straight months, while growth for job stayers falls short, with September's estimate at 3.5%. The gap between the two groups shrank last year, including a brief period where stayers actually saw slightly better wage growth than switchers. The recent trend could be the start of a return to the historical norm of a healthy job-switching premium. "The first half of this year was the anomaly, and the low-hire environment is to blame," said Chris Martin, senior economist at Glassdoor. "Job seekers had to take what they could get, and that often meant compromise: fewer promotions and lower wages." However, some workers don't have the luxury to switch jobs right now. The quits rate has been bouncing between 1.9% and 2% for a little over a year now, far below the 3% rate a few years ago during the " Great Resignation ," suggesting lower confidence among workers. Openings have been similarly sluggish and are substantially down from the March 2022 record of 7.5%. "The return of this premium for job switchers is an early sign of improving prospects for job seekers, though the hiring rate remains low and job searches are taking longer," Martin said. With job openings basically in line with the unemployment level, AI making it easier to send out résumés, and job losses in white-collar sectors , workers might find it tough to say goodbye to their current role. "While job hopping still comes with higher pay, which is especially helpful for workers feeling the squeeze of inflation, the opportunities to job hop are few and far between," said ZipRecruiter economist Nicole Bachaud. People can improve their experience while stuck in their role. Bachaud suggests learning AI skills, which may be helpful in your current position or to note on your résumé. "For workers who are feeling stuck in their current position, it's important not to fall into the complacency trap," Bachaud said. "Beyond wages, the labor market is shifting rapidly as AI reshapes jobs." Whether you're applying for a new higher-paying job or seeking a raise from your current employer, it's not a bad idea to broadcast your accomplishments. People can " loud work " and boast their achievements and contributions to their manager and colleagues as well as beyond the workplace, such as through LinkedIn posts. "We stop ourselves from self-promotion because we think it's bad, but self-promotion is the breadcrumbs that lead to the titles and the promotions and the pay raises ," said Jasmine Escalera, a career expert with MyPerfectResume. events.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days. How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause. Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines. Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today. “It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.” “Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha. Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model. “None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data. Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid). He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers. events.title: Inside Trump, Netanyahu's dilemma: Strike Iran before elections or wait
events.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official. The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later. But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said. " Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said. A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said. Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations." Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran. According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets. Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute all of the various parts of its nuclear program. Israel is especially concerned about Iran potentially operating Pickaxe Mountain as a uranium enrichment site. Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Oct. 2 to discuss next steps in the war and the possibility of resuming strikes. Behind the scenes: An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant. A U.S. official said Trump has been going back and forth on the issue. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the leadership of U.S. Central Command are the strongest backers of resuming strikes in Iran, a source familiar with the discussions said. But most of Trump's advisers favor keeping up economic sanctions and other forms of pressure for now. "They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," the second U.S. official said. Between the lines: Renewed strikes would carry major political implications for both leaders. Resuming the war could dramatically affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke last week with Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and discussed the possibility of resuming full-scale fighting against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a source briefed on the call. Zamir said that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Caine's spokesman, Joe Holstead, declined to comment. It's a big dilemma for Zamir because a strike ahead of the elections could be seen as a political ploy by Netanyahu that would erode public trust in the military, which is largely viewed as apolitical. The intrigue: The White House is aware of Netanyahu's domestic political considerations. "Bibi's got an election before the midterms. He believes his strength is being a wartime prime minister," one of the U.S. officials said. In meetings with his security and intelligence chiefs in recent days, Netanyahu claimed it was Trump, not him, who initiated the discussion about possibly hitting Iran before the elections, an Israeli official said. According to this account, Trump asked Netanyahu if Israel would join. Resuming the war before the U.S. election could backfire on Trump by reminding voters of the unpopular conflict and potentially sending gas prices higher. The big picture: Qatari mediators are still waiting for Iran to respond to the latest U.S. counterproposal to end the war, which includes demands for nuclear concessions. "The negotiations are not really dead, but they're not really alive. We're just here, piling on the pressure and there's a belief that smarter heads will prevail over there," a U.S. official said. "The Iranians thought this president would back down because of the pressure and the midterms. He has shown them the error of their ways," the official added. Trump repeated a familiar refrain Tuesday, telling reporters that "Iran is a failed country" and "we will make a decision on Iran very soon."

events.title: Rivian’s startup Mind Robotics hires former Ford EV chief Doug Field
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics . Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture Rivian created last year. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding. Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field. Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale. Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human . The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer. Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation. “Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said. Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024 . He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.” “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.” Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also , a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized. Mind Robotics and Also operate as stand-alone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026 . events.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says.

A coastal Victorian council has defended its move to increase fees for providers of short-stay rental accommodation as hundreds of community members urge it to rethink the decision. The Bass Coast Shire, which takes in holiday hotspots like Phillip Island on Victoria's south-east coast, is one of just a handful of Victorian areas with local laws regulating short-stay accommodation. The council says the extra fees are necessary to cope with additional costs created by the holiday accommodation industry, but tourism advocates warn it may deter holiday home owners from renting at all, meaning more homes will stay empty for longer. Lisa, who did not want her last name published, bought her Phillip Island holiday home with her partner two years ago and said they worked very hard to afford it. Lisa says she and her partner have worked hard to afford their Phillip Island holiday home. ( ABC News: Georgia Lenton-Williams ) The couple is currently renting the property using an online platform at a base rate of about $220 per night. "We thought we could just share the home with other people and let them enjoy it until we're fully ready to move down here full time," she said. Earlier this year, Bass Coast Shire Council increased its annual registration fee to short-stay providers like Lisa from $324 to $600 — or $900 for homes with more than five bedrooms. The fee hike caught Lisa off guard. "It seems a bit extortionate really," she said. The Bass Coast Shire takes in holiday hotspots like Phillip Island. ( Supplied ) While governments across Australia have taken different approaches to regulating the short-stay sector, a statewide levy of 7.5 per cent came into effect in Victoria in 2025 . Some councils, like Warrnambool, scrapped local fees after the levy was introduced, but a handful retained local laws. That includes the Bass Coast, which has had a registration process in place since 2023 and now has the highest fees in the state . The retention of the local fees has led some short-stay providers to accuse governments of "double-dipping". However, University of Sydney housing expert Nicole Gurran said the state booking levy was likely also being paid by consumers. "It may be a bit of both: a bit of a provider absorbing the cost and a bit of them adding them on to the fee paid by the customer," she said. Professor Nicole Gurran says local councils are facing several challenges with tourism population booms. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) Dr Gurran said short-stay rentals and sudden population booms over holiday periods were difficult for regional councils to deal with. "You've got increased costs associated with waste collection, for instance, associated with managing beaches, parks, public spaces," she said. Bass Coast Shire mayor Brett Tessari agreed, saying the fee was introduced to "control" issues related to short-stay accommodation, including complaints from permanent residents about disruptive behaviour. Bass Coast Mayor Brett Tessari says the new fee is an attempt to address issues associated with short-stay accommodation. ( ABC News ) "The waste, the rubbish, the anti-social behaviour — it's our regular permanents that put up with all that," he said. "The cost is quite significant and we realised before this increase that we were just nowhere near where we needed to be." While Victoria's statewide levy raised $85.8 million in 2025 , that money is directed towards social housing investment rather than being used used to cover local costs. Rental shortage after pandemic migration More than 1,000 short-stay properties in the Bass Coast region have registered with the council. events.title: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States. Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny , with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen. Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed. Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement , Axios' Marc Caputo reported. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired. Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center. . The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR . The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett . How a firing squad works State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves. How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood. A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head. The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner. If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss. Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method. For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank round, while South Carolina has three shooters, all with live ammunition. Hasan uses a wheelchair, potentially complicating how the execution would be carried out at Fort Hood. Yes, but: Firing squads don't always work as intended. Last year, prisoner Mikal Mahdi was executed in South Carolina by firing squad. An autopsy later found that only two bullets struck him and missed his heart. Where firing squad is legal The method is legal in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, according to the DPIC . It is the main execution method in Idaho as of this past summer. The only authorized method for capital punishment in Texas is lethal injection. Yes, but: State laws don't govern military executions. It will happen on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 1pm CT, in Fort Hood. It's unclear if the execution would stream on social media or a website. TikTok and Kick said the event would violate their policies. What we're watching: The Army. Army Regulation 190-55 assigns the Army responsibility to choose the method, date and location of the execution.

events.title: Being chronically online is part of the job description for this top influencer marketer
events.summary: Sophia Sesto is Poppi's VP of culture. Photo Credit: Sophia Sesto If you're lucky, scrolling through TikTok could be part of your job. Sophia Sesto, Poppi's VP of culture, is tasked with keeping the prebiotic soda brand relevant. Poppi's influencer strategy relies on its team of marketers who are deeply fluent in the internet and pop culture. Sophia Sesto has a trick up her sleeve for influencer marketing: staying chronically online. Her role — vice president of culture for the buzzy prebiotic soda brand Poppi — requires her to be tuned in to popular culture. To spot trends and emerging content creators, it's crucial to follow "your own For You Page," Sesto told Business Insider. Sesto was recently featured in Business Insider's 2026 list of most innovative influencer marketers. The search for new, culture-driving creators "is never-ending," said Sesto, who leads Poppi's influencer, partnerships, and social marketing teams. Within Poppi's internal Microsoft Teams , there is a channel called "Seed" where Sesto and other Poppi staff "are constantly dropping" creators and content, accompanied by ideas for how the brand can work with these people in the future. Poppi has a "long-standing" partnership with Alix Earle, Sesto said. Courtesy of Poppi "It is the most manual process," Sesto said, adding that AI tools haven't yet proved useful on this front. "It's all in-house, and we say we get our consumer because we are them." Brands are projected to spend more than $44 billion on influencer marketing in the US this year, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB). As more dollars get pumped into the space, and more creators vie for those checks, standing out and driving conversation carry more weight. Meanwhile, the internet rapidly churns through viral memes and trends. Brands only have a split second to pounce. "A big part of my role is continuously building a model that moves at the speed of culture, while also being able to scale," Sesto said. Poppi's reality TV love affair Poppi's marketing campaigns around the hit reality TV show "Love Island" were right in this sweet spot. While on her honeymoon, Sesto watched "Love Island" and kept up with her colleagues. "We were in the Teams chats like, 'Did you watch last night? What do you think of this? What do you think of that?'" Sesto said. "I promise we get real work done too, but this is when our best work happens." Poppi's team, like many other "Love Island" viewers, grew obsessed with a 2025 cast member, Amaya Espinal . That July, when the plot of the show turned on Espinal, Poppi's staff went on Instagram to show its support with a made-up "Amaya Papaya" flavor. "It's our best-performing Instagram post of all time," Sesto said. What started as a joke turned into a full marketing campaign and flavor launch. By October, Poppi had cast Espinal in a campaign and launched a limited-edition flavor, "Amaya's Island Colada." The drink was sold on Amazon and at Target. Poppi sank its teeth into the "Love Island" fandom even further, working with creators on watch parties and other digital content. According to the company, creator-made content generated more than 212 million views. How Poppi works with pop culture icons Poppi has landed its bright-colored soda cans in the hands of internet celebrities like Alix Earle , Jake Shane, and Charli XCX. Poppi has a "long-standing relationship" with Earle, Sesto said. The brand worked with Earle at Coachella in 2024 and later launched a branded can with her in 2025. Earle's partnership goes deeper than sponsorships, too. She became an investor in the soda brand in 2024. Poppi is a frequent sponsor of Jake Shane's podcast "Therapuss." Courtesy of Poppi The brand has leveraged these faces in some of its highest-budget advertising campaigns, such as its Super Bowl commercials . Poppi recently partnered with actor Shay Mitchell's luggage brand , Béis, on a collection of suitcases. Like many brands, Poppi leveraged an IRL event to coincide with the launch. Poppi isn't only focused on the biggest stars. Sesto said its "always-on influencer program" is a crucial part of the brand's strategy to stay relevant and in front of consumers. When Poppi rolled out its "Shirley Temple" flavor at the end of 2025, it sent cans of the soda to influencers without any context, Sesto said, hoping the creators would post about it. "We gave them the opportunity to launch the flavor for us," Sesto said. Poppi recently partnered with Shay Mitchell's luggage brand Béis. Courtesy of Poppi Big Soda, bigger opportunities After Poppi was acquired by PepsiCo for nearly $2 billion in 2025, a new motto defined the brand's transition: "Let Poppi be Poppi," Sesto said. Poppi's new parent company is "leaning in" to Poppi's cheekiness, Sesto said, and letting Poppi's team "do our thing." The new ownership is also opening up doors. Since the acquisition, Poppi inked a partnership with Starbucks, landing the prebiotic soda on the coffee chain's shelves. Meanwhile, Poppi is also venturing into international markets and launched in the UK this year. "We're working on — spoiler alert — more places where you'll see Poppi," Sesto said. Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently. According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time. The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences. Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses. The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences. The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025. Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them. events.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit. There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel .) And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space. Longshot Space Technology , a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission. When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs. The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far. The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says. These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.) “If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.” The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites. “The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes. But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price. It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.

events.title: Private school fees loophole a sticking point in Labor's trust tax plan Greens say
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens concerned private school fees paid out of trusts could escape Labor's 30pc tax Nick McKim has accused Labor of 'watering down' its trust taxation plans. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke/Matt Roberts ) The Greens say a "loophole" for private school fees is a sticking point in Labor's proposed trust laws. Jim Chalmers will introduce legislation for the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts on Wednesday, amid stiff business opposition. Labor requires the support of the Greens in the Senate to pass the tax hike, given that the Coalition is opposed. Parents who pay private school fees from their trust funds could escape Labor's proposed trust tax, in what the Greens say is a "loophole" that must be closed. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will today unveil a bill to impose the 30 per cent minimum tax on some trusts. The budget proposal has enraged the business lobby and unnerved Labor backbenchers anxious about small business hostility. The Greens, whose votes are required in the Senate, have the opposite concern. On Tuesday, the party called for a Senate inquiry into the bill, saying an early draft was "watered down" and the proposal would not get a "free pass". The ABC can reveal the Greens' main concern is an exemption for money paid from trusts to charities, non-profits and other tax-exempt entities, including private schools. "People who are wealthy enough to set up trusts should not get a tax break to pay for private school fees when this option is denied to people who can't afford expensive accountants," Greens economic spokesperson Nick McKim told the ABC. "The treasurer needs to knock this out of the legislation." In a draft proposal last month, the government indicated it would cap the amount of exempt money each year, but that cap has not yet been set. The proposal does not change the tax treatment of private schools, since this avenue already exists, but the Greens will argue that carving charitable payments out from the new higher rate of tax will make it more attractive. "There is far too much leniency," Senator McKim said. "Labor is just trying to funnel ever-increasing revenues into the private education system when public schools are being starved of funds." Mr Chalmers said the Greens had not raised their concerns with him directly but that there were "good reasons" for the charitable exemption. "We've tried to make sure that there are reasonable arrangements for charities, for not-for-profits … This is a very specific sliver of what's being proposed here," he told ABC Radio National. "We can't lose sight of why this reform is really important … There are legitimate reasons for trusts, but they also allow a small proportion of people to manage their tax in ways that are not available to most working Australians." The 30 per cent minimum tax applies only to so-called "discretionary" trusts, a term the tax office uses to identify trust structures that give their owners the flexibility to shift their money into the names of family members, holding companies, or others. Tax experts say these complicated structures allow a minority of very wealthy, highly motivated people to achieve dramatic reductions in the tax they pay. The government expects to raise $4.5 billion from the tax in its first year of operation. Government offers small businesses a trust tax workaround Those with discretionary trusts can be exempt from the new minimum 30 per cent tax if they agree to hold their trust distributions constant. But business lobbies and the opposition have argued discretionary trusts are used for a range of legitimate purposes, including by small business owners. The government has outlined several exemptions, including for family farms that are placed within trusts, charities that operate as trusts, and trusts that are set up to manage deceased estates. But Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the tax still sent "the wrong message" and targeted business unfairly. "We urge all members of parliament to … listen to the views of those small businesses who will be affected: small and medium-sized home builders, family pharmacies, newsagents, small retailers, restaurants and cafes," he said on Tuesday. The government estimates that 350,000 active small businesses — roughly one in six — used discretionary trusts in 2022–23, the last year of available data. Treasury analysis suggests 140,000 of those would not need to pay the new tax.

events.title: Ukraine isn't focused only on making drones and missiles — it's also prioritizing the jet engines inside
events.summary: Ukraine relies heavily on jet engines for drones and missiles. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy/Screengrab via X Ukraine relies heavily on mini turbojet engines for drones and missiles. The country's defense minister said he expects monthly demand for one specific model to rise to 10,000. Local jet engine production has become a priority for Kyiv as its weapons become more advanced. Mini-turbojet engines have become a growing priority for Ukraine's defense industry as the country relies on them to power the next generation of high-speed interceptor drones and long-range strike weapons. Ukraine has long sourced weapons and components from partner nations. But as the country builds more of its own drones and missiles , reducing that dependency and increasing its self-sufficiency has become more important. Yevhenii Khmara, Ukraine's defense minister, told reporters over the weekend that Kyiv views jet engine production as a "critical area" for its local defense industry. For one specific engine model, he said, projected monthly demand could reach 10,000 units. Khmara said that the demand would be spread across just 20 Ukrainian manufacturers. Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, said that supporting domestic jet engine production has been a priority for the past year and a half. The 20 active projects include a mix of government and private initiatives. Large-scale mini-turbojet engine production is "crucial for effectively protecting our skies, and we are working hand-in-hand with the Defense Forces to deliver it at pace," Brave1 told Business Insider in a statement on Tuesday. Ukraine puts jet engines in medium-range drones, which it has used to hit Russian logistics and supply routes across occupied regions of southern Ukraine, and deep-strike weapons, including its cruise missiles that can reach military and energy targets hundreds of miles across the border. Jet engines are also essential for Ukraine as it builds a next generation of interceptors to counter a rise in Russian jet-powered attack drones. Earlier Ukrainian interceptor models were designed to counter Russian drones powered by piston engines, which could reach speeds of up to 115 mph. But Moscow is increasingly using jet-powered drones that travel much faster; some variants can reach up to 375 mph and are much harder to intercept. Ukrainian defense firms are now developing faster interceptors , some of which are powered by turbojet engines. The next generation of interceptors has already downed several of Russia's fastest drones. Following a meeting with military leadership in late September on the Russian drone threat, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that "new decisions" had been made concerning domestic jet engine production, according to a statement from his office at the time. events.title: What it takes to trust AI with real-world fixes
events.summary: Copilot to autopilot: Why no single safeguard is enough We designed a layered model that lets an AI agent resolve production network incidents on its own within defined identity, authorization, tooling, and human-approval boundaries. It’s 2:00 am. A pager goes off. A link somewhere in a datacenter has started flapping, a handful of alarms have correlated into one incident, and the on-call engineer is now doing what on-call engineers have always done: opening five tabs, one per system, and reconstructing what happened from fragments. We built an AI agent to do that reconstruction. It works. It pulls the device state, reads the telemetry, correlates the recent changes, classifies the failure, and writes a clean summary into the incident before the human has finished logging in. It also knows the fix. And that is where the demo stops being a demo. Because the agent “knows the fix,” the question is whether the system should allow it to shut a BGP session on a device that’s carrying live customer traffic. A “read” is something you can double-check. A “write” is an action that already happened. The moment an agent can change production, every property you were relaxed about at the read stage becomes a potential source of customer impact and risk. This post is about what we learned building an agent that’s trusted to take that action, as well as the uncomfortable conclusion we kept arriving at: There is no single thing you can build that makes an agent safe to run in production. Not a smarter model, not a stricter prompt, not a clever guardrail. Safe autonomy requires a stack. Ask 10 builders for a definition, and you’ll get 10 answers—and most of them are really examples (“You know, like a coding agent”) rather than definitions. That’s fine; we’re still in the relatively early days of agentic AI. But the fuzziness hides what matters here. An agent is not the model. The model is the brilliant, non-deterministic part in the middle. The agent is the deterministic software wrapped around it—the part that decides what the model is asked, what it may do with the answer, which tools it can reach, and what happens when it is wrong. The model supplies intelligence. The agent supplies judgment about how far to trust that intelligence and what to let it touch. Seen that way, the interesting engineering in an agentic system is usually the wrapper. And the whole safety question reframes with that distinction: Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it. Concretely, the harness we wrap around the model during execution is a mostly-deterministic workflow with a few narrow, schema-checked model steps inside it. It is what turns “the model worked something out once” into “these steps run the same way every time.” You don’t need its full mechanics yet—that’s another layer. For now, just hold the picture: a deterministic workflow with the model kept on a short leash inside it. Harness, agent, orchestrator, playbook, call it what you like. The load-bearing idea is the same: deterministic software putting a non-deterministic model to work, on purpose, within limits. The “holy grail” of agentic development is an agent that can investigate a problem, work out a fix, and carry it out without a human directing every step. But getting there in production means building safety into each step. More autonomy should not mean fewer controls. Imagine giving that agent a service account with broad access, a shell that can run anything, and a stern system prompt listing everything it must never do. It might have everything it needs to fix the problem. But what actually prevents it from taking an action it shouldn’t take? A broadly privileged service account can give the agent more access than the person who invoked it. An unrestricted shell can put anything that account and machine can reach within the impact radius. A system prompt helps guide behavior, but it can’t enforce permissions. The model can misinterpret an instruction or be influenced by malicious text in a log or tool response. Production safety can’t depend on instructions to the model alone. The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence. Modern models are frighteningly good at figuring out the fix. The real question is: “What is this thing allowed to do, under whose identity, through what interface, and with whose sign off?” It’s boring, it’s deterministic, and it’s the whole game. The mental model: Four boundaries, layered Once we started stacking boundaries, the architecture fell into four layers. Each answers a different question. None of them are sufficient alone, and that’s the point. Read bottom to top, it’s defense in depth across identity, tool, mutation, and time. Read as a sentence: The agent acts only as the human who summoned it (identity), reaches production only through a controlled interface (tool), can read freely but must pause before it changes anything (mutation), and gets less reliant on live reasoning the more it runs (time). Two of these are security controls in the literal sense: identity and tool access are where an attacker or a hallucination does its damage, so that’s where the hardest walls go. Layer 1: The agent never has more access than you The agent doesn’t get its own powerful account. It acts on behalf of the human who invoked it, bounded by that person’s real permissions. Where a service identity is unavoidable, it gets the narrower of the two. Identity is compound: the human plus the agent, and the stricter one wins. Access policies are owned by the teams that own each tool, defined per tool, and changed through a normal pull request (PR) with the tool team as a required reviewer. Merging a PR grants access; reverting it revokes access. Layer 2: One tool interface, not a bare shell The agent never gets a bare shell. Every capability it has sits behind a single typed tool interface, each tool is individually authorized, and each call is structured and logged. Note the careful wording: The enemy is not the command line; it is the unbounded one. A raw shell cannot be governed, because you cannot put a permission boundary, a schema, or a clean audit trail around bash. But a command line invoked as one narrow, declared tool, behind the interface, is fine. This is why the framing of “MCP vs. CLI” is a false dichotomy. You want both, chosen by trust level. Put everything behind the tool interface, then pick the implementation per call: a plain function or a sandboxed CLI for low-risk local work inside the trust boundary, and MCP for anything that crosses it, because MCP gives you least privilege, credential isolation, structured audit, human approval hooks, and rate limiting for free. You can secure a CLI, too, but only by paying for per-user sandboxes with tightly limited access, and even then, you can’t match per-tool granularity. Layer 3: Read freely, pause before you write Diagnostics run on their own.

events.title: The White House is in its Trump-fueled SI era
events.summary: President Donald Trump has said that those who continue to use the term artificial intelligence will be considered an "enemy" of his White House. Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images AI.gov is now fully si.gov. The White House rolled out the new URL on Tuesday. President Donald Trump has said that he wants AI to be called super intelligence now The White House has finally addressed a remnant of the AI era. On Tuesday, the Trump administration rolled out si.gov, giving a new URL to the site that was first launched during the Biden administration. The new site describes President Donald Trump 's artificial intelligence policies, though much of the text itself was changed before Tuesday. "The Super Intelligence era is here. 🇺🇸," Michael Kratsios, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, wrote on X. The new address falls in line with Trump's wishes that artificial intelligence, or AI, now be called super intelligence, or SI. The president formalized his preference in a September 29 executive order. Last week, Trump declared that if others did not go along with his rebrand, they would be considered an "enemy" of his White House. The president has said that using the term "artificial intelligence" makes the technology sound fake. AI and tech leaders have split over how to handle Trump's request. Over the weekend, SpaceXAI followed through on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk 's promise to rebrand the company's AI division as SpaceXSI. On Saturday, days after Trump bestowed an honor on him, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella published a lengthy statement titled: "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era." AI and artificial intelligence were not among the 805 words Nadella wrote. As for OpenAI, whose name contains the very abbreviation Trump wants gone, its CEO, Sam Altman, previously ruled out a rebrand. "No plans to do that," Altman told the Politico Decoded podcast. "But we have been talking about super intelligence a lot, and we will continue to talk about it." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
events.summary: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting for them to halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. events.title: UK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young people
events.summary: Retailers call on John Healey to reduce national insurance contributions threshold in his first budget Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget. At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics). Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment . They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets. Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts. “It felt like they were listening,” the source said. Healey has vowed to ease the cost of doing business amid mounting pressures on firms from rising energy bills. Another attender, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium trade body which represents most big retailers, said: “Retail is a major driver of growth, supporting jobs, investment and communities across the country, and providing vital first jobs and career opportunities for young people. “But after whacking up retailers’ taxes by 20% in two years, including an extra £6.5bn in new employment costs, any new costs will be paid by consumers at the till and make it harder for retailers to create jobs. “The chancellor recognised these pressures, and we had a positive discussion about our shared ambition for growth and tackling youth unemployment. His first budget is the chance to turn that ambition into action by easing costs, making tax fairer and unlocking investment.” Meanwhile it was reported that Healey has rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed. He has come under pressure to increase the rates of capital gains tax (CGT), which is levied on the sale of assets – including second homes and shares – at significantly lower rates than wages. In her first budget in 2024, Reeves increased the rate of CGT from 10% to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers, and from 20% to 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. That compares with a 20% basic rate of income tax, a 40% higher rate and 45% additional rate for top earners. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Economists have suggested an equalisation of the rates could raise £11.3bn a year for the exchequer. However, according to the Financial Times, Healey has dismissed such calls because of fears it could deter inward investment, but may yet opt for a smaller increase in CGT short of equalisation. It comes after senior Labour figures floated CGT increases among options to repair the government finances while funding priorities ranging from public services, support for households and long-term infrastructure projects. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, suggested the idea of equalisation during his ill-fated May pitch to be the party leader as a “wealth tax that works”. And the first secretary, Louise Haigh, a close ally of Andy Burnham, argued in an article in the journal Renewal in May – while on the backbenches before her return to cabinet – that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”. A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”
