events.title: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests
events.summary: Exclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil project Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands . With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation. A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated. It is understood the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands . An oil project known as Sea Lion in the North Falkland Basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei , has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors. In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood. Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.” She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.” It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character. Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has told MPs that the UK will protect businesses working in the Falklands from pressure from Argentina through measures under protection of trading interests (PTI) legislation. The legislation allows the UK to issue orders and directions forbidding British individuals and companies from complying with specific foreign laws or trade controls. It also opens up the possibility that those affected by Argentinian legal pressure could claim damages in UK courts. Miliband said: “The UK’s support for the Falkland Islands is steadfast. Argentina’s attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion. “We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development.” The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders. Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against . Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project. A draft national sovereignty bill introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers. The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.

events.title: Walmart heir Olivia Walton didn’t get the postpartum care she needed. Now, she’s investing $100M to halve the U.S. maternal mortality rate in 5 years
events.summary: Walmart heiress Olivia Walton is pledging a part of her family’s multibillion-dollar fortune to tackle the maternal health crisis affecting women across the U.S. The CEO of Ingeborg Investments founded her nonprofit Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America in April, dedicating $100 million over the next five years to cut the country’s maternal mortality rate in half.  Her mission is deeply personal: As a mother of three young kids, she ran into serious gaps in maternal care herself, despite having access to the resources of a family worth an estimated $500 billion. “It’s personal,” Walton told leadership editor and summit cochair Claire Zillman onstage at Fortune ’s annual Most Powerful Women conference in Santa Barbara, Calif., on Monday. “I went through it myself, and I saw that even with all my resources, with my family, with my education, it was still really hard.” When Walton had her middle child in 2020, she said that she didn’t get the “postpartum care she needed” from facilities in her home state of Arkansas. And when she took a step back to look at the full picture, she quickly recognized other women in her state were suffering, too. Arkansas has one of the worst maternal mortality rates in the country , Walton noted, which is around double the national average.  “Women are dying in Arkansas from complications from giving birth at the same rate they are in Cuba. And don’t forget—never forget—that for Black and brown women, the mortality rate is three times higher,” Walton said. “We have the medicine, we have the science. What we need is the political will. We need the awareness.” Now she and her husband, Tom Walton, are hoping to turn awareness into action with their bipartisan nonprofit campaign. Through Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America, they’re using “every tool in the toolbox” to drive change—from storytelling and advocacy work, to coalition-building and catalytic grant-making. Arkansas and Kansas will each receive $10 million from the foundation to improve their maternal health. The issue could worsen as we head into the next year, due to Medicaid cuts and changes in the way the American Medical Association bills patients, Walton said. But she said she has hope people on both sides of the political spectrum can agree on one thing when it comes to maternal health care: “Everybody wants healthy families.” However, a $100 million pledge isn’t enough to sustain that progress on its own. Walton stressed the importance of bolstering the maternal health workforce with more midwives and doulas. And beyond getting more workers into the industry, she called on employers to improve their pregnancy and postpartum benefits. After all, large, self-insured companies that improve their perinatal benefits see their costs come down and outcomes improve, Walton said. “Expand your benefits,” the philanthropist said. “Take better care of moms, not because it’s the right thing to do, but because it’s usually the smart thing to do for your business.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: After traveling to all 50 states, I think these 6 state parks are some of the country's most incredible hidden gems
events.summary: In my opinion, Devil's Lake State Park in Wisconsin is one of the best lesser-known US state parks. Emily Hart I've traveled to all 50 states and love exploring the country's lesser-known state parks . Letchworth State Park in New York and Matthiessen State Park in Illinois have gorgeous waterfalls. Utah's Kodachrome Basin State Park feels like stepping into another world. The US national parks are incredible, and I understand why so many people flock to these iconic landscapes to see some of the most breathtaking scenery in the country. However, after traveling solo to all 63 US national parks and all 50 states, I've discovered that some of the most stunning and underrated places aren't part of the national park system — they're state parks. These hidden gems offer the same beauty, adventure, and solitude, often without the crowds, reservations, or permit hassles that come with national park visits. Here are some of my favorites. Devil's Lake State Park in Wisconsin has something for everyone. Emily Hart Despite being Wisconsin's most-visited state park, I find that many people I talk to don't know about Devil's Lake in Baraboo. However, it's my favorite of Wisconsin's 50 state parks. In my opinion, the park's East and West Bluff trails offer some of the best panoramic views in the Midwest. Additionally, the massive rock formations — like Balanced Rock and Devil's Doorway — make it a favorite for hikers and rock climbers alike. Beyond the cliffs, the park offers kayaking, swimming, and peaceful lakeside picnic areas, making it a perfect year-round destination. Coopers Rock State Forest in West Virginia is the perfect place to watch the sunset. Emily Hart West Virginia is another one of my favorite states for outdoor recreation. Its state park system is full of gems, but I always recommend visiting Coopers Rock State Forest. I love hiking in this park or simply enjoying a sunset at Coopers Rock Overlook, which offers a panoramic view of the Cheat River Gorge. The park also has many unique rock formations scattered throughout the forest along the miles of scenic trails. Letchworth State Park in New York is home to stunning waterfalls. Jim Vallee/Shutterstock Often nicknamed the "Grand Canyon of the East," Letchworth State Park is a natural wonder where the Genesee River carves through a deep gorge, creating three stunning waterfalls framed by towering cliffs. With 66 miles of hiking trails, scenic overlooks, and endless opportunities for outdoor recreation, Letchworth is a paradise for nature lovers. The park is especially magical in the fall, with its vibrant autumn foliage, making it one of the most spectacular leaf-peeping destinations in the Northeast. Visiting Utah's Kodachrome Basin State Park feels like stepping into another world. Emily Hart When visiting Utah, many travelers aim to see one (or all) of the state's "Mighty Five" national parks . However, Utah is also home to 46 state parks — my favorite being Kodachrome Basin. Just over 20 miles from Bryce Canyon National Park, Kodachrome Basin feels like stepping into another world entirely. The less-crowded landscape is a stunning mix of red, orange, and yellow hues, and striking "sand pipes" — tall, thin spires of rock that the park is known for. Hike, camp, or drive through the rock formations of this hidden gem park for a peaceful adventure. Matthiessen State Park in Illinois feels magical. Joseph Hendrickson/Shutterstock Matthiessen State Park is a hidden gem known for its dramatic canyons, cascading waterfalls, and towering forests, creating a stunning, almost magical landscape. With peaceful trails and fewer crowds than nearby Starved Rock State Park, Matthiessen is a must-visit for nature lovers in the Midwest. I especially love visiting in the fall to enjoy the changing foliage. Eldorado Canyon is one of my favorite state parks in Colorado. Emily Hart With four major national parks and over 40 state parks, Colorado is known for outdoor recreation. However, I've found that, outside of the locals, many people don't know about one of my favorite places to visit — Eldorado Canyon State Park. Just 9 miles outside Boulder, the park is known for its dramatic canyon views, rock climbing, and scenic hiking trails. Its towering golden sandstone cliffs make it one of the top climbing destinations in the US, with over 500 routes. Visitors can also choose to cross-country ski or snowshoe in the winter months. events.title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: overdue, but proceed with care | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: an overdue show of ambition The prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewards T he German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision. Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off. A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin. That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk. Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield. For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold. As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat. It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country. events.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it. “Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said. Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon , October 13. Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. “I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision. “We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said. At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world. The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale. Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom. Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision. “It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.” While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop. “They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said. Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world. “There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.

events.title: Only 13 albums have spent at least 10 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 this century — here they all are
events.summary: Adele, Taylor Swift, and Morgan Wallen. Kevin Mazur/Kate Green/Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images The Billboard 200 tracks the most popular albums every week in the US. Only 13 albums have spent 10 or more weeks at No. 1 on the chart so far this century. Taylor Swift, Morgan Wallen, and Adele all have multiple albums on the list. Since 2000, only 13 albums have spent double-digit weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart, widely considered the definitive weekly ranking of best-selling albums in the US. Taylor Swift is the only woman to have four albums spend at least 10 weeks atop the Billboard 200, joining The Beatles and Elvis as the only artists in history to achieve this feat. Keep reading to see a complete list of the chart's longest leaders in chronological order. 1. "Fearless" by Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's sophomore album, "Fearless," was released in 2008. Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's sophomore album spent 11 weeks at No. 1 and was certified diamond by the RIAA . It's still known as the most-awarded country album of all time. Prior to "Fearless," the top-charting album of the millennium was Usher's "Confessions," which spent nine weeks at No. 1. 2. "21" by Adele Columbia Records Adele's sophomore LP spent a whopping 24 weeks at No. 1, the biggest nonconsecutive sum for any album by a woman. "21" won album of the year at the Grammys and was later crowned the top-performing album in the history of the Billboard 200. 3. "Frozen (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)" by Various Artists Walt Disney "Frozen" spent 13 weeks at No. 1, the most for any film soundtrack since "Titanic" in 1998. 4. "1989" by Taylor Swift "1989" was released on October 27, 2014. Taylor Swift Swift's fifth studio album spent 11 weeks at No. 1 and went on to win album of the year at the Grammys, becoming Swift's second win after "Fearless." (She has since won four times, more than anyone else in history.) 5. "25" by Adele "25" was released in 2015. Columbia Adele's third album spent 10 weeks at No. 1 . It also won album of the year at the Grammys, beating Beyoncé's "Lemonade." 6. "Views" by Drake Young Money Drake's fourth studio album, "Views," spent 13 weeks at No. 1, besting Adele's "25" for the top-charting album of 2016 . 7. "Dangerous: The Double Album" by Morgan Wallen Big Loud/Republic Morgan Wallen's second studio album spent 10 consecutive weeks at No. 1, becoming just the third album in history to spend its first 10 weeks atop the chart, joining Whitney Houston's "Whitney" (1987) and Stevie Wonder's "Songs in the Key of Life" (1976). 8. "Un Verano Sin Ti" by Bad Bunny "Un Verano Sin Ti" was released on May 6, 2022. Rimas Entertainment Bad Bunny's fourth studio album spent 13 weeks at No. 1 . "Un Verano Sin Ti" was ranked among Business Insider's best albums of 2022 and nominated for album of the year at the Grammys, but lost to "Harry's House" by Harry Styles . 9. "SOS" by SZA "SOS" was released on December 9, 2022. Daniel Sannwald/RCA SZA's sophomore album, "SOS," was the first R&B album by a woman to spend 10 weeks at No. 1 since Mariah Carey's self-titled debut in 1991. It later returned to the top for a total of 13 weeks . 10. "One Thing at a Time" by Morgan Wallen Big Loud/Republic Morgan Wallen's third studio album spent 19 nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1, surpassing "Un Verano Sin Ti" for the most weeks atop the chart this decade. It's also the biggest country album in the history of the Billboard 200; Garth Brooks previously held the record with "Ropin' the Wind," which reigned for 18 weeks in the early '90s. Wallen's commercial success has come despite a string of controversies , including canceling concerts at the last minute, using a racial slur , and partying without a mask during the pandemic. 11. "The Tortured Poets Department" by Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's 11th album, "The Tortured Poets Department," was released in 2024. Taylor Swift Swift's 11th studio album spent its first 12 weeks at No. 1, the longest post-release run by a female artist since Houston's "Whitney." " The Tortured Poets Department " joined Wallen's "One Thing at a Time" and Wonder's "Songs in the Key of Life" as the only three albums to spend their first 12 weeks in the chart's top position. (Wonder holds the record with a 13-week streak.) "Poets" later returned for five more weeks atop the Billboard 200 for a grand total of 17, the longest reign of Swift's career . 12. "I'm the Problem" by Morgan Wallen "I'm the Problem" was released in 2025. Big Loud Wallen's "I'm the Problem," his fourth studio album, spent 14 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. 13. "The Life of a Showgirl" by Taylor Swift Taylor Swift's 12th album, "The Life of a Showgirl," was released on October 3, 2025. TAS Rights Management Swift's 12th studio album, " The Life of a Showgirl ," has spent 14 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl' is one of her biggest albums on the Billboard 200. Here's how her others rank.
events.summary: Taylor Swift performs during The Eras Tour in Dublin. Charles McQuillan/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl" has spent 14 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. It's her second-longest reign atop the chart, surpassing "Fearless" and "1989." "The Tortured Poets Department" holds the record in Swift's catalog with 17 weeks at No. 1. Taylor Swift gave us fair warning in her newest album: "I'm married to the hustle." Swift's 12th studio album, " The Life of a Showgirl ," not only broke the record for the biggest debut sales week ever , but it continued to amass sales and streams in the US for a year after its release. With 14 nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 , "Showgirl" has surpassed "Fearless" and "1989" as Swift's second-longest reign on the all-genre album chart. The impressive tally comes shortly after Swift set a personal-best chart record with " The Tortured Poets Department ." Keep reading for a ranking of her 16 studio albums (including both originals and rerecords) based on their Billboard 200 performances. 10. "Taylor Swift" Taylor Swift's debut album, "Taylor Swift," was released in 2006. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 5 Swift's self-titled debut is the only studio album in her catalog that hasn't reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200. "Taylor Swift" debuted at No. 19 and scaled the chart for more than a year, peaking at No. 5 in 2008. 9 (tie). "Lover" Taylor Swift's seventh album, "Lover," was released in 2019. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for one week Swift's seventh studio album was the first one that she owned outright, thanks to her new label contract with UMG. "Lover" was promoted by several singles, including "You Need to Calm Down," " The Archer ," and " The Man ." Four years later, after Swift kicked off the Eras Tour with "Cruel Summer" near the top of the set list, the fan-favorite song climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and remained there for four weeks, becoming the album's biggest hit. 9 (tie). "Red (Taylor's Version)" The cover art for "Red (Taylor's Version)" was photographed by Beth Garrabrant. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for one week The extended tracklist for " Red (Taylor's Version) " included the storied extended cut of "All Too Well," a longtime fan-favorite song in Swift's catalog. "All Too Well (10 Minute Version)" was released alongside a short film directed by Swift and promoted by a convention-breaking performance on "Saturday Night Live." It became the longest song to reach No. 1 in the history of the Hot 100. 8 (tie). "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" was released in 2021. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for two weeks "Fearless" was the first rerecorded album that Swift ever released. The "Taylor's Version" series was inspired by the sale of Swift's masters to Scooter Braun in 2019, which she described as her "worst case scenario" in a passionate open letter. Swift decided to remake and rerelease her first six albums in a bid to reclaim ownership of her life's work. Braun later sold Swift's masters to a private equity firm. In addition to faithfully recreating each tracklist , Swift decided to add never-before-heard songs "from the vault" that were written during the album's original creative process but cut from the final product. "I've spoken a lot about why I'm remaking my first six albums, but the way I've chosen to do this will hopefully help illuminate where I'm coming from," Swift explained. "Artists should own their own work for so many reasons, but the most screamingly obvious one is that the artist is the only one who really knows that body of work." "For example, only I know which songs I wrote that almost made the 'Fearless' album," she continued. "Songs I absolutely adored, but were held back for different reasons." Many were skeptical that the "Taylor's Version" project would be embraced by fans, let alone achieve commercial success . Those skeptics were forced to eat their words when "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" began to outpace the original on streaming platforms. According to Billboard , "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" earned more equivalent album sales in its first week of release than "Fearless" earned over the entire next year. Four years later, in May 2025, Swift announced that she bought back her masters from Shamrock Capital, giving her complete control over her musical catalog and rendering her "Taylor's Version" project moot. 8 (tie). "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)" "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)" was released in 2023. Taylor Swift/UMG Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for two weeks The rerecorded version of Swift's third album featured six songs from the vault , including two duets with Fall Out Boy and Hayley Williams. 7 (tie). "Reputation" The album cover for "Reputation." Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for four weeks "Reputation" arrived after an extended period of silence. Swift's longtime feud with Kim Kardashian and Ye (then known as Kanye West) had reached a fever pitch; in response to a massive social media hate campaign, Swift decamped to London and withdrew from the public eye. She returned with a new snake-infested aesthetic and "Look What You Made Me Do," a cheeky lead single that poked fun at her own persona — and quickly rose to No. 1 on the Hot 100. Swift also declined to participate in interviews or media appearances while promoting her sixth album. Instead, she relied on a simple tagline: "There will be no further explanation. There will just be reputation." 7 (tie). "Evermore" Taylor Swift's ninth album, "Evermore," was released in 2020. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for four weeks "Evermore" was surprise-released just five months after Swift's previous album, "Folklore." The two were billed as "sister albums," created under near-identical conditions with the same team of collaborators. "To put it plainly, we just couldn't stop writing songs," Swift explained on social media. "Evermore" was nominated for album of the year at the 2022 Grammys, but lost to Jon Batiste's "We Are." 6 (tie). "Speak Now" Taylor Swift's third album, "Speak Now," was released in 2010. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for six weeks Swift's third album had a lot to live up to, following the blockbuster success of "Fearless." In response to skeptics — who questioned whether the teen phenom was relying too heavily on her collaborators — she decided to write "Speak Now" entirely by herself. Swift is the only songwriter credited on the standard tracklist. 6 (tie). "Midnights" Taylor Swift's 10th album, "Midnights," was released in 2022. Taylor Swift Billboard 200 peak: No. 1 for six weeks Swift's 10th studio album sold over 1 million copies in its debut

events.title: Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' is her newest No. 1 hit. Here are all 16 of her songs that topped the chart.
events.summary: Taylor Swift onstage at the Eras Tour. Shirlaine Forrest/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift's newest single, "Patient Zero," debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Swift has the fourth-most No. 1 hits in history, trailing Elvis, Mariah Carey, and The Beatles. Swift's biggest hits also include "Blank Space," "Anti-Hero," and "The Fate of Ophelia." Since releasing her first No. 1 album in 2008, Taylor Swift has enjoyed a historic run on the charts, topping the Billboard 200 and Billboard Hot 100 over a dozen times each. Swift's collection of chart-toppers includes both radio-friendly pop singles and understated gems pushed to the top of the chart by passionate fans. Most recently, "Patient Zero" joined the ranks of Swift's biggest songs. On the all-time ranking of most No. 1 hits , Swift only trails Elvis, Mariah Carey, and The Beatles. All of Swift's No. 1 songs on the Hot 100 are listed below in chronological order of their peak dates. 1. "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" was released as a single in 2012. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Three Despite writing ubiquitous hits like "You Belong With Me" and "Love Story" earlier in her career (which peaked at No. 2 and No. 4, respectively), "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" was Swift's first-ever song to top the Hot 100. The country-pop crossover smash was released as the lead single from Swift's fourth album, "Red." It rose from No. 72 to No. 1 in its second week of tracking and remained atop the chart for two more weeks. 2. "Shake It Off" "Shake It Off" was released as a single in 2014. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Four "Shake It Off" was released as the lead single from Swift's fifth album, "1989." It became her first No. 1 debut on the Hot 100. 3. "Blank Space" "Blank Space" was released as a single in 2014. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Seven "Blank Space," the second single from "1989," debuted at No. 18 on the Hot 100. It rose to No. 13 before soaring to No. 1 in its third week — dethroning "Shake It Off" and making Swift the first woman in history to replace herself in the chart's top spot. "Blank Space" went on to become one of Swift's biggest hits, reigning atop the chart for nearly two months. 4. "Bad Blood" featuring Kendrick Lamar "Bad Blood" was released as a single in 2015. Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One In May 2015, a remix of "Bad Blood" featuring Kendrick Lamar was released as the fourth single from "1989." It rose from No. 53 to the chart's top spot after the music video premiered at the 2015 Billboard Music Awards and broke the Vevo record for most views in 24 hours. 5. "Look What You Made Me Do" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Three Despite mixed reactions from critics, Swift's lead single from "Reputation" rose to No. 1 after its first full week of tracking, breaking the weekly streaming record for a song by a woman. Once again, Swift's music video broke the record for most views within 24 hours , racking up 43.2 million views in its first day. 6. "Cardigan" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One Swift announced the arrival of her eighth album, "Folklore," just one day in advance. The second track, "Cardigan," was released alongside the album and promoted with a whimsical music video. "Folklore" debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 while "Cardigan" simultaneously debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, making Swift the first artist in history to open atop both charts in the same week. 7. "Willow" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One Just five months after "Folklore," Swift repeated her pandemic-era strategy and surprise-released her ninth album, "Evermore," alongside its lead single. Again, "Willow" debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 while "Evermore" simultaneously debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. 8. "All Too Well (Taylor's Version)" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: One " Red (Taylor's Version) " was the second rerecorded album Swift released. It was accompanied by the long-awaited 10-minute version of " All Too Well ," a fan-favorite track from the original album. "All Too Well (10 Minute Version) (Taylor's Version)" was promoted with a self-directed short film starring Sadie Sink and Dylan O'Brien, a convention-breaking performance on "Saturday Night Live," and plenty of theories about the song's muse . It debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, becoming the longest song in history to top the chart. The record was previously held by Don McLean's "American Pie (Parts I & II)" at 8 minutes and 37 seconds. 9. "Anti-Hero" Taylor Swift/YouTube Weeks at No. 1: Eight "Anti-Hero" was released alongside Swift's 10th album, "Midnights," and promoted as the lead single. It dominated the Hot 100 for eight weeks, surpassing the high-water mark set by "Blank Space." The same week that "Anti-Hero" debuted at No. 1, Swift became the first and only artist in history to occupy the entire top 10 on the Hot 100. The hit single was flanked by "Lavender Haze" (No. 2), "Maroon" (No. 3), "Snow on the Beach" (No. 4), "Midnight Rain" (No. 5), "Bejeweled" (No. 6), "Question...?" (No. 7), "You're On Your Own, Kid" (No. 8), "Karma" (No. 9), and "Vigilante Shit" (No. 10). 10. "Cruel Summer" John Shearer/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Weeks at No. 1: Four "Cruel Summer" was originally released as the second track on Swift's 2019 album "Lover." Although it was identified early as a fan favorite, the song was never promoted as a single and debuted modestly at No. 29 on the Hot 100. Four years later, Swift transformed "Cruel Summer" into a showstopping spectacle on the Eras Tour . Streams of the song began to surge, and it reigned atop Billboard's Pop Airplay chart for two months. Swift's label sent the song to pop radio in June 2023. Finally, following the release of "The Cruelest Summer" EP — which includes a live version of the song and a remix by LP Giobbi — the song reached No. 1 on the Hot 100, marking Swift's milestone 10th chart-topper. 11. "Is It Over Now?" Kevin Winter/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Weeks at No. 1: One "Is It Over Now?" was released as the final vault track on " 1989 (Taylor's Version) ," a rerecording of her beloved fifth album. Although it wasn't initially slated as a single, its enthusiastic reception from fans pushed Swift's team to serve the song to pop radio. "Is It Over Now?" debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100, dethroning "Cruel Summer." Swift remains the only woman in history to replace herself in the top spot, a feat she's now achieved twice. 12. events.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon. Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said. Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet. Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach. Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense. Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating. That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts. When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway. “In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.” Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying. “We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said. In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools. To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do. What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation. “We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained. The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.

events.title: Elon Musk becomes biggest donor of US midterms cycle with $366m spent
events.summary: Musk’s midterm donations, mostly for rightwing candidates and causes, surpass his contributions to Trump in 2024 Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections Elon Musk has become the biggest political donor of the 2026 US midterm elections cycle, funneling about $366m into political groups and campaigns as he backs conservative candidates and rightwing causes. The world’s richest person has poured more than $276m into politics since July alone, some of the most rapid political spending in US history. He’s targeting key races that will determine which party controls the US Senate . The New York Times first reported the spending numbers, which will be released in a federal filing on Thursday. Musk’s spending outpaces his 2024 presidential election contributions, in which he sunk nearly $300m into Donald Trump’s re-election campaign. Musk’s political spending reasserts the SpaceX and Tesla CEO as the top Republican mega-donor and furthers his rightwing political influence. Musk, who led the Trump administration’s efforts to gut federal agencies last year, has become an international linchpin for far-right political movements in recent years as he aligns himself with anti-immigrant, conservative leaders. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives The tech mogul’s spending spree is also a reversal from a period in the middle of last year when Musk claimed he would step back from making such large-scale political donations. The failures of his so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) and costly public backlash to his political influence, as well as a dramatic falling out with Trump, appeared to have dampened his interest in Washington politics. Musk’s spending is spread throughout a series of political action committees, according to Reuters and the New York Times, including his own America Pac. His largest single spend was a $158m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund, a Super Pac working to help Republicans retain control of the Senate. Musk has also given $10m to a Pac supporting Ken Paxton, the Texas Republican Senate candidate who is facing Democratic nominee James Talarico in a closely watched and intense race. Other blockbuster Musk contributions include $76m for America Pac, $20m for the Congressional Leadership Fund Republican Super Pac and $10m for the Republican Governors Association. Musk also gave $10m in January to Nate Morris, a Kentucky Republican Senate candidate who withdrew from the race in May after accepting an offer to become the US ambassador to Colombia. Some of Musk’s money is going to advertising and messaging campaigns that focus on anti-transgender rhetoric and accuse Democratic candidates of being radical socialists. Musk has long used X, the social media platform he owns, to target his political opponents , push election misinformation and attack trans rights. Over the weekend, he reposted a video from America Pac that showed Talarico’s previous statements on gender, calling it “madness”. Musk’s immense spending involves some of the largest political donations in US history, but is still only a tiny fraction of his nearly $1tn wealth. The $366m in midterms spending represents about less than 0.04% of his net worth.

events.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
events.summary: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout. For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies . LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.) Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly. LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck. “A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.” Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors. The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.” Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck. The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said. events.title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Related to AI’s impact on app development, Google said it’s also building better ways to curate the Google Play experience — for instance, by leveraging Google’s AI to create a personalized game recommendation engine, called Game Finder. The feature, first available in the U.S. in English, will be based on what the user likes to play combined with Google’s knowledge derived from its game community’s 1.2 billion players. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. events.title: The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people | Letters
events.summary: The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people Terry Peach responds to Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech, while Penelope Turton writes on her promise to cut inheritance tax Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech rehearsed the argument that Andy Burnham’s economic policies were warped by his “nostalgia” for the 1970s, unlike her own forward-looking programme for “a better tomorrow” ( Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan, 7 October ). She appears not to see that her preference for a lesser-regulated capitalist market economy, with lower public expenditure, taxes and national debt, coupled with “tough love” welfare policies, is itself harking back to arguments that have circulated for centuries. Admittedly, her position is not as extreme as the one espoused at the beginning of the 19th century by the leading political economist David Ricardo, who argued that Great Britain would be happy and prosperous if the “evil” of the national debt was extinguished completely, and the country embraced a system in which trade is left “perfectly free” and taxation reduced to a bare minimum. His own “tough love” proposal was to scrap the Poor Laws, as they encouraged overbreeding by the working class, thereby depressing market-determined wages. Terry Peach Chester Kemi Badenoch says “people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort” and regards inheritance tax (IHT) as unfair double taxation on people who have already paid tax on their earnings. In fact, most IHT revenue is driven by inherited and asset-derived wealth, which expands through unearned capital appreciation and is untaxed during a person’s lifetime. Badenoch has elsewhere called IHT immoral . The real moral injury is borne by all those low-paid, hard-working people who face a choice between heating or eating, and for whom acquiring sufficient wealth in a lifetime to leave money to their children is an unimaginable dream. events.title: US home sales rose in September, but slowed from a year earlier
events.summary: Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers. Existing home sales rose 1.5% last month from August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday. One of the factors in the monthly increase is that sales in August were revised lower. Sales fell 2.2% compared with September last year. The latest sales tally is slightly above the 3.98 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet. Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2-million. September is the second month in a row that the annual sales pace has remained below 4 million. Home prices continued to rise nationally last month. The U.S. median sales price increased 1.3% in September from a year earlier to $417,500, an all-time high for the month of September based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis for 39 months in a row. “This is a very tough market out there, especially with mortgage rates rising,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. This year, sales have been in a rut in large part due to rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have marched higher in the months since the war between the U.S. and Iran started in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher. The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage hit 7.4% last week , its highest level in nearly three years. It briefly dipped below 6% before the war started. Many of the homes purchased last month likely went under contract in August and July, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.43% to 6.69%, according to Freddie Mac. Mortgage rates are not likely to drop meaningfully any time soon, given the ongoing uncertainty over oil prices, geopolitical tensions, the exploding U.S. government debt and other factors that have been driving rates on home loans higher, Yun said. Jordan, Austin Butler in 1st look at 'Miami Vice '85' Homebuyers should consider mortgage rates at 7%, or slightly above 7%, “the new normal,” he said. The sharp rise in mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, has led many would-be home shoppers to put their home shopping plans on hold. However, those who can afford to buy at current rates, or pay all cash, have a much wider selection of homes to choose from than they've had in years as properties sit on the market longer. Although home inventory levels remain below historical norms, there were 1.6 million unsold homes at the end of last month — the highest level of unsold inventory on the market since November 2019, NAR said. All told, unsold home inventory rose 1.9% last month from August and climbed 4.6% from September last year, NAR said. September’s month-end inventory translates to a 4.8-months’ supply at the current sales pace. Traditionally, a 4- to 6-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers. The more balanced market gives home shoppers potentially more leverage in negotiating better terms with sellers, especially if a property has not fetched offers in weeks or months. Consider, in September, the national median home listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250 as about 21% of listings had their initial price lowered, according to Realtor.com. “The market is clearly tilting in favor of buyers able to negotiate for better prices,” Yun said. events.title: CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle case over opioid prescriptions
events.summary: CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids WASHINGTON -- CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of prescribing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.” It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.” The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids. The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden's administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills," or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says. Under the settlement, CVS must also "implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently. Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart. events.title: Cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems hits 700 supermarkets
events.summary: Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France PARIS -- Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France’s food supplies but acknowledged that the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” ″It was a wake-up call for everyone,” he said. The Paris prosecutor’s office said Tuesday that its cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack, including the extent of damage caused by spoiled food and possible fires. Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French grocery chain Cooperative U, said 80 of the company’s 2,000 stores were affected. Most managed to prevent disruptions to refrigeration, but some had to discard food, he said in a post on X. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products is an attack on the French food supply chain. It is unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable,” Schelcher said. Danish technology company Danfoss, which supplied the refrigeration management software, said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates. “Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall,” the company said. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Danfoss said it was working with affected customers to limit the damage. events.title: UK's Burnham weighs approval for oil and gas drilling in the North Sea
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces a crucial decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea LONDON -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing a key test of his environmental policies as he decides on whether oil and gas companies should be allowed to drill in the North Sea. Burnham's government has been under heavy pressure from climate campaigners and businesses over whether to approve two oil and gas fields in waters north of Scotland, including one said to be the U.K.'s largest untapped oil resource. Environmental groups have urged Burnham to refuse permission for the projects, known as Rosebank and Jackdaw, saying they would accelerate climate change at a time when the U.K., like the rest of Europe, faces record extreme heat linked to human actions including burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. But opposition politicians, the oil and gas industry and U.S. President Donald Trump have piled pressure on Burnham to give the green light, arguing it would protect jobs, cut household bills and boost Britain’s energy security. British officials have been expected to make a decision since August, when public consultations on the two projects closed. Rosebank is an oil field that also will produce gas. Located 80 miles (130 kilometers) north of Scotland's Shetland Islands, it is estimated to be the largest undeveloped oil and gas field in the U.K., reportedly with capacity to produce 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil within about 25 years. Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles east of Aberdeen on Scotland's northeast coast. Production there was expected to last under a decade. The Shell Group, one of the project's co-developers, predicts the field can produce around 6.5% of the U.K.’s gas production at its peak. The opposition Conservative Party, which has pushed for the developments to go ahead, said the Jackdaw field could start heating 1.4 million homes in the U.K. this winter if approved. The former Conservative government previously approved production at both sites, which were scheduled to start operations later this year. But a court in Edinburgh ruled last year that the approvals were unlawful, after considering a legal challenge from Greenpeace and another nonprofit. “The public interest in authorities acting lawfully and the private interest of members of the public in climate change outweigh the private interest of the developers,” judge Andrew Stewart ruled at the time. Critics have argued that the oil and gas reserves in Britain's North Sea holdings are small and would make little difference to energy bills because prices are decided by international markets. They contend that new developments would increase carbon emissions while failing to contribute to Britain's energy security. Analysts at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a London-based nonprofit, estimated that more than 90% of the oil and gas likely to be produced from the North Sea has already been extracted. “We’ve just had record-breaking heat waves this summer, wildfires, half of the country’s still in drought. We’re facing potential crop failures and food shortages this winter from a super El Niño ,” said Victoria Smith, a Fossil Free London activist protesting on Tuesday. events.title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming. The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space. “When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch. So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt , a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch. The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher. Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure. “The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites. Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground. Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year. A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software. Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders. The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said. Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business. One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.” Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites. “If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.
