events.title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’
events.summary: The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI , said Geoffrey Hinton , “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself. The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done. There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s most valuable company singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack. “I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, told the podcaster Ezra Klein . Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it, and particularly his warning that there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades. “That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.” But Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said. “I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.” Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story. The recent unwanted hack of the tech company Hugging Face by a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise. “This used to be the domain of science fiction. You’re going to have AI agents and they’re gonna go rogue. Oh, come off it. And they’ll go rogue and they’re going to learn how to communicate with each other, even though we didn’t think there was a way. Oh, come off it!” said Hinton. “ And when they figure this out, they’re going to have big emotional expressions like, ‘oh my God! ’ Well, of course, they don’t really mean ‘oh my God’. They’re just parroting the words we use. They’re going to learn to sacrifice themselves for the common good! ’ “All this stuff just a few years ago was written off as complete fantasy. And it’s all happened.” He heartily concedes that neither the warnings of AI critics nor the promises of its boosters can rely on precise predictions of what the technology will do. But, he argues, uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. “The unique problem with AI is that if it goes wrong, if it takes over, you don’t get a second chance. We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.” It’s worth noting that Hinton has a record of seeing things where others did not. He toiled in relative obscurity at the University of Toronto during two AI “winters” when his branch of the field – trying to teach machines to operate in a manner similar to the human brain – was considered obscure. He was fixated on the idea that, like the brain, computer systems could be designed to learn patterns from data, rather than to follow only explicit, prewritten rules. “We believed that if you could figure out how the brain learned, machines learned the same way, and you had enough compute power, they would do amazing things,” he said. But the nascent field of neural networks was mocked by his peers.

events.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
events.summary: The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance. Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control. The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power. Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services. The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex. The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives. Google has been developing its own Tensor Processing Units for years, with its latest generation including separate versions optimized for training AI models and running inference. OpenAI is developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom, initially focusing on inference workloads. The company said in August that its first chip was outperforming Nvidia hardware on certain workloads and that it was already developing subsequent generations. Amazon has its own ⁠ Trainium family of AI chips, which are being used by customers including Anthropic. OpenAI has also committed to using Amazon's custom silicon as part of a massive infrastructure agreement. Anthropic confirmed in August that it is exploring its own chip designs, even as it continues to rely on chips from Nvidia, Amazon and other suppliers. Meta also has an internal chip development program, while continuing to buy substantial computing capacity from Nvidia and other suppliers. Between the lines: Nvidia isn't necessarily losing business just because its customers are developing competing chips. Nvidia's revenue more than doubled to $96 billion in the second quarter, a reminder that overall demand for AI computing leaves room for Nvidia chips and new offerings from Microsoft and others. Like Microsoft, most Nvidia competitors are focused on inference, where margins are highest, while Nvidia remains dominant for training. Still, Nvidia has begun to leverage its balance sheet to bankroll the AI buildout , so any competition that even slightly reduces its strength is noteworthy because it could weaken its centrality to continued growth. What they're saying: Building competitive AI hardware requires designing entire systems, optimizing everything from memory and networking to software and power consumption, Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Innovation, told Axios. "We prioritize Maia for inference," Borkar said, describing it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing and an area where Microsoft can distinguish itself on cost and efficiency. "For us, it's not an either-or strategy," she said. "We want a broad ecosystem while investing deeply in our first-party silicon." Yes, but: Microsoft's plans to make Maia its primary inference platform apply specifically to Microsoft's own services, not necessarily to third-party Azure customers, including OpenAI. Borkar also cautioned that the shift won't happen overnight. Maia 300 deployments will begin in 2027, but reaching multi-gigawatt scale will take time, extending beyond next year. The catch: As Axios ⁠ previously reported , companies developing their own chips remain dependent on the same limited manufacturing capacity, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia relies on. That means even if custom chips can reduce dependence on Nvidia, they don't eliminate broader supply-chain constraints. The bottom line: Nvidia remains central to the AI boom, but its biggest customers increasingly want to control more of the technology powering their own services — and capture more of the economic benefits for themselves.

events.title: Dems' red-state showings raise prospect of a bigger 2028 map
events.summary: Data: RealClearPolitics , American Presidency Project ; Note: Nebraska's Senate race is between a Republican and an independent; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Move over Wisconsin and Arizona. With Democrats making Republicans sweat in a host of red-state Senate races , a new batch of swing states may be emerging. Why it matters: Some of the closest Senate races are in Nebraska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and even Kansas. Sure, this could be a blip — or a reminder that it's a 50-50 moody nation, even in a bunch of red states. The conditions that helped Barack Obama carry conservative states like Indiana and North Carolina in 2008 — an unpopular war, a bruising economy, an electorate hungry for change — could resonate again in 2028. State of play: Democratic and Republican Senate candidates are running margin-of-error races in red states that not long ago were thought to be forbidding, or even a wasted effort, to many Democrats. The Senate races in Kansas and Ohio are tied. So is Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn is trying to knock off Sen. Pete Ricketts. Democrat James Talarico has consistently led polls in Texas, though that race appears to be tightening as money pours into the state on behalf of Republican Ken Paxton. Alaska is also a toss-up. President Trump won all these states by double digits in 2024. Zoom in: Republican operatives told Axios they're far from convinced that what's happening now will create a new slate of swing states in the 2028 race for the White House. They see the current campaign as more of a one-off — a combination of dismay with Trump, high prices and uninspiring candidates. "None of those states will be targeted [by Democrats] in the 2028 presidential. I will bet big money on that. But … all are in danger this year," one GOP consultant told Axios. "It's a function of the atmosphere that we're playing defense in R+15 states. There's lethargy on our side," a Republican pollster said. "I don't think they're the new swing states per se." But Democrats say better-than-expected performances by their candidates in several red states would at least open the door to an expanded map — with a big "if." "An opening, yes," Obama's former chief strategist, David Axelrod, told Axios. "A guarantee, hardly." Obama, he said, spent an enormous amount of time in rural communities and got to know voters. The Democrats who are faring well in those places this year have made a point of speaking with, not at, conservatives. Yes, but: There's no certainty that Democrats will prevail in red states this year, much less set a path for 2028. Polls are narrowing in several other Senate battlegrounds besides Texas, and the polling industry has had enough misses and challenges in recent elections to raise questions about whether we're getting an accurate picture of the political landscape at this time. Either way, it's safe to say Democrats have made things interesting for the Nov. 3 election. The big picture: The backlash against Trump has set the tone in many of these surprisingly competitive Senate surprise states, but Democrats also have also benefited from factors specific to each race. In Ohio, former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is better known than the incumbent, Sen. Jon Husted (R). In Texas, Democrats have a seminarian candidate in James Talarico who's emphasized the Bible's teachings as Republicans have tried to tag him as a radical leftist. His opponent, Ken Paxton, has been dogged by corruption allegations throughout the race. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is the pastor of the largest United Methodist church in the country. His opponent, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, has been hurt by reports that his former medical practice sued patients for even small unpaid bills, and that his 2020 campaign stiffed a bakery on a $700 bill. What we're watching: To build on any openings Democrats might realize this year, the party will need a 2028 candidate who can appeal to center-right voters the way Democrats in red states have this year, Axelrod said. "Part of the long-term problem for Democrats has been that it's still a party of working people, but it often approaches working people — especially in small towns in rural areas, in the spirit of missionaries and anthropologists," Axelrod said. Like, "we're here to help you become more like us." So in 2028, he added,"it depends on who the candidate is, and what kind of bonds of trust that candidate can build."

events.title: What Flock Actually Costs Cities Across the Country
events.summary: In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety , the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount. In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet. WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from public records requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism . Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station. It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment. Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story. WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight. “Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.” When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using. A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia . In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access. “We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.” Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000. As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI , Ring , and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country. “A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work. In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova. Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates. The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment. Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.

events.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
events.summary: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

events.title: He Waited Nine Years in Prison for His Lawyer to File a Single Brief. In This State, There’s No Rule Against It.
events.summary: Mark Harris for ProPublica. Source images: Alejandro A. Alvarez/The Philadelphia Inquirer, courtesy of Patrick Hickson, court records. In 2020, seven years after he was appointed to represent a client who claimed he was wrongly convicted, attorney Scott Galloway told the judge that he was still looking into the case and needed more time.   “I am still in the process of interviewing individuals,” the lawyer wrote to the judge in Delaware County, outside Philadelphia, who had already granted him 32 extensions.  His client, Nolan O’Neal, had been a 20-year-old high school student when he was arrested for murder by Chester police, who had four eyewitnesses identifying him. At his 2005 trial, those witnesses all recanted, saying police had pressured them to accuse O’Neal.  By the time Galloway joined the case, in 2013, O’Neal had already spent eight years in prison insisting he was innocent. The lawyer’s job was to help him file a petition under Pennsylvania’s Post Conviction Relief Act. That law provided a narrow path to freedom if Galloway could find crucial new evidence or prove that previous lawyers had mishandled the case. But court records do not show that the attorney did much other than ask for more time.  In 2022, after nine years, one unsuccessful request to access evidence and 41 extensions, Galloway filed a two-page petition addressing just one of the many issues O’Neal had wanted him to raise. It would not be enough to get O’Neal his day in court.  Nolan O’Neal visits with his sister, Erin O’Neal, earlier this year at the State Correctional Institution Chester, where he is incarcerated. Courtesy of Erin O’Neal For more than half a century, Pennsylvania has promised people who claim they didn’t get a fair trial the right to “effective” post-conviction legal representation, regardless of their ability to pay. That’s more than most states promise people after they have been convicted and lost their appeals.   Yet Pennsylvania has done little to fulfill that promise. The Philadelphia Inquirer and ProPublica previously reported that Pennsylvania lets lawyers resolve cases quickly using a practice that is discouraged in several states: filing “no-merit” letters, also known as Finley letters, urging judges to reject their clients’ handwritten or typed claims. In Philadelphia, dozens who had received such letters later had their convictions or sentences overturned based on issues their lawyers had rejected or overlooked .  But the problems go deeper than that: The state’s loose rules and its failure to fund post-conviction work have made the type of breakdown O’Neal encountered a recurring feature of this system.  By filing public records requests with courts serving all 67 Pennsylvania counties and analyzing a decade of court dockets, an Inquirer and ProPublica investigation found that the system Pennsylvania set up to protect the right to counsel instead allows, or even encourages, shoddy representation. The news organizations found that: Unlike in other types of appeals, attorneys handling post-conviction cases work under no particular timeline and are allowed numerous extensions. The state also has no standards regarding how many cases lawyers should be assigned, and many counties ask lawyers to sign contracts that set no limit on the number of cases courts can assign them. At least 250 people have languished in prison for five years or longer while waiting for their lawyers to act. Unlike some other states , such as North Carolina and New York, Pennsylvania requires no specific training, experience or qualifications for appointed post-trial lawyers, and it holds them to few standards. Lawyers are not required to speak to their clients or take other basic investigative steps before withdrawing from cases by writing no-merit letters. Pennsylvania, which lags behind almost every other state in funding legal defense for poor people, known as indigent defense, dedicates no money for post-trial work. Instead, it leaves it up to each individual county to set pay rates. A majority of county court systems use flat-rate fee structures that some other states ban. While almost every county in the state has a public defender office, most post-conviction cases are handled by private lawyers who are paid hourly, by the case or by the year and work with little to no supervision. Our review of court records found pay as low as $500 per case and delays as long as 19 years without a single court filing.  In some counties, contracted lawyers’ backlogs spanned dozens of cases. In Chester County, an affluent region west of Philadelphia, a lawyer left cases untouched for as long as two years before the county ended his contract last fall.   Delaware County, where O’Neal was convicted, relies on a group of part-time lawyers to handle most of its post-trial matters. One is Galloway, who has handled 20 or 30 post-trial cases per year for the county in addition to running his own law practice and, for a time, holding local elected office. Galloway said that his ethical obligation to confidentiality prevented him from commenting on O’Neal’s case. Judge George A. Pagano, who granted him 41 extensions on O’Neal’s case, declined to comment. In the years Galloway was on the case, O’Neal wrote him dozens of letters from state prison, proposing legal arguments and sending leads to investigate.  “It is a daunting and exhausting task to navigate this legal process and be heard,” O’Neal said in an interview. “We at times even have to fight the attorneys who are supposed to represent us.”  In 2020, he received a letter from the brother of the murder victim, admitting that his testimony against O’Neal was a lie. “I want to fix it. I know my brother would want me to. It’s been long enough,” he wrote. O’Neal said he pleaded with Galloway to track down the man.  In 2022, Galloway attached the brother’s signed statement to a sparse two-page brief, which mentioned none of the other issues O’Neal had raised nine years earlier or the other witnesses who’d come forward over the years. The judge started the process of dismissing the claim. One reason: The filing had been made too late. O’Neal is still fighting his case, now with a new court-appointed lawyer. Dear Judge Pagano: I am writing to your attention as I have grave and urgent concerns about my current appointed attorney Scott D. Galloway, who you have appointed to represent me on my PCRA petition pending in your court. This is the best I can do to bring matters to your attention as my filings are going unanswered. Delays and Extensions Before they are assigned a lawyer, Pennsylvania prisoners must write the first draft of their post-conviction filing on their own within a strict one-year deadline. events.summary: Drivers in three key swing states are about to see even more billboards blaming President Donald Trump for rising prices, according to details shared first with Semafor. Home of the Brave is nearly doubling its billboard campaign in Michigan, Ohio, and Iowa, adding $1 million in new billboards on top of the $1.25 million the group already spent. The new plans bring the group’s total billboards across those three states to more than 350. The billboards hit Trump for higher grocery prices, ding Republicans for supporting Trump’s tariffs, and link gas prices to the unpopular Iran war. They’re intended to help Democratic Senate and House candidates that will determine congressional control. “Job number one is winning back Congress. Once we do that, we can start finally holding this administration accountable,” said Home of the Brave advisory board member Sarah Longwell.

events.title: Dubai inflation eases even as fuel costs rise
events.summary: Dubai's inflation rate eased slightly in September from the previous month, even as rising oil prices pushed up the cost of petrol. Inflation on an annual basis stood at 5.03 per cent, down from the 5.54 per cent recorded in August and the 5.7 per cent peak for this year reached in June. The figures were released by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Dubai’s General Monthly Consumer Price Index decreased by 0.05 per cent month-on-month in September on falling airfares and cheaper holiday packages. Airfares on a monthly basis fell by 23.44 per cent and holiday packages dropped 12.47 per cent from the August level. However, on an annual basis, the transport division was the biggest contributor to the rise in consumer prices in September, climbing 14.7 per cent. The increase in transport charges was driven by a 37.52 per cent rise in the cost of fuels and lubricants for personal transport, as well as a 13.48 per cent rise in passenger transport by air, according to the latest government data. Biggest contributor The transport segment, which accounts for 9 per cent of Dubai’s Consumer Price Index basket, has been the main driver of inflation in the emirate over the past several months amid a rise in prices petrol prices . The UAE lifted fuel subsidies in 2015 and prices are evaluated on a monthly basis, based on movements in global markets. Petrol prices in the Emirates rose for a third consecutive month for October as prices in global oil markets remain elevated amid escalating geopolitical concerns in the Middle East. Global crude prices, which surged by nearly 109 per cent during the peak of the war, now in its eighth month, are still more than 70 per cent higher on concerns of a possible resumption in fighting between the US and Iran . Brent crude, which hovered around the $110 per barrel mark in September, has largely remained above $100 over the past few weeks. The West Texas Intermediate benchmark passed $105 a barrel in September as the Strait of Hormuz remained a flashpoint. Increasing attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the Red Sea by the Houthi rebels in Yemen have added another layer of risk to energy supplies from the region. Rebound Despite economic headwinds, Dubai's economy has largely skirted the deeper slump experienced by some neighbours. Non-oil private sector business activity in the emirate, which is one of the largest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Purchasing Managers' Index stood at 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, indicating a “solid improvement” in Dubai, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026, S&P Global Markets Intelligence said earlier this month. The boost to the emirate’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven by a “sharp and accelerated increase in output” as new orders also rose markedly and employment in the emirate rose, according to the PMI survey data. The tourism and retail sectors in the emirate have also bounced back from the initial shock of the war. Property, among the top contributors to the emirate’s economy, has also held up relatively well. The food and drinks category increased by an annualised 8.05 per cent last month, while housing, water, electricity, gas and domestic fuel rose by almost 6.23 per cent, “as a result of the growth of the average residential rental prices in most areas of the emirate during September”, the latest government data shows.

events.title: Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
events.summary: Why Germany is backing tougher EU trade defenses against China Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base. Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices. In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate. Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue. Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means." China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week. Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction." Before the COVID pandemic , the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent . Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026. Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking , precision engineering and chemicals industries. Why Berlin's China policy is changing German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025. Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures . In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports. "After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW. Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments." Industry pressure grows for trade defenses Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt: "We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August. According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026. While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home. Business groups question industrial policy proposals The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies. Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory. How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials? The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally." Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

events.title: Market turns cold on luxury after LVMH’s China letdown
events.summary: LVMH on Oct 12 posted a 5% drop in organic sales at its fashion and leather goods division, which generates nearly half of group revenue. LVMH’s weaker-than-expected quarterly fashion and leather goods sales, hit by a deterioration in Chinese consumer demand for its flagship Louis Vuitton brand, have raised fresh doubts about the luxury industry’s recovery prospects. Four sell-side analysts have cut their target price on LVMH shares by an average 9% following the results, the first quarterly report by a major sector player, expecting the miss to also signal weak performance at some of its competitors. LVMH shares were down 1.5% by 7.30am GMT ( 3.30pm Singapore time) . Its peers Hermes, Kering and Richemont were down by a similar degree. Europe’s leading luxury groups, mired in a three-year slowdown, have lost around €330 billion ( S$472.79 billion ) in market value since the start of 2026 , with LVMH alone shedding roughly 40%. “Despite the recent share price weakness, we expect some further pressure on the space as a whole today, with confirmation that the Chinese cluster seems to have taken a material (and bigger than feared) step down”, JPMorgan analysts said in a note to clients. LVMH on Oct 12 posted a 5% drop in organic sales at its fashion and leather goods division, which generates nearly half of group revenue, missing expectations in a Visible Alpha consensus for a 1.8% decline. The group said a “less buoyant environment” in China impacted its revenues, contributing to 1% organic sales growth overall, excluding currency swings, to €18.5 billion, below expectations for 1.3% growth. Asked about Louis Vuitton’s recovery prospects in a call with analysts, the group’s Chief Financial Officer Cecile Cabanis said: “It takes a bit of time, but I don’t think there are a lot of shortcuts here”. Adding to investor concerns, growth in LVMH’s watches and jewellery division, home to brands including Bulgari and Tiffany, slowed to 6% from 9% in the first half of 2026 , marking a changing trend in one of luxury’s few bright spots. events.title: IMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’
events.summary: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’ John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain. Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. “The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.” Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok. Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January . But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”. In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll. Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.” The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July . UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise. However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%. Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer. The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve , European Central Bank and Bank of Japan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets. The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher. Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive. “There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said. The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year. It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs. Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter. A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

events.title: What to know about the Nord Stream pipeline explosions trial opening in Germany this week
events.summary: A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago BERLIN -- A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany this week over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago in one of the biggest acts of sabotage in Europe since the Second World War. The suspect faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure, according to prosecutors . The attack laid bare Europe's dependence on Russian energy but also raised sensitive questions about Ukraine and its Western allies. While international observers initially blamed Moscow, there are now increasing suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies. According to German privacy rules, the suspect will be identified in court only as Serhii K., although he was publicly named as Serhii Kuznietsov in extradition proceedings in Italy . Here's what we know about the alleged ringleader of the attack and one of the most politically charged court cases of wartime sabotage that will be heard at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg starting this Wednesday. The explosions on Sept. 26, 2022, damaged pipelines that were built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations. The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that set off from the German port of Rostock. It had been hired from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries. The explosions ruptured the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which was Russia’s main natural gas supply route to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which never entered service because Germany suspended its certification process shortly before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The suspect allegedly organized and carried out the detonation of at least four bombs between 14 and 27 kilograms (around 31 to 62 pounds) at a depth of 70 to 80 meters (230 feet to 263 feet) near the Danish island of Bornholm. He was detained in August in an Italian village, where officers raided a bungalow where he was staying with his family. Police said he surrendered without resistance. He was extradited to Germany in November. A second suspect was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August. He has applied for asylum in Croatia to fight his extradition to Germany. The pipelines were long a target of criticism by the U.S. and some of its allies, which warned that they increased dependence on Russian gas. Russian officials, however, have claimed that U.S. and British intelligence agencies were involved in staging the explosions, which Moscow declared “an act of international terrorism,” and have launched their own investigation. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Russia has also accused NATO of involvement in the attack, while several Western countries initially blamed Russia. More recently, the Kremlin has expressed hope that those who orchestrated the explosions will be held accountable. Asked what Moscow expects from the trial, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that “we expect objectivity.” “We expect … that both the perpetrators and those who ordered it will be named. That would be very important. I think no one doubts who it really is,” Peskov said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts. He also told reporters in August that Ukraine’s prosecutors and Foreign Ministry were already cooperating with partners and that Kyiv was “absolutely open to joint steps on the investigation,” stressing the importance of keeping Europe’s trust. Nonetheless, “all the evidence points very clearly to the fact that Ukraine blew up the Nord Stream pipelines, not the Russians, whom they initially tried to pin the blame on,” says Joachim Weber, a security expert at the Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies at the University of Bonn. “This is, of course, highly explosive politically, because, as is well known, Germany is one of Ukraine’s closest allies, supporting the country on a massive scale with huge sums of money and also by taking on considerable political risks,” Weber said.

events.title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
events.summary: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments. Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not. Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work. I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness. You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit. You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged. It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July. You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way. A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September. The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600. I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss. You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record. Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: ‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothes
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively? The small stockroom of St Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, south London, is rammed with donations. “On average, we get 30 to 50 bags a day,” says Caroline Worley, the commercial manager, “but it’s not unusual to receive over 100.” This might sound like a good problem to have, but the sheer volume of stuff is the shop’s biggest challenge. “Sometimes, there’s only [enough] floor space to tiptoe,” says 48-year-old store manager, Colin French. Rummaging through the donations, it’s clear that much is unsaleable: a smelly, soiled bathrobe, tatty trainers, heavily bobbled jumpers, old socks, an empty Swarovski jewellery case. “Absolutely typical,” says Worley. They’re also overwhelmed with deluges of low-quality fashion – a shift in donation habits that accelerated during Covid, because, says Worley, all that time at home enabled people to sell their best stuff on Vinted. The experience here echoes that of author Tansy Hoskins, whose latest book, Charity Shop World , paints a picture of a charity retail sector in crisis. She spent 16 months working in a London charity shop, sorting through “daily avalanches” of clothing, which swamped “all the other categories put together”. Everyone Hoskins interviewed said similar: “quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste.” The problem is nationwide. Since the book came out, she’s “been contacted by managers of charity shops around the country – for example, Nottingham, Accrington, Newcastle – all saying that most of what they’re getting is waste.” It is, of course, our waste. According to Jose Baladron of Traid, which has 12 shops across London, shopping for new clothes is “through the roof – the UK is the highest consumer of clothing in Europe by far ”. “That obviously translates to more donations, which is far too much to process in small shops.” Hoskins routinely found that ultra-fast-fashion donations would “still have tags on – it was clear people had received their online purchases and gone, ‘What the hell is this?’ It wasn’t even wearable so they’d just donate it.” On average, charity shops only manage to sell about 25% of clothing donations, according to Baladron (a figure replicated by a University of Southampton study ). “So they rely heavily on the ragman” to shift the rest. Yet the price of rag has “plummeted”, according to Merryn Haines-Gadd of the environmental action charity Wrap, “due to the saturation of low-quality fast fashion”. Ten years ago, a charity might have been paid 50-60p per kilo. “Now you’re lucky to get 10p,” says Baladron. Plus there’s only so much the ragman can take. For anything they can’t take, charity shops have to pay to have it collected as waste. At St Raphael’s, some of that has included, according to Worley, saucepans with food still in the bottom, babies’ soiled sleep-suits and used sanitary products. “[Staff] can get a bit worn down when people are donating stuff that isn’t saleable,” says Libby Gordon, CEO of Fara, which has 39 charity shops in London. “Plus there’s a time cost for us to process it all.” Factor in rising utility costs and national insurance payments, and “charity shops are in a perfect storm”, says Hoskins. In June, the British Heart Foundation announced plans to close 150 of its 651 stores; its latest accounts indicate that its retail arm lost £3.3m last year. Cancer Research is part-way through a 190-shop closure programme, and rumours are swirling that up to 100 Oxfam shops might close (which the charity has denied ). Some are fighting back. Fara’s new in-store poster campaign advises would-be donators: “If you’d be happy to give it to a friend, we’d be delighted to receive it.” Items should be “clean, complete, and in good condition” , states their online guide . But just as people “wish cycle” by chucking unrecyclables into the recycling, so do people “wish give”. I certainly struggle to accept that something with life left in it, however worn, can’t be useful to someone. This mentality, however, creates unpleasant work and costs for charities – even more so when people leave donations outside a closed charity shop (technically, it’s fly-tipping, and charity shops do often check their CCTV, record numberplates and report such crimes). These bags are often soiled by foxes or dogs, ripped open and/or rained on. At St Raphael’s, staff have found soiled mattresses, ripped sofas and even an old toilet dumped outside: “It leaves us with a big problem,” says Worley. Disposal at scale is an expensive business.

events.title: Visa approved to prepare domestic payments business in China
events.summary: Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa won approval from the People’s Bank of China to prepare a domestic bank card clearing business, after seeking entry since 2017. The firm must finish preparatory work within one year before applying for a licence, joining Mastercard and American Express in China’s huge payments market. The move ends a long trade dispute issue, but Visa faces a market now dominated by Alipay and WeChat Pay, with 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation in 2025. BEIJING – Visa received approval to begin preparations to establish a domestic bank card clearing business in China, as the firm follows rivals Mastercard and American Express in serving the country’s massive payments market. “We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” Visa chief executive Ryan McInerney said in the statement. The company’s Beijing unit won the green-light from the People’s Bank of China, the official Xinhua News Agency reported on Oct 13. It must complete preparatory work within one year before applying to commence operations and obtaining the clearing business licence, Xinhua added. Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion (S$184 trillion) payments market and marks the end to its years-long pursuit. Visa applied for the licence in 2017, local media reported. Competitor Mastercard received approval to establish its bank card clearing business in 2020, and Amex’s joint venture in the country was approved to start bank card clearing services several months after that. For years, the battle for entry into China’s massive domestic clearing market was a primary friction point in the broader trade dispute between the world’s two largest economies. Earlier in 2026, US President Donald Trump said he brought up Visa’s request for access to China’s market during a meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing . Visa’s CEO McInerney accompanied Trump on that May trip to China. Xi later met his counterpart in Washington in late September, with both agreeing on a trade truce extension . The two are scheduled to talk again in person on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November. China first signalled an opening in the sector in June 2015, announcing that foreign bank card clearing providers could apply for licences by establishing local units or through acquisitions. The move was designed to dismantle the longstanding monopoly held by state-run China UnionPay. While the approval marks a significant milestone, Visa is entering a market that looks very different from the one it first sought to enter. China’s payments ecosystem is now dominated by domestic mobile platforms Alipay and WeChat Pay, which have largely bypassed traditional card networks and become the primary channels for everyday transactions. China had 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation at the end of 2025, with transaction value totalling 963.6 trillion yuan (S$184 trillion) in 2025, according to the People’s Bank of China. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Cost of living struggles inspire 'social supermarket'
events.summary: Thomas Cliffe and Laura Steele welcomed customers into the store for the first time on Monday "Instead of going to a food bank, being handed a bag and getting back home then finding out that they won't use all those items, at least here they can buy the tokens and shop around for the items they would choose to buy." Founder Thomas Cliffe hopes the first "social supermarket" in Newcastle-under-Lyme, designed to help people struggling with the cost of living, will offer the "freedom to shop with dignity". Set up by Community Cupboard NUL CIC, the store allows members to buy groceries at cost price or below, with more choice than other outlets. Customers can sign up for a membership costing £1 for 12 months. They are then able to purchase tokens to spend on items throughout the store. Newcastle's first 'social supermarket' Cliffe said the idea was inspired by his own experience after leaving work because of anxiety. Although his wife was still employed, he said the couple struggled financially and found they were unable to access some forms of support. "It was horrible because you start to panic and think: 'What am I supposed to do? Where am I going to get the next food from?'" "We either had to choose a meal or choose the bills." Cheryl Peeper found that the store was helpful to keep her ticking over to the next big shop without spending to much. The supermarket opened for the first time on Monday. Such stores aim to cut food waste while helping people facing food insecurity by selling surplus goods at lower prices. "It was exciting to have everyone come through the doors for the first time and give them that freedom to shop with dignity," Cliffe said. Voluntary co-director Laura Steele said the level of need in the area often went unnoticed. "One in four children experience poverty from what we have found, and the average income is £29,000." "There was nothing really for the people of Newcastle and it was crying out for it really," she said. Cheryl Pepper, a carer who visited after finishing a night shift, described the supermarket as "absolutely brilliant". "The food's cheap. If you go to Tesco you spend £100, but you come in here, I've put £20 on and I still have some tokens left," she said. Fiona Morris was one of the first to purchase items from the store. Recent research on the growth of social supermarkets , external backed the idea that they were less off-putting than food banks and large commercial stores for those facing food insecurity. But lead researcher, Dr Claire O'Malley from Teesside University, said: "While social supermarkets can improve access to affordable food and reduce waste in the short term, they should not be viewed as a complete solution to food insecurity." The report called for them to supplement, rather than replace, government support for those struggling to put good food on the table. Fiona Morris, who has ADHD, said she had often found large supermarkets overwhelming. After visiting the new store, she said she immediately felt understood by staff. "It feels like Supermarket Sweep - I feel like I'm robbing the place," she said. events.title: Singapore firm eyes hub in Japan for start-up talent in Asia
events.summary: Insignia Ventures Partners’ Yinglan Tan said the academy will train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to bridge the two regions. Insignia Ventures Partners and Iwate Prefecture plan a start-up academy in north-eastern Japan to train talent from South-east Asia and Japan and link the two regions. Yinglan Tan and Governor Takuya Tasso are due to sign an agreement in Morioka, but the opening date has not yet been decided. Iwate hopes the project will boost regional revival and offset ageing, while the site in Hanamaki may need housing, transport and renovation support. SINGAPORE – A Singaporean venture capital firm is planning to launch an academy in north-eastern Japan in partnership with a local Japanese government to develop start-up talent in and around Asia, according to sources familiar with the project. Insignia Ventures Partners and the Iwate prefectural government are crafting a plan to create a start-up hub in Iwate Prefecture by drawing international talent into the broader Tohoku region – a development the two sides hope will lead to increased investment in Japan by fast-growing South-east Asian economies. Yinglan Tan, founding managing partner of Insignia Ventures Partners, and Iwate Governor Takuya Tasso are scheduled to sign an agreement for the project on the sidelines of the Iwate International Convention, set to take place from Oct 29 to Oct 30 in Morioka, the prefectural capital. However, the two sides have yet to decide on a date to open the hub. Founded in 2017, Insignia Ventures Partners has invested in more than 90 companies in Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore and Taiwan, among other markets, and manages $1 billion in assets. The firm and the Iwate government started talks on the project after Tan and Tasso met during the Summer Davos forum in Dalian, north-eastern China, in 2024. Tan said the academy aims to train young people from South-east Asia and Japan to serve as a bridge between the two regions by combining knowledge of Japanese business culture with an understanding of the diversity of South-east Asian markets. According to prefectural officials, Iwate hopes the project will spur regional revitalisation and ease the impact of its ageing population. The facility will serve as the Iwate campus of the Insignia Ventures Academy, which is based in Singapore. According to the plan, the Iwate campus would offer in-person programmes. Insignia Ventures Partners reports that the Singapore academy has produced more than 250 graduates through its 12-week core programme on venture investment fundamentals. Graduates have joined portfolio companies or launched businesses, and the Iwate campus would be its first base outside Singapore. According to Iwate officials, the planned site of the academy is in Hanamaki, which is south of Morioka. The Iwate government plans to sell the 41,900 sq m Towa High School property, which closed in 2010, to the Singaporean firm. The Iwate government is considering earmarking renovation subsidies for the project, the officials said. Serving as a transportation hub in the Tohoku region, Hanamaki features Iwate Hanamaki Airport, Shin-Hanamaki Station on the Tohoku Shinkansen Line and the Tohoku Expressway. Tomokazu Sugawara, the executive director of the Management Support Division of the Iwate prefectural government, addressed the host prefecture’s need to develop accommodation and transportation for prospective students and faculty. “We recognise the need for such infrastructure so that instructors and students can travel from Singapore and other parts of the world to stay at the school,” Sugawara said. events.title: NVIDIA Lands in Europe for GTC Berlin
events.summary: NVIDIA is in Europe, showcasing the future of technology together with the region’s developers, researchers and industry leaders. It all leads up to NVIDIA GTC Berlin, taking place October 20-22. This is the place to find the latest — stay tuned for rolling coverage of the events and news. October 12 – 24, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers France Gathers for Innovation — and Huang Meets With President Macron Salle des Tirages, a historic hall on Place Vendôme, has hosted events of consequence for more than a century. On Tuesday evening, it held France's latest ecosystem moment as founders, policymakers, researchers and press gathered for NVIDIA's France AI Ecosystem Reception. NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang took the stage to discuss NVIDIA’s investments in Europe and the need for safe and secure technology development. “Europe is one of the great regions of industrial manufacturing,” Huang said. “This is the beginning of the AI journey for the EU.” Roland Lescure, France's Minister of the Economy, joined Huang onstage to talk about France’s strategy for innovation and economic growth. “We want Europe to enjoy this revolution that’s going to create prosperity, jobs and revenue,” Lescure said. “For this we need pioneers.” As attendees mingled at the reception, crowds gathered around a couple tiny guests: Microducks, 10-inch biped robots by Hugging Face that run on open source software. Huang also stepped outside to address the press gathered at the venue about secure technology deployment. “Containment and monitoring are the fundamental pillars of AI,” he said. Later that evening, Huang met with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace to discuss NVIDIA’s contribution to France’s thriving AI ecosystem through investments spanning startups, AI-native companies and computing infrastructure. They also spoke about the importance of open source for France and Europe, AI safety and NVIDIA’s recent launch of its Open Agent Safety Platform. NVIDIA Brings Build-a-Claw to the Heart of Paris On the afternoon before NVIDIA's France Ecosystem Reception, hundreds of developers gathered at Pavillon Vendôme to build physical AI — and get a surprise visit from NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Pavillon Vendôme sits just off Place Vendôme in the 1st arrondissement — one of the most storied addresses in Paris. On Tuesday afternoon, it was full of claws. NVIDIA’s Build-a-Claw came to France with developers from the nation’s startup community and big companies alike packing into the pavilion. The excited crowd was lined up around the block to try their hands (and brains) at building AI-powered robotic claw machines using open models and NVIDIA’s platform. NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang dropped in on the robotic fun chatting with the crowds inside and outside, and showing off NVIDIA DGX Spark and RTX Spark AI computing powerhouse machines. “The world’s first computers that unite all the software the world has ever created,” Huang said. Huang then raffled off one of each of the machines, signing the DGX Spark and handing out an autographed “IOU” for the wildly popular RTX machine, since it’s sold out at the moment. The crowd of developers did not miss a beat, claws were waiting, and went back to building. The Paris Build-a-Claw was NVIDIA's second event of the day, after a morning Build-a-Claw in Barcelona drew another big crowd at the Palacio de Pedralbes. He next headed to the nearby Salle des Tirages for an evening ecosystem reception with France's AI leaders. A single day, and already there is a sense of the huge excitement and ambition across the tech ecosystem in both countries. More news, and more countries to come. At GTC Berlin’s First Stop, Barcelona’s Builders Put Physical AI to Work Before NVIDIA's keynote in Berlin, the road to GTC began in Barcelona — with a royal palace, hundreds of developers and a very particular kind of robot. The Palacio de Pedralbes sits at the edge of Barcelona on land that once belonged to the Spanish royal family. On Tuesday morning, it belonged to builders.
