events.title: From Earth to Orbit, France’s Ecosystem Delivers Agentic Computing at Scale With NVIDIA
events.summary: NVIDIA Announces New Investments in France’s Startups Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack. NVIDIA has been investing in France’s startup ecosystem, having previously invested in leading technology companies including Alice&Bob, Gradium and Scintil Photonics . Across all of Europe, NVIDIA has committed nearly $10 billion to the technology ecosystem. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Doctolib, Entalpic , Genesis AI and Pigment . These startups are innovating to solve challenges across healthcare, materials discovery, physical AI and business planning. Doctolib , a European healthcare technology company, builds agents that free up healthcare professionals to deliver better care, while providing patients with a digital health companion that improves access to care and supports more preventive, continuous medicine. Entalpic , a Paris-based startup, accelerates the engineering of advanced materials at the atomic scale, with particular expertise in surfaces and interfaces for semiconductor manufacturing and next-generation electronics. Genesis AI is a global robotics company developing general-purpose robots with frontier intelligence and capabilities through its foundation models, data collection systems, simulation infrastructure and robot hardware. Pigment , a Paris-based enterprise software company, builds a planning platform that helps businesses forecast performance, model scenarios and make decisions across finance, sales, workforce and operations. France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology. Bull is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2. Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by Loft Orbital and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks , a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space , the satellite is flying NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit. NVIDIA Nemotron open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data. LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement , making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations. In financial services, SBS is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA. Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries. Fondation Inria , with NVIDIA’s support, is launching a working group on open source advanced modeling and tool adoption, with findings to come in the spring of next year. Across retail, public services, telecommunications and science, the pattern is consistent: open models and NVIDIA infrastructure are driving results in France. L’Oréal is integrating NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflows so scientists can explore formulation possibilities in silico and better help guide laboratory research. Combining computational predictions with hands-on experimentation can make the discovery process up to 100x faster than traditional methods and maximize the potential of the group’s proprietary active ingredients. Mirakl has onboarded more than 70 million products with fine-tuned and open models running on NVIDIA GPUs and inference software, cutting seller catalog onboarding to under two hours. Photoroom and Vestiaire Collective a re demonstrating the measurable business impact of advanced visual modeling on marketplace performance. Omi helps brands bring accurate products into AI-generated marketing visuals at scale, combining its approved 3D digital twins with open models optimized on NVIDIA for 4x faster inference. In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila built a digital-twin agent — powered by NVIDIA Cosmos open world models, Nemotron and Omniverse libraries — managing nearly 5,800 kilometers of roads and buildings, cutting total operating costs by 10% and targeting 30% as deployment progresses. Port Sud de France runs goods processing and port security on ThinkDeep’s DeepBrain platform powered by Nemotron and Cosmos. Enchanted Tools, a robotics company headquartered in Paris, is deploying social robots to support patients in healthcare settings including pediatric cancer care. In telecom, Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, powered by NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure, to offer all of its employees the ability to build their own agents, securely and in a controlled environment In quantum, Alice & Bob has integrated the NVIDIA NVQLink platform for its superconducting cat qubits, showing how GPUs can make quantum error correction more efficient, including for faster qubit modalities. Quandela has also been using NVQLink to build an integration between a DGX Spark system and its photonic qubits — advancing QPU-GPU supercomputing and exploring hybrid quantum-classical applications. events.title: NutryFarm shareholders demand CEO’s immediate suspension, CFO to take over in interim
events.summary: The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended on the SGX since April 11, 2022. On Oct 9, shareholders holding at least 10% of paid-up capital asked to remove Niu from the board and all group roles, and to consider Charlie In as CEO. NutryFarm is reviewing the allegations and seeking legal advice. The row comes as the company stays suspended from trading, despite leaving judicial management in February. SINGAPORE – Shareholders seeking to oust NutryFarm International chief executive Niu Liming have stepped up their demands, calling for his immediate suspension and the appointment of the company’s chief financial officer as interim CEO. The former durian distributor said in an Oct 12 stock exchange filing that it had received an urgent demand notice from shareholders identifying themselves as acting on behalf of the group seeking a special general meeting. Their demands included suspending Niu as CEO and executive director, and appointing the current CFO to temporarily lead the company. NutryFarm’s notice did not name the CFO, but filings on the exchange show that Derek Ong Chee Beng, 60, was appointed group financial controller on June 8. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the notice and seeking legal advice. It also did not detail the grounds for suspension or announce any management changes. The Oct 12 demand follows several letters concerning Niu’s position at the firm and his right to vote on behalf of a major shareholder. On Oct 9, shareholders identifying themselves as holding at least 10% of NutryFarm’s paid-up capital requested a special general meeting to remove Niu from the board as well as his appointments across the group. They also sought to elect shareholder Charlie In as a director, and asked the board to consider appointing In as CEO. In another Oct 9 letter, the shareholders demanded Niu’s immediate removal from executive positions and his recusal from board discussions and voting on the matter. Niu Liming’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the allegations, which its announcement did not detail. The company subsequently received an objection to Niu’s proxy voting rights granted by shareholder Jia Lijie, including any conflict of interest arising from the arrangement, on Oct 11. Under a share pledge arrangement, Niu has a deemed interest in NutryFarm through Jia’s 21.7 million shares and another 13.3 million belonging to Cheng Meng, according to the company’s 2024 annual report. Including his own 360,000 shares, his direct and deemed interest in the company is 25.72%. Niu also has an ownership interest in Corpbond IV, the creditor that applied to place NutryFarm under judicial management in June 2022 . He became executive director and CEO in December that year. The High Court discharged NutryFarm from judicial management on Feb 2, but its shares have remained suspended since April 11, 2022 .

The exchanges are soliciting public comment on revisions to the rules and punishments until Monday. The announcements came just days after the China Securities Regulatory Commission convened a meeting with market participants, signalling possible stabilisation measures if stocks fell further. Top policymakers have placed great emphasis on financial stability this year, as the capital markets are a critical part of Beijing’s tech self-reliance drive, given their ability to generate funding for home-grown companies.

events.title: ACCC takes egg 'cartel' to court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACCC takes civil action against egg companies for alleged cartel behaviour Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Sunny Queen is alleged to have breached competition laws. ( Facebook: Sunny Queen Farms ) The ACCC has launched legal action against 12 egg producers and suppliers, alleging they coordinated on production and supply decisions. The consumer watchdog alleges "widespread anti-competitive conduct" has affected egg supply in Australia since at least 2020. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen, Australia's largest egg supplier, has denied all allegations. Australia's competition regulator has launched legal action against some of the country's biggest egg producers, alleging "cartel conduct" and other anti-competitive behaviour. Sunny Queen, the largest egg supplier in Australia, and 11 other producers and suppliers are alleged to have breached competition laws by coordinating on the production and supply of eggs since 2020. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today, alleging the companies had coordinated on a range of decisions. The ACCC alleges that since at least October 2020, the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on a range of business decisions, including buying a property in Queensland to stop a rival supplier acquiring it. The legal filing comes more than a year since the ACCC launched court action against several large vegetable producers, alleging they formed a price-fixing cartel in supplying supermarket Aldi. The ACCC alleges the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on decisions about production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply in a way that likely "substantially reduced competition for many years". ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said eggs were an important household staple, and the alleged behaviour could result in less competitive prices for consumers. "When you have good functioning competition then you have more choice, you also have price competition, so lower prices," she told Victorian Country Hour. "Our concern is that when parties are not competing and they start working together … consumers can ultimately miss out. Gina Cass-Gottlieb says the ACCC is concerned consumers could miss out on lower prices. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) Sunny Queen is Australia's largest wholesale egg supplier, holding about one-third of the market for supply of eggs to retailers such as Woolworths, Coles, Metcash, Aldi and Costco. The company has warehouse and distribution facilities in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia. The proceedings involve allegations against entities including Sunny Queen, Doug Hall Poultry Pty Ltd, Alpair Pty Ltd trading as McLean Farms, Ellerslie Free Range Farms Pty Ltd and Kinross Farm Pty Ltd along with seven other companies. The ACCC alleges Sunny Queen, Hall and McLean Farms's coordination extended to purchasing a property in Pittsworth, Queensland, to prevent rival egg suppliers acquiring it. "We also allege this had the effect of substantially lessening competition," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. The competition regulator also alleged Sunny Queen restricted how many eggs its rival Kinross could sell to customers, and prevented Kinross from selling its eggs to Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, Metcash or Costco. A spokesperson for Sunny Queen denied all allegations. "Sunny Queen has cooperated fully with the ACCC throughout the course of its investigation," the spokesperson said. The company said the allegations related to the terms of its agreements with its shareholders and main egg suppliers in Queensland and Victoria. It said it would remain "business as usual" while the matter was before the courts. Doug Hall Poultry, McLean Farms, Kinross Farm, Yallamundi Farms and Ellerslie have been contacted for comment. Sunny Queen is one of 12 egg producers named in the Federal Court matter. ( Supplied ) It is the first case the ACCC has brought involving concerted practice allegations since the prohibition was introduced in 2017. A concerted practice involves cooperation between businesses that goes beyond them acting independently in response to market conditions. "It can involve competitors coordinating their behaviour in ways that harm competition, even if there's no formal agreement," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said. "It can involve communication between competitors, as we allege here, a regular exchange of information … in ways that reduce independent decision-making.

events.title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits Silvana Tenreyro, IMF chief economist The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. Gulf outlook The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Arab world's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. Conflict and AI boom lift inflation The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) The Basel Committee has published assessment reports on the implementation of its leverage ratio framework (LEV) in Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Australia, Japan, Korea and Switzerland are assessed as compliant; Canada and the United Kingdom are assessed as largely compliant. This publication concludes the first round of multi-jurisdictional assessments of the leverage ratio. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published assessment reports on Australia, Canada, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and the United Kingdom’s implementation of the Committee’s leverage ratio framework (LEV). Australia, Japan, Korea and Switzerland were assessed as compliant with the Committee’s global standards, the highest overall grade. Canada and the United Kingdom were assessed as largely compliant, which is one notch below the highest overall grade. These assessments form part of the Committee’s Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP), which evaluates the consistency and completeness of Basel standards’ implementation across member jurisdictions. With the publication of these reports, the Committee has concluded the first round of multi-jurisdictional assessments of the leverage ratio. In line with its work programme, the Committee initiated in H1 2026 jurisdictional assessments of the Basel III revisions to risk-weighted assets and continues to assess the implementation of the leverage ratio.

events.title: Scoop: Top Trump operative enlisted to rescue Kansas senator's campaign
events.summary: A top Trump political operative has been tapped to help boost Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall 's campaign in the weeks before the Nov. 3 election , the latest sign of how Republicans are scrambling to defend the red-state seat. Why it matters: The hiring of veteran strategist Chris Grant reflects the GOP's growing anxiety over Kansas' Senate race . Marshall is running neck and neck with Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state President Trump won by 16 points in 2024. Republicans fear losing Kansas could be a domino in costing them their Senate majority . Driving the news: GOP operatives have become increasingly frustrated with Marshall's reelection campaign, which they believe hasn't been aggressive enough at a time when soaring fuel prices have particularly hurt farmers in Kansas and elsewhere in the Midwest. Grant, who helped lead the main pro-Trump super PAC in 2024 and has remained involved in Trump's political operation, will be a senior adviser to Marshall and help guide strategy in the final three weeks. Grant also worked on Marshall's 2020 Senate campaign. What they're saying: "Chris is an absolute pro who has been a longtime friend to Team Marshall. Having him help land the plane these last three weeks is a no brainer," Brent Robertson, Marshall's chief of staff, told Axios. Zoom in: Two GOP outside groups — the Senate Leadership Fund and Club for Growth — are pouring millions into the Kansas race. SLF, the principal super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, is spending $14 million in Kansas after shifting resources from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has a significant polling lead over former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley. Trump said in a social media post Monday that he would campaign for Marshall "very soon." A Democrat-aligned super PAC has announced plans to spend $5 million to help Hamilton. Between the lines: Marshall has faced damaging headlines recently, including a New York Times r eport that his medical practice sued more than 700 former patients over unpaid medical bills, and that 81 were later arrested for missing court appearances. The other side: Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, has won endorsements from two former Republican governors in Kansas, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.

events.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
events.summary: The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?

events.title: What we know about Lady Violet Bridgerton ahead of Netflix spin-off
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Netflix has announced a Bridgerton spin-off focusing on Lady Violet. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) This article contains spoilers from seasons one to four of Bridgerton. In previous seasons of the Netflix and Shondaland series Bridgerton, Lady Violet has expressed a great affection for her late husband Viscount Edmund Bridgerton. She experienced intense heartbreak and sorrow when he died. Now, fans of the television show will get to see their love story. In the same way Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story delved into the early life of Queen Charlotte, a yet untitled series will chronicle the early life of a young Lady Violet. It promises to tell the story of Violet's romance with Edmund (Rupert Evans). There have been two actors so far who have taken on the role of Lady Violet. Ruth Gemmell plays her in the main series and appeared in the Queen Charlotte spin-off, in which Connie Jenkins-Greig played a younger version in flashbacks as a then Violet Ledger. Lady Violet is depicted in Bridgerton as a kind, warm and wise matriarch with the interests of her family at heart. As we gear up for the spin-off, here's a trip down memory lane exploring some of what we already know about Lady Violet and her relationship with Lord Bridgerton. Violet Bridgerton (née Ledger) holds the title the Dowager Viscountess Bridgerton. Lady Violet is the family's matriarch and has eight children. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) A Dowager Viscountess is the widowed wife of a viscount who retains her aristocratic rank after her husband's death. Violet was pregnant with Lord Bridgerton's eighth child Hyacinth when he died from anaphylaxis. He'd suffered a severe allergic reaction after being stung by a bee. He was in his late 30s at the time. He'd been out hunting with eldest son Anthony and was picking hyacinths for his wife when it happened. In a conversation with Anthony in season two, episode eight of Bridgerton, titled The Viscount Who Loved Me, Violet tells her son she would go through the pain of losing her husband again because the beauty of love overpowers the risk of grief. "Losing Edmund was the most difficult time of my life," Violet said. "And the pain that I felt … beyond description. "But there is one thing that has given me at least some modicum of solace. "It's knowing that I would still choose the life I led with him, each and every time. "And I would undoubtedly feel the same pain I felt all over again if I had to because real, true love is worth it no matter what." Lady Violet is close friends with Lady Danbury (right). ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) Violet is keen to see each of her eight children marry, but she wants them, too, to experience true love, rather than marry for the sake of it. While no marriage is perfect, the union between Violet and Edmund is so idealised that each of her children aspire to live a similar fairytale. In season one, episode eight called After the Rain, Violet points out to her daughter Daphne that marriage is hard, and the reason why hers worked was because they chose to love each other through each obstacle. "It is a rarity, I have come to realise," Violet said. "That is not to say it was without its trials. "Your father and I faced many difficulties, indeed, but we overcame them. "We made a decision early on to do so. "We chose to love each other every single day. "It is a choice, dearest, one that is never too late to make." Lady Violet remains devoted to her late husband throughout the first few seasons of the television series. Lady Violet develops feelings for Lord Marcus Anderson, but not enough to marry him. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) That is, until Lord Marcus Anderson (Daniel Francis) catches her eye. He is Lady Agatha Danbury's (Adjoa Andoh) younger brother, and they meet in season three of Bridgerton. In season four, they kick it up a notch into a steamy, passionate, but secret dalliance. Finally, Violet is exploring her own desires after mostly focusing her efforts on matchmaking her children. Lord Marcus wants to marry her, but the "not yet" response to his offer of engagement turns into a "not ever" in his eyes. With Queen Charlotte being as juicy as it was stunningly heartbreaking, this author cannot wait for the Lady Violet spin-off, dearest gentle reader. The spin-off will be written by showrunners and executive producers Shonda Rhimes and Nicholas Nardini. Bridgerton is based on the popular historical romance novels written by Julia Quinn. The TV show debuted on Netflix in 2020 and captivated global audiences. Season five is currently in production.

events.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
events.summary: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government. Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect. Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition". In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil Published 10 September Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick says heating his home now feels more like an investment than a regular household bill Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil Published 10 September Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick says heating his home now feels more like an investment than a regular household bill Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". events.title: New report shows US chip industry's reliance on China
events.summary: More than 5% of equipment and materials supplied to US chipmakers originate in China, which also possesses some 90% of the rare earths required to manufacture semiconductors, a new report showed. The figures highlight the structural reliance of US tech on China, and the difficulties of erecting a materials and software firewall against Beijing. “We’re so deeply intertwined,” Brookings’ AI specialist Kyle Chan told The Washington Post: “ There’s a lot of actual dependency .” Beyond materials, the US tech startup ecosystem also relies on cheaper, open-source Chinese AI, so much that when the Trump administration considered banning it, nearly 300 US firms spoke out — marking “the moment open intelligence itself becomes a geopolitical dependency,” an analyst wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Feds search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration probe
events.summary: Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state. It's also an unusual move against a candidate less than a month before an election , something the Justice Department has typically avoided . The latest: President Trump said authorities are looking at Omar "very carefully" when asked whether he knew about the search of her home in advance. "I've always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said . "I think she's a terrible person. She comes from a country that is a non-country." What they're saying: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar said in a Monday afternoon post to X. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement. A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. DHS referred Axios to the DOJ. The other side: Omar's office blasted the search. "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar spokesperson Jacklyn Rogers said in a statement. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong." House Democratic leaders separately issued a joint statement calling the search "deeply disturbing" and part of a "rogue abuse of power" by the administration. Zoom out: Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details. Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee. Between the lines: Trump has for years demanded that Omar leave the country or be deported , citing, among other things, unsubstantiated claims that she married her brother to help him circumvent immigration laws. Omar has dismissed the claims about the marriage in question as "baseless rumors." Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks. Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to " fight back " against the state's Somali population. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from President Trump, as well as statements from Omar, her House office and House Democratic leaders, and with more context. Andrew Solender and Torey Van Oot contributed reporting.

events.title: Uber struggles to solve Broome's late-night transport issues
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late-night transport issues remain in Broome despite arrival of Uber Travellers say they opt for e-scooters after failing to book an Uber. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Residents and tourists in Broome have long raised concerns about the lack of transport options late at night. The arrival of Uber was touted as a potential solution, but those in Broome say they have struggled to book a ride through the app. Police say the issues people have getting a ride home are no excuse for drink driving. Global rideshare giant Uber has struggled to fill the void of late-night transport in Western Australia's far north. Like many remote locations across Australia, transport options in Broome, 2,000km north of Perth, are progressively limited as the evening wears on. Buses cease at 7pm during the peak tourist season, and many taxi operators stop their service from a similar time. While some drivers continue throughout the night, residents say they face long wait times with expensive fares. Limited taxis operate during the night in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) Uber was touted as a potential solution during its July launch, but those in town said the app has had little impact. Jenny Antonipillai recently travelled to Broome from Perth, and attempted to find a ride home from the pub. "We tried to get a taxi or an Uber, but there's not much available out here. It's very hard," she said. "We went on the Beam [e-scooter] and my boyfriend fell, so not a good idea." Jenny Antonipillai says she was not able to order an Uber home from the pub, despite the app launching in Broome two months ago. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Travellers Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon said they had also had no luck with Uber and opted for e-scooters to get around. "There was nothing available at all in the area," Mr Clancy said. "We got taxis quite easily earlier in the day, but later at night it's a bit more trouble." Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon opted for the e-scooters to get around in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Resident Lili Walker said she was used to long waits and expensive fares costing up to $60 for a 10-minute ride. The state government increased the flexibility of taxi authorisation in 2020, resulting in a number of drivers offering a private service throughout the evening. But their contacts are not always readily available. Matty Arai says many people struggle to organise a taxi through automated answering services. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Pub security guard Matty Arai said it was common to see patrons huddled out the front looking for a way home after close. "There are a couple of good guys around town that will be out all the time, but then trying to pick them up is also hard," he said. Partygoers said expensive fares, long wait times and limited options created a dangerous incentive for drink driving. Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe says educating the community on safe e-scooter use is a priority. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) But Kimberley District traffic Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe said inconvenience did not justify breaking the law. "I understand there are difficulties … transport, distance, everything else like that, but it's not acceptable," he said. Sergeant Di Giuseppe said police had been working to educate community members they were subject to the same road rules on an e-scooter as they were driving a vehicle. Broome and Karratha were the first off the rank for Uber's regional WA expansion in July. Broome Private Taxis owner Paul Rewell said he was not surprised the rideshare service has reportedly struggled to take-off. "If people like our group are struggling to find drivers, Uber won't be any different," he said. Paul Rewell says he is not surprised the app has struggled to attract drivers. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Mr Rewell has been operating taxis in the town for the past six years, and said his business had trialled working throughout the evening. Repeated incidents of vandalism during the night led to the decision to close after 6 or 7pm. He said he welcomed Uber's arrival should they have enough drivers. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said she recognised the challenges of catching taxi services at night in remote towns. She said the government was committed to "providing accessible and affordable" public transport for regional communities, pointing to an expansion of Broome's bus timetable put in place for this year's tourist season. events.title: Phillip Island business operators prepare for MotoGP's final lap
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Phillip Island has relied on the MotoGP to bring in tourists and revenue. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP race at the end of October before the race moves to Adelaide in 2027. The GP and World Superbikes inject about $80 million into the island's economy each year. Businesses, councillors and the island's tourism board are calling for government support. Every October, Phillip Island emerges from a sleepy winter season and roars to life with the sound of motorcycles travelling in convoy to the MotoGP. The weekend of racing turbocharges the island's summer tourism season, culminating in the World Superbikes event in February. But Cowes and the broader island community are preparing to host their final MotoGP later this month at the picturesque cliff-side track, before the race moves to its new home in Adelaide from 2027. The loss has hit businesses and residents hard, with many reeling emotionally and financially. During the 1990s, Bass Coast Shire Council Mayor Brett Tessari worked at a caravan park on the island. "The vibe of the motorbikes coming in and the people, it was awesome," he said. Brett Tessari says the region's tourism future will need to rely on new ideas. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "I remember being stuck on the [Phillip Island] bridge, trying to get over back to Wonthaggi and people were starting up barbecues and cooking sausages on the side of the road because we were at a standstill," Cr Tessari said. "Things like that are just etched in your memory. "To be the mayor, unfortunately, at the last one, it's pretty surreal and quite sad." For the past decade, Samantha Hampstead has run a tattoo business in Cowes with her husband Jason. They are both members of the social motorcycle club Trust No One, and are key organisers of the annual community motorcycle convoy that heralds the start of the motoring weekend. "We do it because of the love of the ride," she said. "It's a full-blown rush when you have all these riders together. "You look in the mirror and you can see this full parade of bikes behind you and it just goes on forever." Samantha Hampstead organises a community motorcycle run in Cowes. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Ms Hampstead said for many business operators the weekend was their busiest time of the year. "It's part of the island," she said. San Remo Fisherman's Co-Op chief executive Wolfgang Platzer said the GP brought thousands of visitors to the island who may not otherwise have visited the region. Wolfgang Platzer says the community needs develop fresh ideas to attract tourists. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There would be a large portion of people that come here for the GP and see that the island and the area is very beautiful and then might think about, oh, we'll come back because we liked it and it was so beautiful," he said. Phillip Island is the state's most tourism-reliant region. According to Destination Phillip Island (DPI), more than $80 million in annual economic activity is linked to the World Superbikes and the MotoGP. The accommodation sector is the island's largest employer, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, accounting for almost 4 per cent of jobs. Cafes and restaurants are the third-largest employer. San Remo is the gateway to Phillip Island. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) DPI chief executive Kim Storey said while the event's loss had accelerated the need to broaden the island's outlook beyond motoring events, the role the track had played could not be understated. Economic uncertainty, a lack of infrastructure such as a car ferry and the potential toll of the H5N1 virus on the island's wildlife were all cited by DPI as upcoming barriers to success. "The MotoGP has provided that platform of security and the resource for businesses," Ms Storey said. DPI and Bass Coast Shire Council have called for government funding to help develop new events, such as The Hills are Alive music festival, the Island Whale Festival, the island hot springs, and a new festival of motorsports to capitalise on the island's motoring history. One Nation candidate for Bass Nikole Schellekens, Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead and Labor candidate Chris Buckingham were asked what commitments they would make to the island's economy if elected at the November state election. All three candidates stressed the importance of tourism for Phillip Island and support for ongoing development of the island's resources.

events.title: Oil company wins tenders in Channel Country with supply to stay in Australia
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bridgeport Energy already has oil wells in the Cooper-Eromanga basin. ( Supplied: Bridgeport Energy ) An Australian oil company has won tenders to explore for more oil and gas in the Channel Country. Bridgeport Energy has been allocated 270,000 hectares of land with new supply to stay within the domestic market. Traditional owners and graziers want assurances that "significant" flood plains will not be damaged. The head of an Australian oil company says any fossil fuels taken from new land in Queensland's Channel Country will stay in Australia, but it could take years before oil or gas flows. Bridgeport Energy has been declared the preferred tenderer across an extra 270,000 hectares of land between Innamincka and Thargomindah along the South Australian-Queensland border. Bridgeport already has about 90,000 hectares of "oil-producing acreage" in the Cooper-Eromanga basin and processes oil at Queensland's only inland oil refinery in Eromanga. The land allocated for exploration is on the Queensland-South Australia border. ( Supplied: Google Maps ) The state government has been ramping up land allocations to mining companies since 2025. Bridgeport Energy chief executive Christian Lange said he wanted to work "very, very closely" with landholders including graziers and traditional owners before any exploration began. "We need to be cognisant that our disturbance on that land is zero effectively by the time we pack up and leave," he said. Agriculture-conservation alliance wants assurances Western Rivers Alliance is a cooperative between graziers, traditional owners and conservationists advocating to stop new oil and gas activities on Channel Country flood plains. The latest sites are not within the protected Channel Country flood plains where fracking was banned two years ago , but parts are within 5 to 10 kilometres of the boundary. Coordinator Riley Rocco said the alliance was "neutral" on mining outside the flood plains. "But the activity could come quite close to the flood plain and obviously we are keen to make sure that any oil and gas or any industrial activity stays managed well outside of the flood plain in order to not have an adverse impact on those significant river and flood plain areas." In May 2013, a major oil spill in the Channel Country at a Santos-owned well involved the loss of 250,000 litres of crude oil, which flowed for 2 kilometres before the leak was stopped. The Queensland Department of Environment did not prosecute Santos at the time but admitted damage could have been severe if the leak had occurred during floodtime. Mr Lange said impacts on groundwater, fauna, flora, roads and other "land disturbances" would be considered before new exploration begins. He said the small-scale company would use seismic waves to determine whether there were enough "commercial flows" of oil or gas underground. "I would anticipate that it's probably the best part of two years to obtain your authority to prospect, and then preparing to do seismic surveys, whether it's 2D, 3D or a combination of all those things," he said. Gas exploration was banned in some parts of the Channel Country in 2024. ( Supplied: Pew Charitable Trusts ) The latest round of tenders also included 62,500 hectares for the ASX-listed Vintage Energy in the Channel Country, while a four-business consortium won 30,600 hectares of land in the Taroom Trough. In a statement, Queensland Resources Minister Dale Last said increasing the supply of fuels was the "only solution to bring down the cost of energy". The state government has awarded 12 sites for oil or gas exploration since 2025.

events.title: Renewed mineral sands mine bid 'a turd in glitter', resident says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian government 'manipulating' planning laws to win critical minerals race, expert says Kane Busch and his family have been farming vegetables in the Lindenow Valley for 100 years. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) The Victorian government is assessing a mineral sands mine project it has already rejected. The global critical minerals race is behind the renewed attempt to green light the project, experts argue. The company behind the proposal says claims the project has not been altered since its previous rejection are "misleading and false". The Victorian government is "manipulating" its own planning system to fast track approval for a mining project it already rejected, a leading planning expert claims. The Fingerboards Mineral Sands Project proposed for eastern Victoria was knocked back by the government in 2021, because it would "pose a significant risk to the environment and valuable horticulture industry". But the government is now considering what it calls a "new and modified" bid to get the project off the ground, a description that RMIT emeritus professor of planning and environment Michael Buxton said was a "blatant deception". "The project is not a different project and it's not substantially altered," he said. Michael Buxton worked at the Victorian planning department for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Sean Warren ) Nearby residents who have spent years fighting the mine have a different description of the latest proposal. The company behind the project, Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM), rejected these claims and said its new bid for approval included significant changes. GCM said the site was a rich source of a range of minerals, which had been deemed critical by the Australian government. Miners have been exploring the Lindenow Valley, 270 kilometres east of Melbourne, for mineral sands since the 1970s. Irrigated areas of the Lindenow flats. ( ABC Rural: Emma Field ) Between 2015 and 2023, global demand doubled for mineral sands, which contain concentrated amounts of heavy minerals such as rare-earth elements. Organisations from mining giants such as Rio Tinto to junior mining companies have had a stake in the region, but no project has ever been considered commercially or environmentally viable. After almost a decade of review, in November 2021 the Victorian government rejected a mining project proposed by Kalbar Resources, later Kalbar Operations. In 2023, Kalbar was renamed to Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM) and submitted a "rescoped" proposal. Gippsland Critical Minerals has dug a test pit on its Fingerboards mineral sands site. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) Dr Buxton, who has been involved in planning for 50 years, including at the Environment Protection Authority and state planning department, said the government failed to follow proper process by accepting the Fingerboards project for a second review. "The minister could have just refused to consider this application — and in my view, should have," he said. Australia's strategic focus on critical minerals for economic and national security reasons was behind the renewed push for the East Gippsland mineral sands mine, he said. "This has provided companies with the opportunity to argue that it's a critical resource." Under the state government's critical minerals road map launched in December 2024, which outlines efforts to build a globally competitive critical minerals sector, eight mines are at various stages of approval. University of Sydney professor of global governance Susan Park said she was "not surprised at all" that rejected minerals projects were getting a second look. Dr Park said trade and security agreements between Australia and allies such as the United States were driving state and federal support for mining projects. The proposed Fingerboards mine site, 25 kilometres west of Bairnsdale. ( Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals ) In February, the Australian government gave the Fingerboards proposal Major Project Status, which gives "strategically significant projects" extra support to navigate regulatory approvals. GCM bills the project as a major source of "ex-China production" of the rare-earth oxides dysprosium and terbium, elements on Australia's critical minerals list. China controls almost all of the world's production and rare-earth refining. Terbium and dysprosium oxides, used in renewable energy and military technologies, are almost completely supplied by China. The Lindenow Valley is a highly fertile region known for its leafy salad vegetables, brassicas and sweet corn. Up to 2,000 workers harvest about 200,000 tonnes of food every year.

( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Australia wastes about 7.6 million tonnes of food each year, costing the economy more than $36 billion. Less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspect their food waste, and operational methods mean it can go unnoticed. The federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030, but some experts are concerned about progress. When Karl Riseborough realised how much food went to waste each week at his Sydney pub and brewery, he was shocked. Grain left over from the beer-making process was thrown out, as well as food waste from the kitchen. What surprised him most was the volume of waste on top of the spent grain. "The food scraps coming back, the plate waste, the kitchen prep waste … you don't really notice when it was all going straight into the bin," Mr Riseborough said. Food waste expert Belinda Chellingworth said many traders had no idea how much waste they were generating, or how much it was affecting their bottom line. The capacity of landfill is reaching a critical level in some areas. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale/File photo ) Every year about 7.6 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia at a cost of more than $36 billion to the economy . Of that wasted food, 70 per cent is edible and there are critical knock-on effects for landfill management, food security and the climate. With the support of Ms Chellingworth, who happily calls herself a "garbologist", Mr Riseborough has stopped throwing away 50 kilograms of spent grain from each batch of beer he brews. Karl Riseborough is saving thousands a year after some simple changes. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "Now I have regular users who come and collect it once I've brewed and use it for the benefit of their gardens or their animals," Mr Riseborough said. "We had two 240-litre bins that were getting collected each week. We're now down to one bin collected each fortnight." He said that saved him about $5,000 a year. Australia's hospitality sector wastes 1.2 million tonnes of food each year, according to the Sustainable Restaurant Association. The economic impact of food waste in the food service sector is about $6.4 billion , averaging about $66,000 annually per business. Belinda Chellingworth says many businesses do not realise how much food they waste. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Ms Chellingworth said less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspected their food waste. "Typically, many businesses, if they've got food left over at the end of their operations or the end of the day, then it will be landfilled," she said. "For many businesses, and particularly large businesses, the cost of food waste across their operations isn't fully realised because they incur it multiple times, but it's not obvious." Food waste will be a point of discussion at the COP31 conference. ( ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch ) For example, over-ordering food is a cost to the kitchen. If it is not sold, that is a revenue cost, and then whatever goes into the bin also involves a cost for collection. "So they're paying for it multiple times, but they're different departments, different cost centres, and it's often not added together, so they don't understand the full cost across the whole business," Ms Chellingworth said. To combat the economic and environmental impacts of food waste, the federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030 . But UNSW food and health professor Johannes le Coutre does not believe the plan is on track. Johannes le Coutre says tackling food waste will help to ease food insecurity. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "I'm not sure if that's attainable or achievable with the current landscape," he said. events.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
events.summary: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected. The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack. More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them. Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. The firm added in a statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date. "Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to." The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France. Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed. In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon. The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible". Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported. As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires. French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C. Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions. French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality." In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible". He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable". Have you been affected by this cyber attack? Share your experience .
